We had the opportunity to try practice questions before the interview began. Once ready, HireVue will then ask questions, which we’ll record our responses to via video. We were asked two questions. The questions were typically what you would expect during an HR interview round. I don’t have a very clear recollection of the questions. But I guess the first question was along the lines “mention a time in your life when you made a mistake at work or school\" and the second was “describe a time in your life when you did something overwhelming or overambitious”. The answer to each question was not supposed to exceed two minutes. We had one opportunity to re-record each response if desired. If we chose to re-record a response, the updated response would automatically be submitted as final. The deadline for completing the video interview was 14th March 2021. Tips for the video interview? 1. Prepare! You have Tips for Success and resources to guide you. 2. Find a time and place which ensures a quiet, distraction-free environment with good lighting. 3. Dress professionally and make sure the camera and sound on your computer or mobile device are working. 4. Make sure to try the practice questions before your interview begins. Based on the performance in the coding test and the video interview, 18 students were shortlisted for the final Code For Good event. CFG Bootcamp Ahead of the 2021 Code for Good Hackathon, a series of optional workshops and Q&A sessions were conducted to help us settle into a collaborative virtual environment and prepare for the big event. The CFG Bootcamp was designed to introduce us to key tools and platforms that would assist us in having a successful hack over the event weekend, especially for someone new to the hackathon space. Line-up of sessions: ● Introduction to Git (29th June 2021, 5 pm) A walkthrough of the fundamental concepts and commands in Git to help prep for a collaborative coding environment. ● The Art of Powerful Questions (1st July 2021, 5:30 pm) To learn all about how Powerful Questions helps to build better relationships with clients and create more inclusive designs by encouraging a mode of inquiry, varied perspectives, and co-creating solutions. ● Git Q&A ( 2nd July 2021, 5:00 pm) Now that we had learned the 101s of Git and had the chance to try it out, we had a session lined up where we could engage with JPMC’s subject matter experts on Git to clear any doubts/questions that we had. ● Code for Good Event Q&A (6th July 2021, 5:00 pm) A 1.5-hour session focused on reviewing the hackathon event structure and the Code for Good virtual platform set-up. We could seek any clarifications we needed regarding the hackathon format. Code for Good ( 8th - 11th July 2021 ) JP Morgan’s annual coding challenge – “Code For Good” - is dedicated towards solving real-world problems for nonprofits. The Code For Good is also a hiring event and the only means by which we could apply for Internship opportunities under the “Software Engineer Program (SEP) 2022” at JP Morgan. The Code for Good challenge gives you the chance to put your coding skills to work helping nonprofits. It’s also a great opportunity to see whether a career in financial services technology is for you. Over the course of a weekend, you’ll work with a team to develop a technology solution for a leading nonprofit. You’ll work alongside JPMorgan Chase technologists, learning from their experience as you creatively solve real-world problems faced by social organizations. This is a great way to put your creative ideas into practice to help those who need them most. About the event: Teams of five to seven (5-7) students will compete against each other on behalf of a charity assigned to them in order to provide a technological solution to a problem that the charity faces. The team or teams which, in the opinion of J.P. Morgan Services India Private Limited (“JPMC”), make the best attempt at developing such a solution will receive a prize for themselves. Based on their performance during the Code For Good, students that truly stand out as exceptional will get an offer to join the Firm for the Software Engineering Program Internship. There were a total of 95 teams this year. Platforms Used: The organizers had provided every team with a private GitHub repository. A Code For Good slack workspace was also created for announcements and activities that were to be conducted. The Hackathon was conducted on the BeMyApp platform. All teams were given unique Zoom links for discussions throughout the hackathon. Here is a detailed breakdown of the Hackathon: Student Networking (8th July 2021, 5:30 PM) Since the teams were formed by the CFG organizers, it was very likely to find team members from different Colleges and even different states within India. This necessitated the need for a student networking period wherein we could get to know each other better, understand the strengths and weaknesses of our team, discuss the tech stack everyone was familiar with and strategize for the hack. To help us bond better, each team was given a unique zoom link. There were several activities we were asked to do as a team. We had an Icebreaker round wherein we had to find out our common interests as a team, favorite meme/GIF, favorite framework to work with, the trickiest framework to work with, and so on. We also had many activities to do some of which included using a meme to best describe our team and post it on the #TeamMeme slack channel. The meme we chose to describe us was the “perfectly balanced” one. The reason for choosing this meme? Well, we had decided to make both a Web and Mobile Application. So we had three members who were familiar with React (who would make the Frontend for the Web App), two who were proficient with Nodejs and APIs, etc.(who would do the Backend), and two of us who would make the Mobile App in Flutter. Also, a few of us had worked previously with AI/ML. Hence we thought we were a perfect balance as we had a decent mix of tech stacks. Hackathon Survival Guide (8th July 2021, 6:30 PM) This was basically a speaker session wherein we were given a lot of advice and many tips and tricks to surviving the hack. While there were so many things to take away from this session, a few have been summarized here: ● Brainstorm ○ Think out of the box. ○ What unique touch are you going to provide? ○ Evaluate each idea. ○ Discuss, talk and set targets. ○ Be realistic. ● Organize your Team Decide high-level roles and responsibilities ○ Pick a leader - to speak on behalf of the team, settle disputes, remove roadblocks, and set directions. ○ Pick a timekeeper - that will keep you on task and schedule. ○ Regroup and do it often. Quick cycle time is an important advantage. ○ One person can serve in multiple roles. ○ You should change roles as needed. ● Use tools ○ These will save you time ○ Save time getting project structure and build files created. ○ Using tools like Spring Initializer and Create React App help set up projects and initial dependencies. ○ Most of these resources are CLI tools or web GUIs that create the project’s structure, define its required dependencies files(pom.xml, package.json, etc.), and set up a few simple run scripts. ● Scientific Method to the rescue! ○ Reach out to SME/ Team mentors, leverage the resources available to you. ○ Understand the situation ■ Got an error? What does it say? ○ Identify the root cause of the problem ■ Changed something recently? Revert!? ○ Develop an effective action plan ■ Got an idea? Decide how you are going to test it! ○ Execute and modify, until the problem is solved. ■ Run your test, evaluate the result, modify as needed, test again. Hackathon Tool Prep (8th July 2021, 7:45 PM) This was Another Speaker session by an Ex-CFG participant. This session was focused on how to improve productivity and how to use project management tools like Trello, Github Projects, etc. during the hackathon. Our team decided to go ahead with Trello. So we created a workspace in Trello. We created 3 boards one each for Web Frontend, Backend, and the Mobile App. We then made a list of things to be done and categorized them into three lists called On-Going, Completed, and Ambition(for extra things that we would do only after completing the bare requirements) for each board. After the events scheduled for the day were over, we decide to join our team zoom meet again and discuss and strategize a few more things. After which everyone went off to learn things from the resource pool that we had collected. 9th July 2021 There were a lot of events scheduled on this day, like the Opening Ceremony, FLARE Workshop, a session on Power of Empathy in Coding but we didn’t much attention to those sessions as we were engrossed in discussions for the Hack. We decided on going through problem statements of previous year's CFG and see how we as a team would come up with solutions for the same, what all features would we include, and were we able to think of something out of the box. Mentor - Team Huddle (9th July 2021, 7 PM) This was the most awaited of all the events. Do remember that the mentors play a very important role in you getting the internship at JPMC. The Mentor - Team Huddle was where the mentors would get the first impression of each one of us. At JPMC, there is no hierarchy and no one is considered superior or inferior to another. Hence we were expected to address everyone by their first name. It did feel very awkward at first to address our mentors by their first name rather than calling them Sir or Ma’am. But eventually, we got slightly accustomed to it. Just like we had an Icebreaker and Activities lined up for us during the Student Networking event, we had them for the Mentor - Team Huddle as well. The Mentors were very kind and supportive and there was a lot to learn from them and their experiences. It was a lot of fun carrying out these activities with our Mentors. We really needed that time off the pressure and stress of the Hackathon that was to start the next day. Challenges go Live! (10th July 2021, 7:00 AM) At 7:00 AM the Problem Statements were live on the CFG platform. There were around 11 Non-Profit Organizations each with a problem statement. Each Problem Statement consisted of a Mission, Context, Challenge, Additional Considerations, and Technology Baseline. We had one hour to read through the challenges and decide which one we wanted to go ahead with. Challenge Presentation(10th July 2021, 8:00 AM) Each Organization presented its problem statement and elaborated a little more on what type of a solution they were expecting from us. As the Organizations were presenting, we were simultaneously discussing our preferences. At 9:00 AM, the preferences form was rolled out, and we had to fill them ASAP as the Challenges would be allotted on a first-come-first-serve basis. Each Organization was allotted only to the first 5 teams that chose it as their first preference. Team Challenge Alignments (10th July 2021, 9:30 AM) The final allotments were out, unfortunately, we didn’t get our first preference but we were glad we at least got our second preference. Q&A with the Social Good Organization(10th July 2021, 10:15 AM) This was a Q&A session wherein we could clear our doubts regarding the problem statements with the Organization we had been allotted. This was our chance to get to know what exactly the Organization wanted us to come up with, as we found the problem statements pretty vague. The more questions we would ask the more details we would get, thereby giving us a clear idea of what we wanted to implement and what features would be crucial for the solution. However, we didn’t want to waste any time as the hackathon had started. So we decided to split up, two of us stayed back in the zoom meet to attend the Q&A and gather as much information as we could while the rest started coding the basic features of the App that we had discussed earlier. After the Q&A session, we joined the rest and explained all the requirements of the Organization that were expected to be in our solution. We then split up into breakout rooms. We had three breakout rooms one for the Web Frontend, one for the Backend, and one for the Mobile App. The mentors were also there in our team zoom meet. They were carefully listening to our conversations, giving us feedback and suggestions from time to time. We did have frequent group discussions to check on everyone's progress. We also occasionally moved between breakout rooms to help with errors, API failures, App crashes, etc. We also leveraged the help of SME’s whenever we were stuck. Everyone was so engrossed in coding that the Mentors literally had to tell us to take a break XD. Submission Requirements (10th July 2021, 9 PM) Just like the Q&A session, to save time only two of our team members joined the meet where they explained the submission requirements while the rest of us continued to code. We were supposed to submit our project on the BeMyApp platform. All instructions on how to submit the project were given during this session. The two team members noted down all the things that would be required for submission. Some of which included the GitHub repository link, screenshots of the App, project description which should include how our solution solves the challenge presented to us, drive link of the video demonstration, etc. The two of them joined us again after the session was over. And the coding continued. The Mentors were there in the meet for a significant amount of time. They kept motivating us. They also spoke to us on topics other than the hack like what our future plans were and the like. They also lightened the tense environment by occasionally cracking jokes and taking team pictures. The mentors wished us luck and left the zoom meet at around 12 AM. We continued coding even in the wee hours. Some of the team members decided to take a small break while the rest of us continued coding, knowing very clearly that we wouldn’t be able to rest for even a second until the App was complete. The CFG organizers had also arranged fun games and activities during the event and participants were encouraged to take part in them whenever they felt like taking a break. But no one from our group took part in any of them XD. Coding Cut-off (11th July 2021, 10 AM) We had to stop coding, and could not commit anything to our Github repository after this. The Mentors joined us again to see our completed project. We now had one hour to submit our solutions. We had the option to do a live demo or a pre-recorded video presentation for the technical judging round that was scheduled at 11:30 AM. We didn’t want to risk a live demo and hence we decided to go forward with the pre-recording option. It was at this moment that we realized that the Web App was suddenly not working :( We began to panic a little but the Mentors told us to record the Mobile App that was working and to focus on the pitch, as pitching the solution was very important. They told us that not all the people judging from the Non - profit Organizations have a technical background and hence pitching to them about how our solution solves their challenges was essential to ace the round. Since we were using Flutter, we decided to tell the judges that it can be used as a Web App as well as a Mobile App. We didn’t lose hope and began to record our presentation. Since we were short on time, we reckoned that if everyone spoke about a portion of the App, It would take a long time. So it was decided that I would do the presentation and speak about our solution approach, all the features of the App, and how it solves all the challenges presented in the problem statement. We did have many bloopers in the process while recording XD. We finished recording exactly 1 minute before the deadline. We immediately uploaded it to the drive, added the link to the BeMyApp platform, and were able to submit our project just in time. Technical Judging (11th July 2021, 11:30 AM) We presented our solution to the social good organization that had been allotted to us. They then proceeded to ask us a few questions and we were able to answer them. After looking at the solutions of other teams, we were mind-blown with the level of innovation and creativity they had used in their solutions. We knew for sure that we didn’t stand a chance to qualify for the next round. Unfortunately, but not surprisingly, we didn’t make it to the next round. But we were glad that we did our best. It was a complete roller coaster ride filled with ups and downs. There was a lot to learn from each and every person that I interacted with during the hackathon. It was definitely the experience of a lifetime. Event Shortlists: Roughly less than a month after CFG, the list of students selected for the Internship was out. 13 students were selected from our college, and surprisingly I was one of them. Optimal use of two power resources: Two power resources and their initial power capacity were given as input. At every step we have to optimally choose between one of the resources. At every step capacity of chosen resource gets reduced by 2 and that of the unchosen resource increases by 1 so you can only choose a resource with capacity greater than 1. Repeat this until one of the power stations capacity becomes zero. Return the number of steps required if we use the resources optimally. Sample input: 5, 3 Output: 6 It is solved by greedy approach by choosing the greater number at each step. I passed all test cases. 2. Most similar string for a given query: Given a list of strings and a query string, we have to find the string from the list which is most similar or closest to the given query string. To do so we have to calculate the Levenshtein distance ( minimum number of insert a character/delete character / replace character operations to be performed on a string to convert the string to the given query). Return the word with lowest Levenshtein distance. If two words have the same Levenshtein distance, then the a lexicographically smaller word is the answer. Finding the Levenshtein distance is a well known DP problem - Edit distance I partially passed test cases for this problem. 3. Blacklink sorting: Given a string array of webpage titles and an integer array of number of blacklinks on the corresponding pages, we have to return the webpage titles in decreasing order of number of blacklinks in them. Code for Good 2023 Hackathon (15th &16th) The hackathon for my batch was conducted online. Pre-Hackathon: Before the hackathon JPMC conducts online bootcamps on the required technologies during the hack like GitHub and their communication channel slack, etc. You’ll be assigned your mentors and teammates 2-3 days before the hack starts. Team assignment is unknown to us so your teammates can be from anywhere in India. Generally a team of 6 members is formed with 2-3 mentors. A day before, our team got in touch with each other on a Whatsapp group and discussed our tech stack along with our strengths and weaknesses. We collectively decided on MERN stack as all of us were web developers. During the session, everyone got to know each other well, overall very typical. After the session the NGO coordinators presented their problem statements to the teams and all teams were given some to discuss and decide a preference order for problem statements. A form was released then where we had to submit our preferences and the allocation was done on a first come first serve basis. After you are allocated your problem statement, your team along with all the teams that have the same problem statement will have a separate meeting with the respective NGO coordinator to understand their requirements further in much detail and also ask any questions that you may have. The actual brainstorming and coding starts after this. Throughout the hackathon the mentors were present with us on a zoom call and observed the way we ideated, brainstormed and came up with a solution. Unlike other mentors, our mentors didn’t take any one to one interview/ QnA, they purely judged us based on how we performed individually and as a team (in terms of tech stack and team work). My Tips for CFG: Be a leader. I took charge in my team right from the start, whether it was interacting with my teammates or working as a team alongside our mentors. Just remember to lead while also giving everyone a fair chance to contribute to the team. Be quick in decision making and do not be stuck on a small problem for a large amount of time. It's fine if your teammates aren’t as proficient as you in your chosen tech stack. Many of my teammates only knew basic HTML/CSS. You can always divide the work in a manner that plays with everyone’s strengths. Be confident and out there with your ideas and points. Nobody will know how smart you are if you are not heard. Winning isn't everything, securing an internship through this hackathon is about showcasing your best all-around self. This includes not only technical skills but also your personality, teamwork abilities, and work ethic. We did not win the hackathon, but 4 out of 6 (including me) in our team got an offer a month later from JPMC to join as SEP interns for summer 2024. Internship Offer After 1 month, the internship selections were announced, 6 out of 10 received internship offers, and all 6 accepted the offer since the results were announced before the arrival of any other company in the college. Tips In General 1. Keep practicing DSA questions (450Sheet, Blind 75) from Leetcode, CodeChef or any other platform. 2. Be up to speed on core subjects/concepts like OS, DBMS and OOPS (our curriculum is good enough, else you can also refer to GFG). 3. Make sure that you are confident in your English speaking and presentation skills. 4. It’s fine if you aren’t proficient in the entire tech stack (eg. MERN/MEAN) it’s about how good you are at whatever you do. Apart from this I know this entire process can be very draining and mentally exhausting (trust me we all have been there) so make sure that you keep your health, both mentally and physically in check. Do not decide your self worth based on this. Getting an internship is super cool but your worth is not dependent on just getting an internship in a company. Be happy and enjoy the ride! Good luck.   "content": "Deutsche Bank Interview Experience Ritika Chandwani TY BTech IT Online Coding Assessment (90 mins): Only CS/IT and EXTC students with a CGPA of 7.0+ were allowed to take the test. The online assessment was scheduled for 6th November 2022 at 3 pm. The test was proctored and was held on the HackerEarth platform. The test was designed to be of total 90 marks There were 10 MCQs on CS Fundamentals (each of 4 marks). Some of them were pretty basic and a few of them were of medium level. Then there were two coding questions each having 10 Test Cases. 1. Maximum Quirkiness (20 marks): Given an array A of size N, find the pair of index {i,j} such that quirkiness between them is maximum and return the maximum quirkiness. The Quirkiness of two indexes i and j is defined as Q( i, j ) = Sum of array elements from index i to index j + constant*(j-i) Q(i,j) = Sum(An) + c(j-i) Where An is the sum of array elements from index i to j and j>i. Also, indexing starts from 1 for the given array and the constant value was given. Return the maximum quirkiness for the given array. Example: Consider N = 4, c=2, A= [4,1,2,-2] If we take i=1,j=3 we get quirkiness = 7+ 2*(3-1) = 11 This is the maximum quirkiness across all pairs of indexes. So, return 11. Approach: I started with the brute force approach using three nested loops. One loop for choosing ith index, another loop for choosing the jth index and third loop for calculating the sum of array elements between i and j. And each time calculating quirkiness and returning the maximum value. Of course, this led to TLE as time complexity was O(n3). Though I was able to pass 5/10 test cases. Then, one important thing to note here is that we need the maximum sum of the array elements between i and j and also the maximum difference between i and j to maximize the quirkiness. So, I tried finding out the maximum sum subarray. This reminded me of Kadane’s algorithm. So, using Kadane’s algorithm, I found out maximum sum between any two indices and then found out the quirkiness for those indices and returned the value. Although in most cases, quirkiness will be maximum where sum of subarray is maximum, it may happen that because of the indices difference, the quirkiness may not be maximum. With this approach, I got 7/10 test cases passed. Further, I went on to thinking how to simultaneously consider the index position too. I tried modifying Kadane’s algorithm, by taking into consideration the start and end index difference, but I was running short on time. So, I decided to switch questions and first try solving the next question and come back, if time permits. But, eventually, I couldn’t solve it any further before the time. 2. Collecting Coins (30 marks): John is playing a battle game that consists of N heroes and M monsters. The power of heroes and the monsters are represented by arrays H and M respectively. A hero can defeat a monster if his power is greater than or equal to the power of the monster. On defeating a monster, the hero gains a certain amount of coins corresponding to that monster. The coins after defeating a particular monster are represented by an array C of size M. Now, John is curious to know how many coins each hero can collect by defeating any monster in the game. Return an array of N integers containing coins earned by each hero. The health of a hero doesn’t get reduced after defeating a monster. Also, a monster can be defeated by multiple heroes. Example: Let N = 5, M = 4, A = [1,3,5,2,4], B = [1,4,2,9], C = [1,2,8,4] The first hero can defeat only the 1st monster, so he gains only 1 coin. The second hero can defeat the 1st and 3rd monsters, so he gains 1+8=9 coins. Similarly, the third, fourth, and fifth heroes gain 11, 9 and11 coins respectively. Return: [ 1, 9, 11, 9, 11 ] Approach: Again, I started with brute force, simply using two nested loops, traverse the hero’s array, and compare its power with each monster, whenever the hero’s power is greater than or equal to the monster, add coins for that hero and finally return the array. With this approach, I got 5/10 test cases correct. Now, I had to optimize this approach and get the answer in less time complexity. For this, since we need to find only those heroes whose power was greater than the monster’s power, I thought of sorting. Now, here sorting couldn’t be used directly as coins were correspondingly associated with the monster’s power. So, for that, I thought of making pairs of arrays B and C and then sorting the pair according to first value, using comparator function. And then I could get the answer in O(nlogn) time by using binary search on array A, by finding values less than each element of array B. I did mess up a bit with this approach, as this got complicated and I couldn’t think of a better approach, but still, I could pass 8/10 test cases. Results were declared on 8th November 2022 and 8 students were shortlisted for the interview rounds! After the PPT, the interviews were scheduled on the same day. Technical Interview (45 Minutes): It started at 9:30 am. The interview began with the introduction of the interviewer and of course, followed by my introduction. Most of the interviews begin with the standard ‘Tell me about yourself’ question. Be prepared for it and do mention the key points about yourself that you are confident of. Don’t brag unnecessarily as questions may arise from it. Next, he enquired about my favorite subject in CS fundamentals. To which I answered OS, the reason being I was very confident with OS. This question is your golden chance to create a first good impression and brag your confidence about your most prepared subject. Don’t mess up with this and be very sure of at least one of the CS fundamentals. OS: What is deadlock? It’s better to answer the definition and also explain it clearly in layman’s terms. And if possible, provide an example for the same. What are the methods to overcome deadlock? An Example is a must here. I explained all four methods with examples. It’s okay to forget methods, but try to answer as much as possible. The interviewer was very friendly and after OS he asked me my next favorite subject. To which I answered DBMS, as I was confident with it. DBMS: What is SQL? (pretty basic) What all SQL databases I am familiar with? I had used a NoSQL database in my project so, I mentioned about MongoDB. Of course, the next question was SQL v/s NoSQL Whenever asked for comparison, make sure to highlight the key differences and try to add real world comparisons. Why did you use NoSQL? I mentioned that I had to include unstructured data(images and videos) in my project and also the benefits of NoSQL. He was quite satisfied with my answer. Further, he asked me about Joins and Different types of Joins. Be prepared for the most common questions, make notes while studying, and revise them thoroughly before your interview. I could answer it well as I had revised it the last night. Then he moved on to Data Structures and Algorithms (the most important of all) So, he started with a pretty basic question: How to reverse an array in place (i.e without using any extra space) It’s nice to start with brute force, but when clearly mentioned stick to it and start with what’s asked. I answered the swap method (loop through half of the array and swap every element with (n-i-1) element.) He was satisfied with this answer. Then he asked me to count the occurrence of a character in the given string I messed up a bit with this pretty simple question. I directly jumped on to Hash Maps, which weren’t needed at all here. Soon after realizing, I corrected myself and gave the very basic approach of looping through the string. Then he moved on to linked lists. How to detect a cycle in a linked list? A pretty standard Linked list question. Again, started with brute force approach, hashing method and then explained the fast-slow pointer method (hare and tortoise method) Find (n-3)rd node from the given linked list. I started answering with the brute force approach: traverse the linked list and get the length of the list. Then, simply traverse to the (n-3)rd node as you now know n. The process continues until team_size is achieved. Example - score[] = [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 30, 20] team_size = 2 k = 3 Initially, we select first k i.e [10, 20, 10] or last k [5, 30, 20] so, 30 is selected and removed from the list. Second time, we have first k i.e [10,20,10] or last k [15,5,20] we take 20 and remove it. Thus our team reaches a size of team_size so we stop and return 30 + 20 = 50. DSA: For Binary Search, Stacks, Sliding Window (MUST), Heap - Aditya Verma. For DP, Trees, and Graphs - take U forward. 1) Always revise the sorting algorithms, basic data structure questions because they are frequently asked in interviews such as quick sort, merge sort, stack using a queue, queue using stack, graph traversals, etc. 2) Make notes for each topic that you cover. These could be on some pattern that you identified in such questions as finding Kth order statistics in an array being related to a heap or some syntax that you find tough to remember such as the declaration of the priority queue in C++. 3) Don't hit a trial by submitting your code; it just wastes time. Rather do a dry run of example input and expected output. You won't be asking an interviewer to confirm your code multiple times. so develop the habit of verifying it twice and submitting it once. 4) Sometimes you may be asked to write the driver code, and data structure implementation along with the algorithm for the given question - in both online tests and interviews. Do practice writing driver code for a linked list,tree, and graph questions. Given two resources with powers A and B respectively. Every second, the power of the selected resource gets reduced by 2 and the power of the unselected resource gets charged by 1. The software stops when at least one resource has a power of 0. 2. Given a dictionary of N words and a query word S, you need to auto-suggest the best word from the dictionary that is closest to S. Two words are first compared by their Levenshtein distance to the word S. If two words have the same Levenshtein distance, then the lexicographically smaller word is given the priority. All words, along with S, are lowercase. 3. Backlinks are links from other websites to a particular web resource, and they play a crucial role in the SEO of pages. You are given N webpage titles and corresponding arrays that constrain the number of backlinks for each webpage. The objective is to rank the web pages in descending order based on the number of backlinks they have. If two or more pages have the same number of links then maintain their ordering. There is a lot of luck and chance involved in who gets to pass the Coding round of all companies. For odd ‘n’ answer is 0. 2nd Problem: Beautiful String There are 3 kinds of characters, [a-zA-z] letters, [0-9] numbers, and some special symbols [/\\*]. Beautiful string is the string of the form: Starting with a letter, then there are 0 or more numbers, then there is a ‘/’, after that one or more letter or number, then a ‘\\’, lastly one or more letter or number or ‘*’. (I don’t remember exact expression but it was of this form only) You are given a string as input, print number of substring which follows the Beautiful String expression. Input: a4/v1\\v*3 Output: 6 Substrings: a4/v1\\v, a4/v1\\v*, a4/v1\\v*3, 4/v1\\v, 4/v1\\v*, 4/v1\\v*3 3rd Problem: You are given an array of integers (non-descending) and one number ‘n’. From the given array take any ‘n’ elements to make a new array. Now take the minimum difference of the adjacent elements. Do this for all the possible combination of elements from given array. From all the minimum differences of the sub arrays, print the maximum number. Input array: 1, 2, 5, 8 Input n: 3 Possible sub arrays and its minimum difference of adjacent elements: (1, 2, 5): 1 (1, 2, 8): 1 (1, 5, 8): 3 (2, 5, 8): 3 Ans: 3 So I could solve 1st one completely, we had to get to a formula and solution was of complexity O(1). Again it was conducted on their internal platform only and the duration of the test was 100 minutes.\nIt consisted of 3 easy to medium DSA questions covering arrays, math and logic based questions.\nQuestion 1: Given a string containing only digits ‘6’ and ‘9’, replace at most one digit (6->9,9->6) to make the largest integer possible.\nFor example:\nInput: num=”996996” Output:”999996”\nMy approach was to start traversing the string from left to right and replace the first ‘6’ detected with ‘9’.\nCode:\nstring solve(string num) {\n   for (int i = 0; i < num.length(); i++) {\n       if (num[i] == '6') {\n           num[i] = '9';\n           break;\n       }\n   }\n   return num;\n}\n\nQuestion 2: A robot starts at the origin (0, 0) on a 2D X-Y plane. It can move one unit at a time in four directions:\n● ^ → North (up)\n● v → South (down)\n● > → East (right)\n● < → West (left)\nYou are given a string ‘moves’, where each character represents one move made by the robot.\nDetermine whether the path traced by the robot forms the boundary of a rectangle and returns to its starting position.\nExample\nInput: moves = \"^>>>vvv<<<\"\nOutput: true\nExplanation:\nThe robot moves around the perimeter of a rectangle and ends at the starting point.\nCode:\nbool solve(string &moves) {\n   unordered_map<char, pair<int, int>> dir = {\n           {'^', {-1, 0}},\n           {'>', {0, 1}},\n           {'v', {1, 0}},\n           {'<', {0, -1}}\n   };\n   vector<pair<int, int>> path;\n   int x = 0, y = 0;\n   for (char c : moves) {\n       x += dir[c].first;\n       y += dir[c].second;\n       path.push_back({x, y});\n   }\n// Must return to the starting point\n   if (x != 0 || y != 0)\n       return false;\n   int minx = INT_MAX, maxx = INT_MIN;\n   int miny = INT_MAX, maxy = INT_MIN;\n   for (auto [cx, cy] : path) {\n       minx = min(minx, cx);\n       maxx = max(maxx, cx);\n       miny = min(miny, cy);\n       maxy = max(maxy, cy);\n   }\n   // Perimeter check\n   int perimeter = 2 * ((maxx - minx) + (maxy - miny));\n   if (perimeter != (int)moves.size())\n       return false;\n   // Every visited point must lie on rectangle boundary\n   for (auto [cx, cy] : path) {\n       bool onVerticalEdge = (cx == minx || cx == maxx);\n       bool onHorizontalEdge = (cy == miny || cy == maxy);\n       if (!(onVerticalEdge || onHorizontalEdge))\n           return false;\n   }\n   return true;\n}\n\nQuestion 3: You are given a three-digit integer N and an integer K.\nIn one operation, you can increase any digit of N by 1 (a digit cannot exceed 9). You may perform at most K operations.\nFind the maximum possible three-digit number that can be obtained after performing at most K increments.\nApproach\nTo maximize the number, prioritize increasing the most significant digit (hundreds place), then the tens place, and finally the units place. For each digit, use as many operations as possible (up to the amount needed to make it 9) before moving to the next digit.\nCode:\nint solve(int N, int K) {\n   string num = to_string(N);\n   for (int i = 0; i < 3 && K > 0; i++) {\n       int digit = num[i] - '0';\n       int required = 9 - digit;\n       int increase = min(required, K);\n       num[i] = char('0' + digit + increase);\n       K -= increase;\n   }\n   return stoi(num);\n}\n\nResults: 16 people were shortlisted for interviews, and I was one of them. These weren’t very direct, and ate up a lot of my time. 3-4 questions were based on airline ticket prices. Data of different discount schemes available, and different criteria for availing those schemes was given in checked tabular format. For example if C1, C2, … are the criteria, and S1, S2, … are the schemes, if C1 and C3 are satisfied, then S5 can be availed. And the questions were like a family had to book tickets, and each of the members had different characteristics (like frequent flyer, infant), so find the total cost. I took too long to solve the stock and airline problems, so I couldn’t solve the last 4 questions, which were based on some other scenario. So I just marked them randomly. (There was no negative marking. Other tests may have it, so always know this before giving every test.) c. Coding Questions: I must say that I got lucky (and I’ll probably keep saying this throughout this document). Everyone had 2 coding questions to solve in 60 minutes. The questions that I got (yes, problems weren’t the same for everyone) were really easy. i. Count the number of occurrences of a string in another substring. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/frequency-substring-string/ Although there is an O(M+N) solution, my O(MN) solution was accepted, since string length was a maximum of 15 (naive matching). ii. The second problem was similar to the reachability to the end of an array question. It was coated in a long problem statement about a network which has nodes linearly connected, and one can install a repeater at that node so that signals can go further down the array of nodes. Every node has a certain value that represents how many nodes ahead can the signal go if a repeater is installed there. So the problem was to find the sequence (ordered) of nodes at which repeaters should be installed, such that a signal from the first node can reach the last node, and minimum repeaters have to be installed. If there are multiple solutions with a minimum number of repeaters, print the one which is lexicographically smallest. Constraint: N <= 10^3, so I solved this using dynamic programming 22 people were shortlisted for the first round of interviews, the Technical Round. Interviews were taken on Zoom calls 2. Technical Interview: 45 minutes The interviewer started with asking me to introduce myself. Then he asked me about the subjects that I had in my current semester (V). Then he started with the questions. a. OS: Semaphores, difference between threads and processes, paging, cache. b. OOP: Principles (abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance). c. COA (-_-): Pipelining. I didn’t remember the term. d. CN: TCP/IP stack. He then asked me about routing algorithms. I didn’t know that, so I told him that we haven’t covered that yet (I had told him that we had CN in the current semester). He said okay and continued. e. DBMS: He asked me about Normalization, and B+ Trees. I did not know B+ Trees (-_-) f. He asked me about the first project that I had mentioned on my resume. He did not ask any technological aspects of it, just what the project was. g. Since two of my projects used JavaScript, he asked me about OOP in JS. I answered this very haphazardly. h. DSA: He asked me two problems. He asked me whether I wanted to write it on paper and share photographs to him or whether I wanted to use some collaborative editor. I opted for the latter. So he sent me a collabedit link. There was no syntax highlighting, no bracket completion, no auto indentation, so always make sure to write clean and readable code, regardless of the editor. He asked me for the pseudocode, in plaintext, but I ended up writing both questions in C++ :-P : i. Longest increasing subsequence with reconstruction: This is a standard DP problem, with O(N^2) complexity. I solved it and explained each part to him. He asked me to analyze the time and space complexity. Then I told him that an O(nlogn) solution also exists for LIS, but I didn’t know how it worked. He didn’t ask me any questions on this further. ii. Reverse a 32 bit unsigned integer: I thought this was easy, so I just solved it using shifting bits and checking if each bit was 1 or 0. And the interviewer also accepted this solution. After the next round of interviews, my friend made me realize that my solution is not correct. For example, if the number given is 6, or in binary: 0000...0110, the output should be 0110….0000. But my solution would give the answer as 0000...0011, or 3 in decimal. :-) Despite my blunder for the second DSA question, I qualified for the next interview round, along with 14 other people. 3. Senior Manager Interview: As you can guess, the interviewer was someone at a senior position. This interview lasted for 1 hour. a. He asked me to differentiate between Java and C++, garbage collection in Java (because I mentioned this difference) - when exactly is the garbage collector called, and whether setting a class variable to null causes the garbage collector to be called immediately, abstract classes v/s interfaces. He was listening very intently, and he somehow always picked something that I had said in response to the previous question, and then asked a counter question. b. He asked me some DBMS questions, like what are primary keys, can unique keys be NULL and an example based question. He asked me to write a query to select duplicate rows. I told him a query, he said I was close, and went on to asking me questions about GROUP BY. c. He asked me nothing from OS or DSA. d. He asked me exhaustively about my projects, my role in them and some DOM questions because I’d used JS. He patiently and intently listened about my projects, and asked specific questions related to them. e. He asked me about challenges and my roles at SRA and CoC (I had mentioned these on my resume). f. Then he asked me if I had any questions for him, so I asked one. In the middle of answering it, he actually asked me the following question (it was open-ended). I asked for clarifications twice, and I’m still not clear about what he was asking me: Say you’ve been given the task to make an application that takes real time stock prices from a database and relays these prices to some interface (web / API client / whatever), and you’re told to make this application in Golang and in Java. How would you approach this task, and how would you present your application (he stressed on the word “metrics”)? So I think that he wanted to know how I would plan the project activities, and deal with having to code in an entirely new language for me (he knew beforehand that I didn’t know Golang). I mentioned a few points like learning Golang first, and simultaneously designing the application, the inputs, outputs, architecture (I was just saying whatever came to my mind at that point). Then I would implement it in the two languages. Then he asked me about metrics, so I mentioned speed, scalability, code quality. For some reason I also blurted out “Design Patterns” when I was talking about code quality. So he asked me what Design Patterns are, and what the Singleton Pattern is. (That is the one design pattern I was confident about at that time XD). After a long wait (like, 8 hours for me) 8 people made it to the last round, HR. 4. HR Interview: This was just for 15 minutes, and it was really quick XD. The interviewer asked me what I know about Wells Fargo and why I wanted to intern there (pay attention during the pre-placement talk :-) ). He then asked me which companies I had given interviews for before and what I had learned from those interviews. He then asked me if I’m flexible with the locations of the internship. And finally, he asked me if I had any questions for him. All 8 people who qualified for the HR round were selected for the internship. Afterword (or whatever it’s called): 1. I know this document is long, but I wanted to include how interviewers can ask counter questions, how they can be very thorough with your resume, et cetera. 2. If you’ve been preparing well, then don’t get demotivated if you don’t advance to next rounds. There were days when I had become very demotivated due to not even qualifying the online rounds. I had failed learning experiences with a total of 6 companies before being selected for this internship. Learn from your mistakes. 3. One internship drive does not define you or your worth. Stay confident, persistent and enjoy what you’re learning. 4. Plan. I had all my focus on DSA, and I ended up doing OS, DBMS haphazardly. 5. If you’re a person who doesn’t speak too much, try developing a habit of speaking out loud when you’re solving a coding problem. In an interview, it’s much more important to explain to the interviewer your thought process and then arriving at a solution. Maybe it’s not perfect, but it’s better than thinking silently for two long, awkward minutes. 6. People will keep giving you tips (like I am right now :-P), and you should listen to them. But remember that your hard work and your calmness during the interview are the things that will help you the most. If you have any queries, you can email me at akshatshah_21@yahoo.in All the best for your endeavours!",

  "content": "GOLDMAN SACHS SUMMER ANALYST INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE YEAR - 2024 MANAV SHAH COMPUTER ENGINEERING BATCH - 2026 Introduction Hey there, I am Manav Shah, a BTech CE student of VJTI (2023 - 2026). I would like to share my interview experience for the Goldman Sachs Internship opportunity as a Summer Analyst. I hope my experience will help you prepare better for both internship and FTE (Full-Time Employment) opportunities at Goldman Sachs. The selection process included three interview rounds and an online assessment. Each stage was crucial in assessing various skills, such as technical knowledge, problem-solving abilities, and communication. I will share as many details as I remember from my experience, hoping it will give you valuable insights and guide your preparation effectively. Pre Placement Talk Somewhere around 12 July 2024, we received an email from TPO informing us that Goldman Sachs was visiting the campus for intern hiring. In this email, there were links for applying on the official Goldman Sachs Careers page as well as details for a webinar. Platform: Zoom Webinar. Time: 23 July 2024, 5pm - 6pm. The Pre-Placement Talk was engaging and to the point. They started off by explaining what GS does, why GS stands out from the rest and what kind of lifestyle you can expect at GS. Pay close attention to whatever is discussed in this meeting, as it serves as a good way to understand the kind of people the firm is looking for. Additionally, during your interviews, the interviewers may ask you questions about the firm, and the insights shared in this session can help you make a strong impression. Preparing for this talk and taking detailed notes will definitely pay off in the later stages of the hiring process. Online Assessment (OA) Platform - Hackerank (Video and Screen proctored) Duration - Around 1 hour The online assessment consisted of: 10 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) -15 mins 3 coding questions - 40 mins 1 HR-related questions - 5mins As much as I remember, we were allocated 55 minutes to complete the MCQs and coding questions, and an additional 5 minutes for the HR questions. Each MCQ earns you 3 marks for correct answer and -1 mark for incorrect answer. Coding Questions - 3 Questions 1) Modest Number The problem is to identify modest numbers within a given range (inclusive of start and end). A number is considered modest if it can be split into two parts (left and right), such that dividing the number by the right part gives a remainder equal to the left part. The program should check all possible combinations of left and right partitions of a number to verify this condition. Solution Approach 1. Splitting Numbers: Iterate over all digits of a number to partition it into left and right parts. 2. Validation: Check if the right part is non-zero and if the condition number % right == left holds. 3. Iterate Over Range: For every number in the given range, apply the above check. 4. Output: Collect and print all numbers that satisfy the modest number property. This approach ensures all possible partitions are tested for each number within the range. 2) Identifying Unique Colors on Painting Sheets Problem: You are given N rectangular painting sheets and M shots. Each sheet is defined by four integers representing the bottom-left and top-right corners of the rectangle, i.e., (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). Each shot has a set of coordinates (x, y) and a color. The goal is to determine, for each sheet, how many unique colors have been shot within the boundaries of that sheet. For each shot, you need to check if the shot's coordinates lie within the bounds of each painting sheet. If the shot is within a sheet, the color of that shot should be considered for that sheet. Input: N (number of painting sheets) and M (number of shots). N rectangles, each defined by four integers (x1, y1, x2, y2), representing the coordinates of the bottom-left and top-right corners. M shots, each defined by three integers: (x, y) for the coordinates and color for the color of the shot. Output: For each sheet, output the number of unique colors that have been shot within the sheet's bounds. Solution Approach: 1. Store Sheet Data: Each sheet is represented by a rectangle with four coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2). 2. Track Unique Colors: For each shot, check if the shot’s coordinates fall within the bounds of each sheet. If they do, add the color of the shot to the respective sheet's set. 3. Output: After processing all shots, the size of each sheet’s set will give the number of unique colors associated with that sheet. This approach efficiently uses sets to ensure that only unique colors are counted for each sheet. 3) Card The problem involved using a greedy approach and working with arrays. While I can't recall the exact details of the question, it revolved around distributing or sorting cards in some way that required an optimal solution using a greedy strategy. The task likely involved finding a way to minimize or maximize certain values based on the cards' properties (such as their values, positions, or some other attributes). MCQs - 10 Questions 1. Blocks of Different Colours Flock Together: This problem involves calculating the probability of selecting three balls of different colors from a box containing white, black, and red balls, given certain relationships between the number of balls of each color. 2. Printer and Bookshelf Efficiency: This scenario involves a printer and a bookshelf with various operations like printing papers, stacking books, and handling failures (paper getting stuck or books falling down), represented by different operations (X, Y, Z, W). 3. Binary Tree Check: This question is about the properties of a complete binary tree, where you need to identify the correct statement related to the structure and characteristics of a complete binary tree. 4. Reality TV: In this problem, you're asked to calculate the number of ways to form a group of six people from eight teams, ensuring that exactly one team's both members are selected. 5. Probability Games: This question involves selecting three balls from a box containing prime numbers from 1 to 30 and finding the probability that the sum of their numbers is even and their product is less than 500. 6. Sequence Check: This problem asks you to verify or identify properties of a given sequence of numbers or elements. 7. Binary Tree Nodes: This question likely asks about the properties or characteristics related to the number of nodes in a binary tree and how they are structured. 8. Multiple Inheritance: This question tests knowledge about multiple inheritance in object-oriented programming, particularly in terms of how it works and the challenges associated with it. 9. Queue-Stack Time: This question is about analyzing the time complexity of insertions and deletions in a queue, given a specific number of push and pop operations. 10. Linked List: This problem involves operations on a linked list, testing knowledge of how linked lists function and the operations that can be performed on them. HR Question - 1 Question The question was how I would ensure a smooth transition of responsibilities if I were leaving a team. Specifically, the question was: \"If you are leaving a team, how will you make sure you communicate all the important details and responsibilities to another team member?\" The focus was on how to effectively transfer knowledge and tasks to ensure the continuity of the team's work. Results: 27 people were shortlisted for interviews, and I was one of them. We received the results on 25 July 2024, in the afternoon. Interview Day Date: 26 July 2024 Venue: TPO Seminar Hall The day started with a reporting time of 8:30 am, followed by the Pre-Interview Talk scheduled at 9:00 am. We were instructed to bring 3-4 printouts of our resumes and dress formally. I wore a white shirt, black trousers, a belt, and formal shoes. Dressing well is crucial, especially when interviewing with financial firms, so make sure to present yourself professionally. A team of around 6-7 people from GS was responsible for managing the process. About five of them were engineers from GS, while the rest were HR/Managerial personnel. During the Pre-Interview Talk, they gave us an overview of the interview procedure and their roles at GS. They explained that the interview would consist of technical rounds followed by HR rounds. After the talk, the interview process began around 10 am without any delays. A few important tips to keep in mind before the interview: 1. Pay attention to the Pre-Interview Talk: Focus on the introductions and the roles of the people from GS. This knowledge might be useful, as you may end up with one of them as your interviewer. 2. Engage with the questions: If there's a Q&A session or any general questions are asked, make sure to answer. Most candidates tend to stay silent, so responding will make you stand out. 3. Ask about the company: Show your interest by asking questions regarding the technologies the company is working on or other relevant aspects of the organization. 4. Research the company: Before the interview, make sure to gather background details about the company, including its latest news and collaborations. This will help you stand out as an informed candidate and show your genuine interest. Round 1: Technical Interview (Duration: 1 hr) The interviews began at 10 am, but my first technical round didn’t start until 12 pm, which was quite nerve-wracking, especially since some candidates had already completed two rounds by that time. The TPO seminar hall had several cabins, each with one or two interviewers, and candidates were allocated to different cabins. Finally, I was called for my first technical interview. I sat down across from my interviewer, who introduced himself and explained his role at GS. He then asked me to introduce myself. I gave my introduction confidently. It’s important to have a well-prepared introduction—keep it concise and to the point. Avoid going too technical and consider mentioning a hobby or an interesting fact. Remember to maintain good eye contact and positive body language. Then after asking me which language I was comfortable with(C++), he gave me the 1st question and a piece of pen and paper to solve it on. 1. Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree Given a binary tree root, a node X in the tree is named good if in the path from root to X there are no nodes with a value greater than X. Return the number of good nodes in the binary tree. Input: root = [3,1,4,3,null,1,5] Output: 4 Explanation: Nodes in blue are good. Root Node (3) is always a good node. Node 4 -> (3,4) is the maximum value in the path starting from the root. Node 5 -> (3,4,5) is the maximum value in the path Node 3 -> (3,1,3) is the maximum value in the path. It was an easy question, and I explained my approach to the interviewer before writing any code. I described how I would solve it using Depth-First Search (DFS) to traverse the tree and keep track of the largest value encountered in the path from the root to each node. I also mentioned that for a node to be considered \"good,\" its value must be greater than or equal to the largest value in the path from the root to that node. Here’s the approach I explained to the interviewer: Perform a DFS traversal on the tree to visit each node. At each node, compare its value with the largest value encountered so far (curMax). If the node’s value is greater than or equal to curMax, increment the count of good nodes. Recursively traverse the left and right subtrees, passing the updated curMax value. Additional Tips: Always mention the time and space complexity even if the interviewer doesn't ask. Use proper variable naming conventions to make your code more readable and maintainable. Consider various edge cases and test your code against them. Running your code on different test cases impresses the interviewer as it shows thorough thinking and problem-solving skills. 2. Design a Gmail System The second question in my technical round was quite unique and interesting. The task was to design a mail system with various features and operations. The mail system needed to support the following components: 1. Unread: Stores emails that have not yet been read. 2. Read: Stores emails that have been read. 3. Spam: Stores emails that are marked as spam. 4. Deleted: Stores emails that have been deleted. Additionally, there were various operations to perform on the emails: 1. X: Marks email X as \"read\" and moves it from the \"Unread\" queue to the \"Read\" queue. 2. X: Marks email X as \"spam\" and moves it from either the \"Read\" or \"Unread\" queue to the \"Spam\" queue. 3. X: Moves email X from the \"Spam\" queue back to the \"Unread\" queue. 4. X: Deletes email X from the system and add it to delete queue. Approach: I started by explaining to the interviewer that we could maintain separate queues for each component: \"Read\", \"Unread\", \"Spam\", and \"Deleted\". When we receive an email (let's say X), it will first be placed in the \"Unread\" queue. When the user performs an operation like \"read\", the mail X is moved from \"Unread\" to \"Read\". Similarly, other operations can move emails between queues while maintaining the FIFO property of each queue. This was the basic approach I outlined, and the interviewer was satisfied with it. Then, he asked me about the time complexity of the solution. I explained that each operation would take O(n) time because we would need to traverse the entire queue to find the email, remove it from the old queue, and add it to the new queue. Optimization: The interviewer then asked me to reduce the time complexity from O(n) to O(1) per operation. Initially, I struggled to think of how to achieve this, but after a while, I brainstormed different data structures. He provided me with a hint about using linear data structures. Eventually, I realized that I could use a Doubly Linked List to store the nodes and maps to track the positions of emails. Specifically, I proposed using a map like <mail, Node>* to directly locate any email in O(1) time. This way, we could: Remove an email from a queue in O(1) time by modifying the left and right pointers of its adjacent nodes. Add it to another queue in O(1) time by adjusting the pointers. This solution is quite similar to how LRU (Least Recently Used) cache and LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache work and I had already solved those while practicing. Since the code would be large and we were under time constraints, the interviewer asked me to design the map structures and explain the workflow of the operations rather than writing the full code. Outcome: The interviewer was impressed with this approach, as it was a novel solution to a unique and challenging problem. 3. Count Unique Occurrences of Different Characters in a String The third question I was asked was to count the unique occurrences of different characters in a string. This was a relatively straightforward question. Approach: I started by explaining to the interviewer that the problem could be solved by maintaining a map (or a hash map) to store the frequency of each character in the string. After iterating through the string, we could check the frequency of each character and track the unique occurrences. Here’s the basic approach I described: Traverse the string and maintain a map to store the frequency of each character. After processing the string, count how many characters have unique frequencies. This was an easy problem to solve, and I told the interviewer the time complexity and space complexity: Time Complexity: Since we only need to iterate over the string once, the time complexity is O(n), where n is the length of the string. Space Complexity: The space complexity is O(1), as there are at most limited different characters in the string . This makes the space complexity constant because the number of different characters is fixed. The interviewer seemed satisfied with my approach and explanation. I was selected for the second round. I was tasked with designing a system to accommodate this scenario. I started by asking a few clarifying questions to ensure I understood all aspects of the problem and then proceeded to design the solution on paper. My approach was to create a Company class and then Department classes that would inherit from the main class. Each department class would inherit common features and have additional unique features specific to that department. For common features, I suggested creating a separate class that would house all the shared features, ensuring code reusability. Each department class would then extend this common class and add its own unique attributes and functionalities. When the interviewer asked which OOP concepts I would use for this design, I mentioned inheritance and encapsulation. She then asked which type of inheritance I would use, and I initially said multiple inheritance. The interviewer pointed out that Java does not support multiple inheritance, but I quickly adapted and explained that interfaces could be used as an alternative in Java to achieve the desired functionality. She then asked how I would implement this system in React. I explained that I would create modular code using different components, ensuring code reusability across the application. The conversation shifted, and the interviewer asked me a random question related to streaming services. She asked, \"When you watch a movie on Netflix and click on ‘continue watching,’ it starts from where you last left off. But in Zee5, it starts a few seconds before that point. What do you think is the reason for this difference?\" I thought for a moment and suggested that Zee5 might be dividing the video into fixed frames and resuming from the nearest previous frame. The interviewer confirmed my answer for Zee5 but clarified that Netflix uses a sliding window data structure to handle this functionality. I was a bit surprised by this and was curious about how this data structure is implemented. After this, the interviewer asked me if I had any questions. I asked about the reason behind GS migrating from a private cloud to AWS (a public cloud) and how they manage to send years of data to AWS. She answered my query, and that concluded my second round. After a brief pause, I explained that the government likely doesn’t use the funds for profit. Since different people have bank accounts in various banks, and the government maintains the money in a single account, the refund process involves transferring funds to multiple accounts, which takes time. Merge Sort Counts\nAn array has n elements. If the array has less than 2 elements, then the array is returned without any changes. If the array has more than two elements, then it is divided into two arrays, left and right. The left array contains the first half elements of the input array while the right array contains the second half of the elements. If n is odd, the left array takes the middle element. Next, the algorithm calls itself first with the left array and then with the right array. After that, the algorithm produces the sorted array, by merging the left and the right arrays into a single sorted array. In this challenge, keep a count for each of the elements in the input array. Initially, all counts are 0. Whenever an integer k from the right array is merged before at least one element from the left array, add 1 to the count. Find the maximum count value after the merge sort algorithm finishes.\nExample\narr = [2, 3, 1]\nAll counters are initialized to 0. First, the mergesort divides the input array into left [2,3] and right = [1]. Next, it runs itself again with the left array. It divides this array into [2] and [3]. Since both are sorted, it merges them, and during the merge 3 is merged after 2 into the sorted order, so nothing is added to the counter. After the merge, the algorithm returns [2,3] to its caller. Next, the initial mergesort call runs itself for the right array [1] but since it has only one element no merging is performed and [1] is returned immediately. Next, the algorithm merges [2,3] with [1]. Since 1 from the right array comes before both elements from the left array during the merge, we add 1 to the counter. After this merge, the algorithm finishes, and the maximum count after the process is 1.\nFunction Description\nComplete the function largestCountValue. The function must return an integer that denotes the maximum count value after the entire merge sort algorithm finishes for the input array arr.\nExample:\nSTDIN\nExplanation\n6\nArr[] size n=6\n1\nArr = [1,2,3,4,5,10]\n2\n3\n4\n5\n10\narr[] size n = 6\narr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10]\nThe first step, break the array into left = [1, 2, 3] and right = [4, 5, 10]. Now break left into left' = [1, 2] and right' = [3]. Break left' into left\"= [1] and right\" = [2]. Perform the merge to get res\" = [1, 2]. The element from right\" was not inserted before an element of left\", so the count remains 0. Merge res\" and right' to get res' = [1, 2, 3]. Again, no element of right' was inserted before an element of res\", so the count remains 0. The array right uses the same logic to arrive at a count of 0. Finally, merging [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 10], no element from the right array is inserted before any element of the left array has been inserted, so the count remains 0.\nThis was a slight variation of counting inversions problem using Merge Sort.\nI was able to pass 4/15 test cases in this question as I made some silly mistakes.\n\n3. Server Investment\nA network security administrator must protect networks at a number of locations from cyber-attacks. Initially, the ith network has num_server[i] servers, and money[i] funds allocated for security upgrades. To upgrade a server in the ith network, it costs upgrade[i]. Selling a server adds sell[i] to available funds.\nGiven the arrays num_servers, money, upgrade, and sell, each with n integers, determine the maximum number of servers that can be upgraded to ensure optimal network security. The result should be an array of n integers, where the ith integer represents the maximum number of upgraded servers for the ith network system.\nGiven, num servers - [4, 3], money = [8, 9]. sell = [4, 2] and upgrade - [4, 5]\nSystem Description | No. of upgraded servers\n1st | A server can be sold at a cost of 4 and upgraded at a cost of 4. If one server is sold, the total amount left is 8+4=12 and 3 servers will be left. Now each server can be upgraded at a cost of 4 for each | 3\n2nd | One server can be sold for a cost of 2 amounting to total money of 11 units which can be used to upgrade both of the remaining servers at a cost of 10 units | 2\nHence the answer is [3,2]\nI solved the question using the below solution:\nI was able to solve this problem completely.\n\n4. Team Formation\nGiven a list of employees where each is assigned a numeric evaluation score, use the selection process below to find the sum of scores of selected employees.\n1. The employee with the highest score among the first k employees or the last k employees in the score list is selected.\n2. The selected employee is removed from the score list.\n3. The process continues to select the next employee until the team size is achieved.\nNote:\n1. In case multiple employees have the same highest score, the employee with the lowest index is selected.\n2. If there are fewer than k employees, the entire list is available for selection.\nExample\nscore = [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 30, 20]\nteamSize=2\nk=3\n• For the first selection, choose from the first 3 elements: [10, 20, 10] or the last 3 elements: [5, 30, 20]. Score 30 is selected and removed from the list. This makes the score = [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 20].\n• For the second selection, choose from [10, 20, 10] or [15, 5, 20]. Score 20 is selected from the lowest index and removed from the list. This makes the score = [10, 10, 15, 5, 20]. The sum of the selected employees' scores is 30+20=50.\nI tried to solve this questions using multiple approaches but the Multiset approach worked but still it passed only 7/15 test cases.\n\nAfter being not shortlisted for 2 companies consecutively - Deutsche Bank and Oracle, I had a lot of anxiety since this was the last dream company in August and all other companies may be invited by mid september.
