  "batch": "Not specified",
  "preview": "Goldman Sachs interview experience for an internship position consisting of an Online Assessment and three interview rounds focusing on DSA, resume projects, and application design.",
  "content": "Goldman Sachs Interview Experience Ahaan Desai - TY CE Eligibility Criteria CS/IT: 7+ CGPA EXTC/Electronics: 8+ CGPA Application and Pre Placement Talk On 27th July, we received an email from the TPO, informing us about the Goldman Sachs Campus Drive. GS took the PPT on 1st July at 5 pm, where they spoke about what their company does, their values etc. I’d suggest taking notes of the PPT as it might come up in interviews. Online Assessment 1st July The OA was conducted on hackerrank on the same day as PPT, between 7-8 pm. 170 students gave the OA. There were 3 programming questions, 10 MCQs and 1 HR question. Tab switching was not allowed. Video was not monitored. a) Programming Questions i) Given a range (l, r) [l & r not included] , find pairs (x,y) in this range such that: sum of perfect divisors of x = y + 1 sum of perfect divisors of y = x + 1 x != y [Perfect divisors of a number include all divisors except the number itself.] For example, if x = 140 and y = 195, the sum of perfect divisors of x is 196 = 195+1 and that of y is 141 = 140 + 1. Constraints: r <= 50,000. ii) A problem that involved finding aliases for a particular name For example if original names = [\"ABC\", \"DEF\", \"GHI\"] and alias = [\"AXY\", \"DJK\", GPS\"] then ABC -> AXY, DEF -> DJK , GHI -> GPS. Basically, the aliases should be mapped such that the first characters of original and alias names should be the same. iii) You were given station data for 3 weather stations for N days. Station 1 had all the data of N days perfectly, while station 2 and 3 had some missing and repeated days. The task was to find the minimum number of columns to delete such that the data is consistent. Consistency in this case meant that all 3 stations should have the same set of days (even with same counts). The test case below will make this question clear. Station 1: 1 5 7 6 4 3 2 Station 2: 5 3 3 2 2 1 4 Station 3: 3 5 4 4 4 1 6 In this case, a possible case would be to delete columns 3,4,5,7, resulting in 1 5 3 5 3 1 3 5 1 So the columns to delete are 4. We had to find the minimum possible number of columns to delete b) MCQs 10 MCQs were asked on mathematics, DSA topics and Java OOPS . These were easy to medium problems, DSA was just theoretical stuff. I don't remember the exact questions but the rough topics are below Math: Equation solving, finding area of an irregular shape Java OOPS: Stuff about object creation and inheritance DSA: A question on simulation using stack and heap, types of self balancing trees. c) HR question A single HR question was there for which a response had to be typed. The question was: \"What will you do if your classmate can't work on a project anymore?” My Experience: I started with the DSA questions first. I solved two questions out of three, and both in Python. Q1 solution: The bruteforce for this question (generating all pairs and checking the condition) would take O(r^2 sqrt(r)) time complexity. There are r^2 pairs in the worst case and time to calculate perfect divisor sum takes sqrt(r) time (assuming optimal algorithm which just checks till sqrt(n))]. Since r was <= 5 * 10^4 , it would take ~6 x 10^11 operations which is not feasible. (feasible should mean <= 10^8). My approach (while not the most optimal one) had time complexity r*sqrt(r) : ~10^7 operations, which worked. I iterated over the range (x=l+1, x<=r-1; x++) [or range(l+1, r) in python] and for each number x in the range, I calculated the sum of perfect divisors (s). Hence a possible y for this x is s - 1, as per the given condition. Now I calculated the sum of the perfect divisors of this y , and checked if it is equal to x+1. If it is, then (x,y) is a valid pair. (I've left out some key edge cases here - see if you can identify them. These edge cases were the reason it took me so long to solve this problem.) An optimisation would be to precompute divisor sums up to N = 50,000 , which would take NlogN time, and then a y for an x can be found and checked in constant time. But it was not needed for the problem. Q2 solution: A use of a hashmap would easily solve this problem. Each first character should be mapped to the alias, and each real name should be mapped to its first character. Suppose there is AXY (alias) and ABC (real), and map1 stores character to alias mappings, and map2 stores mappings from real name to first character. We could do something like map1[map2[\"ABC\"]] = map1[\"A\"] = AXY. There was some existing code, to which we had to tailor our solution and return values. Q3 Nobody who gave the OA solved this question (at least to my current knowledge). The solution might have involved dynamic programming (especially computing longest common subsequences) and use of sets to filter out invalid days. (Solution left as exercise to reader - contact me if you solve it) OA Results: 19 students were selected from the OA. Interviews 19th July Out of the 19 selected from the OA, 2 people got selected elsewhere. They called one more person on the day of the interviews. So a total of 18 candidates gave interviews. As the hiring team had to catch a flight in the afternoon, all candidates were called at 7 am in the morning. At around 8 am, the hiring team were all at campus, and they introduced themselves and asked if we had any doubts. Then they started the interviews shortly after. 4 people from Goldman Sachs were present to conduct the entire hiring process, plus TPO faculty and student representatives. The interview was conducted at the VJTI racing office and the EV lab, as the main TPO office was under renovation. The team took 3 rounds of hiring, with shortlisting after every round. The first two rounds were: 1. DSA + Resume projects 2. A high level description/design of an application. Some people gave the DSA round first and then the design round, while others had the design round first. Some people only gave the DSA round. But whoever gave the design round also gave the DSA round. I had the DSA round first and then the design round. Round 1 8:30 am Duration: 30 mins I was the second person to give the first round. I went into the interview cabin, greeted my interviewer and got seated. Without further ado, I gave my introduction. She read my resume and started asking questions on my first listed project. Q1. Describe the high level architecture of your application, mention what technologies that you have used for each part of the application, and how they communicate within each other. Now this was a recipe app I’d made as part of the Inheritance mentorship program. The app frontend was made using flutter, and had 3 backend servers, one for the main data (recipe data, user data etc.), one for gathering ingredient prices from various grocery websites and a machine learning model for recipe recommendation. Click here to know more about the project. So I described the architecture on paper and told her how data is being displayed/transferred. She asked how the frontend gets data from the backend so I mentioned that the data from the backend is being exposed via a REST API. Then she asked me if I modeled the application in a sort of microservices type architecture to which I said that I was going in that direction but it wasn't a traditional microservice architecture. Q2. What databases have you used for the application, and where have you gotten the data? I mentioned that I used MongoDB, as at the time of building the project that was the only database I was familiar with. I’d also listed a project using SQL in my project, so she asked a bunch of follow-ups related to the tradeoffs of MongoDB and SQL. 1. Why did you choose MongoDB over SQL? Reason listed above, I did not know SQL much back then, and I mentioned that I only got well versed with it after studying DBMS in college. 2. Would you migrate the database to use SQL? Now there was a lot of discussion here. Initially, I said I would migrate, as the data in my project was structured only and there was no special reason to use MongoDB instead. Then she asked me the differences between MongoDB vs SQL, is SQL more efficient than MongoDB, further questioning on why I would switch to SQL. I highlighted the main differences between them, for the efficiency part I really didn't say much, rambled a bit about joins in SQL, and that joins don't exist in MongoDB (and spoke about the equivalent). I mentioned that my main reason for SQL preference now is that queries in SQL are easier to write, as opposed to mongodb. In mongodb, querying is a bit tedious, json objects are used in queries, where nesting can get a bit deep and hard to understand. 3. Where did I get the data? I got the data from a publicly available dataset on Kaggle. My interviewer was not aware about Kaggle so I gave her a brief explanation about what Kaggle is and why it's used by developers. Q3. How will you implement the addition of new recipes? Well this question started off with “is there any intercommunication between servers?”. There was no intercommunication between the servers as they were mostly standalone. But my ML model was trained on recipe data and I was using the same data as my database. Now my app also doesn't support adding new recipes as of now, so she followed up with “How will you add the functionality of adding new recipes?”. This part was pretty straightforward, I said I'd implement a form in the frontend, and I’d send the form to my backend server, and also my ML server as its being trained on the recipe data itself. In the ML server I was storing vector embeddings of recipe data, so the model could directly use those embeddings to evaluate similar recipes. So the recipe would need to be sent to the ML model too. I mentioned the flow would be 1. An API call to the backend server 2. An API call to the ML server Then she followed up with “what if the ML server failed to add the recipe?”, to which I replied “I’d store a sort of flag variable, which detects if there is any error code returned from the ML server. If the backend server successfully added the data, I’d send a delete request to it.” Then she asked something along the lines of “how would you adapt this if the backend and ML are also connected” (don’t remember exactly what it was) So then I mentioned that my frontend would make one API call to the backend, and the backend would make one API call to the ML server. Then if the ML server fails, it will return the error code to the backend, which would just issue a database query, instead of the more expensive API call in the first solution. This was the last question on my project, and after this she moved on to the DSA portion of the interview. DSA Question Given an array of integers nums and an integer target k, find one continuous subarray whose elements sum up to k. Return the start and end indices (inclusive) of any such subarray. Example: arr = [5,2,3,4,1,2,3], Target = 10. Then l = 1, r = 4 was expected. Python I did not get the entire question at once, rather she started with an array and a required target, and highlighted a certain subarray that would sum to this target. Initially I thought I was being asked the “two sum” problem (would have been crazy), because the first subarray was just of length 2. But then she mentioned another target to which the answer was a longer subarray. I clarified exactly what she required, and started solving. Initially I proposed the brute force solution of checking all subarrays, which would take O(n^2) time. Then I moved on to the optimal solution by proposing use of prefix arrays (she had also built on to the question by use of prefix arrays only). I was a bit skeptical about my solution as I had only solved the variation where we get the count of subarrays, not exact indices. But in the end I provided the correct solution, with a short dry run and python code (code was not required). I also thought of providing a sliding window approach, but time ran out and that would not have worked for negative numbers anyways. def subarraySumOneIndices(nums, k): prefix_map = {0: -1} prefix_sum = 0 for i, num in enumerate(nums): prefix_sum += num if prefix_sum - k in prefix_map: return (prefix_map[prefix_sum - k] + 1, i) prefix_map[prefix_sum] = i return None While writing the code I also mentioned python specific constructs, like how a hashmap is declared in python, how we can’t use the ‘map’ keyword as it is reserved etc. (not needed at all, they just wanted the approach and dry run) After the DSA problem, she asked me if I had any questions for her. During their main introduction at 8 am she had mentioned that she works with Java and Spring Boot. So I brought that up and asked “what was the biggest challenge that you have faced?” to which she answered for about 2-3 minutes. I came out of round 1 at 9-9:10 am a bit anxious and unsure because I felt I had not communicated the DSA solution properly. But, sometime later, I was informed that my round 2 would be conducted in a while. Round 2 - Design Round 10:45 am Duration: 40-45 mins The interviewer for the design round was asking everyone their hobbies, and then asking to implement an application related to a particular hobby. This design round wasn't strictly related to traditional LLD/HLD, but it was just a round to see how I would approach designing any application, no real technical terms were expected. I was asked to design an app which would let an individual learn an instrument. He started by asking what I would add as features in my application. I said that first we should create a registration platform, where the user can choose his previous experience with instruments & music in general. Then the user should be able to start with learning the basics of the instrument i.e. how to play notes, chords etc. The user should also be able to learn particular songs of their choice. I focused on keyboard and guitar as example cases for this application. For the guitar I also mentioned that the app could provide a tuner to tune the strings, but the interviewer said that it's fine if we don't implement that as of now. After this, he asked me to design the high level architecture along with information on what data I would store in the application. I started by saying that someone who wants to learn an instrument would probably find a mobile app ideal due to portability, so we should make a mobile app for the front-end. For the data, I spoke about storing chords, scales, notes and how to play these on different instruments. I also spoke about storing individual songs and the ways to play these on different instruments; I mentioned that we could utilise Inheritance if there is any common factor between ways to play a song/scale by an instrument; for example, a song/scale that just consists of a sequence of notes would play the same on any instrument, only the way to play those particular notes would differ. He asked me how songs are stored on streaming services such as Spotify and Amazon music, to which I replied they directly store .mp3 files as large objects. I was also asked how exactly I would store the songs, to which I provided two options: - A large object (such as a pdf file) of the sheet music of the song - A string consisting of the sequence of notes I think the interviewer also had experience with instruments so I could easily communicate my points across to him. After all this, he asked me how I would implement certain features. Feature 1: The app should be able to detect what note is being played. I said that the phone should be able to detect the frequency of the note being played. But maybe the frequency detected isn’t exactly the frequency that is stored in our database (or in memory), so I suggested that we could store frequencies in a sorted array, and whenever a note is played we just return the upper/lower bound frequency (whichever is closer) to the current frequency using binary search. I don’t remember in what context I said this but I also suggested that we could store note->frequency mapping in a relational database and use an SQL query to return the upper/lower bound. Feature 2: The app should be able to detect what song is being played based on some notes. I talked about using an ML model (as a form of brute force) but I had a feeling that he wasn't looking for that, I also highlighted some drawbacks of using it (such as training the model on different parts of a song individually). After this, he gave two approaches, for which I assumed that the song is being stored as a string of notes. 1) Sliding Window Now before all this, I mentioned that we shouldn’t expect our app to detect songs if only 1-2 notes are played and that a sequence of sufficient length should be played. Given this sequence, we could use a sliding window algorithm to detect if that sequence is part of any song. This would be easy to implement as our input sequence would be of fixed length only. But the drawback here is that every song would have to be searched. 2) Trie My explanation wasn’t complete here, I just mentioned that we could store all the song sequences in a trie data structure. I drew out an example structure and showed how searching could be done. I also highlighted that the Trie method could not be used for detecting sequences in the middle of songs, only for the starting parts, and ended it there. I also thought about mentioning string hashing, but I wasn’t really familiar with it and time ran out anyways. In the end, my interviewer asked me if I had any questions for him. He had not mentioned his role at the firm so I asked him about it, to which he answered sufficiently. The round ended at 11:30 am, after which they told me to come back at 1pm. I used the remaining time to talk to my fellow candidates and to have lunch. But due to more interviews being conducted, they only announced the shortlists for round 3 at 2:45pm, and said that round 3 will start from 3:15 onwards. Round 3 - DSA + Resume 3:25pm Duration: 10-15 mins After eliminations from the first two rounds, 9 people made it to the third round. Some of us had a technical round while others had an HR round. One of us did not have his round 3 conducted at all, maybe due to time constraints. I'll keep this one short, just like the interview itself. 1) I walked in, greeted my interviewer, gave my intro, and the interviewer gave his intro and talked about what he does at the company. 2) The interviewer asked me if I’ve used AI tools (yes), if I’ve used testing tools (no), and asked me to explain the features of one of my projects and the AI feature of my project in depth. 3) He then proceeded to ask me a DSA question - Next Greater Element. I just had to provide an overview of the general working of the algorithm - once I mentioned the term “monotonic stack” and explained how the stack is being used, he was satisfied with my answer. This concluded my round 3. Results At 5pm, results were announced and 6 of us were selected, including me. Final thoughts on the interview I felt that the interview was easier than expected. As I had read interview experiences, I prepared more topics outside of array questions such as Binary Search, Trees, Linked Lists etc. so I was surprised that only array based questions were asked. The monotonic stack question was still unexpected, but I had prepared that too. I was also not asked CS fundamentals (they did not ask last year too) and HR questions (but in any case always prepare for these). The design question was expected due to similar reasons but everyone was asked a different question, based on their hobbies. Also the team had a flight to catch, so they wanted to be done with it as fast as possible. This concludes my interview experience. General Preparation Tips 1. For core DSA concepts, solve any DSA sheet. I’d recommend the Striver A2Z sheet. Avoid solving problems randomly. Instead, progress step by step through the sheet to build concepts systematically. Solve daily problems from LeetCode and GFG to build a routine. 2. Review core Computer Science fundamentals, including Operating Systems(OS), Object-Oriented Programming (OOPS), and Database Management Systems (DBMS). If time allows, explore Computer Networks and low/high-level design concepts. Companies like DE Shaw ask LLD/HLD questions (read Rushabh Mehta’s experience). 3. Focus on key interview questions related to your preferred programming language. Apart from this you should be familiar with at least one of Java and C++, as companies tend to ask language specific questions and OOP questions from these languages. 4. Know your resume inside out. Be ready to answer questions about the technologies used in your projects. 5. Prepare for HR questions too, use the STAR method to answer questions. OA Tips 1. Take part in CP contests to sharpen your problem-solving speed. For OA’s I'd recommend pure CP based contests like on CodeChef and CodeForces (first few questions of contests), as many OA questions are based on pure logic and not on any core DSA concept. Some companies tend to ask extremely hard OA questions, so I’d recommend trying later questions also, and to at least have some knowledge about advanced data structures used in competitive programming. For example, the 2nd question of the HILTI OA was based on advanced data structures for many candidates, and the BNY OA was like a CF contest only (read Siddhesh Pandey’s experience for BNY). 2. Use a language you are comfortable with (preferably the same language used for contests) and have a good grasp on the syntax and inbuilt libraries and data structures for a particular language. Examples would include STL for C++, collections for python and java etc. You should mainly know how to sort, how to use arrays/vectors (depending on your language), HashMaps and HashSets. 3. Read the complexity guide on codeforces, to know what time complexity is expected based on constraints on data. This helps in OAs, contests and problem solving in general. Interview Tips 1. Before going into the interview, research about the company, their goals, their values etc. A good source for this is the Pre Placement Talk conducted by the company, so always pay attention to that. You can also research on the Company’s website. You can incorporate this knowledge into your HR question responses, or ask them questions about it if they allow (usually most interviews ask if we have any questions for them - this is a good chance to show your genuine interest in the company.) 2. During interviews, it’s essential to communicate your thought process clearly. Speaking out loud while solving problems not only helps interviewers follow your logic but also gives them the opportunity to provide hints if you're heading in the wrong direction. It’s equally important to mention edge cases , as it shows your thorough approach to tackling challenges. But always start basic and then work on edge cases. For open ended questions such as design questions, always follow up with the interviewer about requirements. 3. Do some mock interviews with peers or seniors, ask them for feedback on your performance, and use it to improve yourself.",

At every step we have to optimally choose between one of the resources. At every step capacity of chosen resource gets reduced by 2 and that of the unchosen resource increases by 1 so you can only choose a resource with capacity greater than 1. Repeat this until one of the power stations capacity becomes zero. Return the number of steps required if we use the resources optimally. Sample input: 5, 3 Output: 6 It is solved by greedy approach by choosing the greater number at each step I passed 9/10 test cases ( I missed out on one basic condition :) though it was simple so please make sure you read the entire question carefully ) 2. Most similar string for a given query: Given a list of strings and a query string, we have to find the string from the list which is most similar or closest to the given query string. To do so we have to calculate the Levenshtein distance ( minimum number of insert a character/delete character / replace character - operations to be performed on a string to convert the string to the given query). Return the word with lowest Levenshtein distance. If two words have the same Levenshtein distance, then the lexicographically smaller word is the answer. Finding the Levenshtein distance is a well known DP problem - Edit distance I passed all test cases 3. If two pages contain same number of blacklinks then arrange them in order of their index in the input array. Output will be a list of strings. Myself Prashik Manwar, currently pursuing B.Tech in Electronics Engineering from VJTI. My core domain of interest lies in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Analytics & NLP. I have worked on several projects based on these domains – I developed a RAG based Multi-lingual PDF Q&A system (chatbot) using LangChain, Ollama & ChromaDB which allows the user to upload a PDF and ask questions related to it in natural language. This allows the user to take necessary actions on time and prevent the occurrence of the disease. So, that was a brief introduction about me. Thankyou.” Questions about Project - Multi-Lingual PDF Q&A System ❖ What is RAG? Answer – Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a concept by which we develop or train an AI agent/chatbot only using the data which we have. This ensures that the agent/chatbot answers the questions based only on the data which we provide and not any other data. This greatly reduces the chances of hallucinations and ensures responses relevant to our data only. ❖ Why did you use ChromaDB specifically? Answer – I used ChromaDB because the dataset (pdfs) which I had contained both images and text. So in order to ensure that the relevant text is extracted from the images as well (which is one of the unique features of ChromaDB), I used ChromaDB. I could have used FAISS also but it is a preferred option when we have data largely in form of text. ❖ What are embeddings and how are they created...what did you use to create those embeddings and where are they stored? Answer – I said, “Embeddings are nothing but a vector/numerical representation of the text. I am not quite sure about how exactly they are created, but I used nomic-embed-text to create them. I used Ollama’s LLM (“nomic-embed-text”) to create them. These embeddings are stored in ChromaDB vector database along with their respective chunk.” ❖ What is semantic search and multi-query retrieval? Answer – In RAG, I used Ollama to create multiple queries which were similar to the user’s original query. Then, I used multi-query retriever to retrieve the information from the vector database. The multi-query retriever takes the different variations of the user query as input, converts them into embeddings and searches in the vector database for the embeddings which nearly match to these queries. This is called semantic search. ❖ What is document chunking? Answer – Document chunking means dividing the extracted text into various parts or chunks. While document chunking, I also ensured that chunk overlap is taking place. ❖ Tesseract is a very old technology...why did you use it even if you had other alternatives for that? Answer – I used Tesseract because I found it the most accurate in my case. It was giving satisfactory results. ❖ If you want to host your chatbot online, how would you handle the large traffic of users? Answer – I would use haystack. Haystack is a python framework which provides various libraries to deploy production ready chatbots. ❖ What is the value of DPI that you set to extract text from scanned copies? Answer – In range of 300-400 ❖ How did you host Ollama on Google Colab...you must have done something like chat.invoke() ?? Answer – I installed Ollama in Google Colab using “!pip install” command and used in inbuilt colab kernel to operate it. ❖ What are the different parameters available for tuning a chatbot? Answer – Actually there are many, but I told them only about temperature – It is a parameter used to make a chatbot more creative or direct. If the temperature is low, the chatbot will give straight-forward answers & if it is high, the chatbot will give more creative responses. Questions about Project - E-Commerce Sales Insights Dashboard ❖ What is the difference between dimension and measure in PowerBI? I gave a partially correct answer: Dimension – They are the number of rows and columns in the dataset –> Wrong! (Dimension is a data modelling term used to classify the type of information a column. They provide descriptive context (who, what, where, when) of the dataset. Eg. Product Name, City, Date, Customer Name.) Measure – It is something which we calculate by applying DAX formulae to a numerical column. -> Right! ❖ What is the significance of drill-down slicers in your project? Answer – I used them to visualize sales data quarterly as well as for a particular state. Questions about Project - PrevaMed Healthcare Analytics Platform ❖ Which machine learning algorithm have you used (mostly) to predict the occurrence of diseases? Answer – Kaggle ❖ What was the most important performance metric in this project and why do you consider it the most important? Answer – “In this project, I considered recall to be the most important. I worked with one of my teammates to develop and deploy the ML models and the other 2 members developed the front-end of the website and focused on overall integration of ML models and website. The AI industry is currently booming and many people are getting hired for AI related roles. AI is like a new electricity - it is powering every industry’s growth. Personally, I feel that people should learn and adopt to this new technology. This does not mean that we must completely rely on AI to code and solve every problem. How would you allocate the tasks to everyone and ensure that it gets completed within the deadline? First of all, I would get to know about my teammates well, their strengths, weaknesses and their proficiency in any one field. For e.g. as a team leader of my team at Hacksagon, I allocated tasks to each one of my teammates based on their skill-sets (like someone who is good English speaking was given the introduction and explanation of the problem statement, I was able to explain the entire workflow and handle ML model development of the project clearly whereas other 2 were good at web dev part so they designed the frontend). 3) What all did you learn in the last 1 year? Also tell the things you learnt which are not mentioned in your resume. In the past one year, I learnt about implementing RAG systems, designing Power BI dashboards, exploring IoT and everything that is mentioned in my resume. Other than that, I have also been active in physical activities like football and skating. I also did start learning Japanese but it did not interest me much so I discontinued it. 4) Puzzle: You have 8 similar looking balls. One of them is of higher weight than others. You have a weighing scale (taraju). In how many minimum number of iterations would you be able to find the heavier ball? Consider 1 iteration as weighing once. Bruteforce answer – 3. Optimal answer - 2. You can do this by pen and paper by dividing the 8 balls into 2 groups – Grp A (6 balls) and Grp B (2 balls). If we weigh Grp B and the weight is uneven, we have found the heavier ball in 1st iteration. If we want to weigh Grp A, we again divide it into Grp A1 (3 balls) and Grp A2 (3 balls) and put them on the scale. If one of the Grp is heavier (say A1) then we will again divide A1 into 2 groups (2 balls and 1 ball). This way we have found the heavier ball in 2 iterations only. 5) What do you know about Mahindra Finance? Mahindra Finance is a NBFC. It currently holds nearly 34% market share in Tier 2 & 3 cities and holds good reputation and trust in these areas. The organization provides various loan facilities like education loan, vehicle loan, home loan, etc. to its customers from varied backgrounds. It has also taken significant steps towards sustainability ensuring environment protection. Also, the company is continuously working on developing scalable and user-friendly solutions for its customers. 6) Do you have any questions? I asked the interviewer about his role in the company. Thank you for giving me this opportunity.” (You can say this before the beginning and after the end of any interview.) Then we were allowed to go for lunch. We were told that the results were going to be announced the next day (30th Nov). But the results were not announced that day and also the day after (1st Dec). On 2nd Dec, 2025 I was going back to my hostel room after giving first exam of ESE. My phone was on silent and kept in my bag. Upon reaching the entrance of the hostel, one of my friends came towards me shouting, “Bhava! Jhala na Mahindra!”. I exclaimed, “Kaay mhantos!” I hastily took my mobile out of my bag and the first thing I noticed was 5 missed calls from my friends. Mostly, the people who want to get an internship offer start preparing early from Sem 4. I honestly never thought of that and focused more on improving my CGPA. Actually, I was more focused on placement season in the long term. But as companies started to come for internships in Sem 5, I told myself, “Try toh karke dekhte hai.” From starting till the end of Sem 5, I tried and tried again for getting internships. My journey started by approaching CoE at VJTI as they have a place for everybody to contribute to their projects and work as an intern there. Then followed the interviews of Texas Instruments, Citi Bank and Axis Bank. Obviously, I failed in them but learnt something valuable from each one of them, getting better and gaining confidence after every interview. After failing 5 interviews back-to-back, finally, Mahindra Finance had a place for me! Many people (even my seniors) used to say that placements and internships are 30% hardwork and 70% luck (Yeah, they even told the percentages!). They even told me to not expect an on-campus internship offer. Of course, luck plays an important role, but I think that wasn’t so much applicable in my case. So, you will have setbacks and failures during internship and placement season. At one point of time, you may think that all the hard work that you did means nothing (as it happened to me after my Axis Bank interview), but remember that every second you spend doing a project of your own and the countless nights that you spend learning a new skill, will never go to waste. Load Balancer (25 min): You are given n servers such that the ith server is active in between [ai, bi). You are also given k tasks such that tasks[i] gives the time when the current task will require a server. You have to calculate the minimum waiting time for each task to get a server of say that the task cannot be completed. Ex: servers = {{2, 3}, {5, 10}, {12, 13}, {15, 25}} tasks = {1, 7, 30, 4} answer = {1, 0, -1, 1} Explanation: For task 1 it takes one unit time to get server {2, 3}. Print the answer modulo 10e9 + 7. Ex: For k = 3, the possible strings are 0, 00, 111, 000, … Queries = {{1, 3}}, Answer = 4. Sol: I decided to follow a recursive approach, and generate all the strings of size (max of the query). Then used memorization to make it efficient. Now dp[i] contains the string of length i using the given rules. The using prefix sum we can calculate the answer efficiently. Q3. Max Sum (35 min): You are given a matrix of size 10 * 10 where the elements can be positive or negative. You are given a number n, now you need to find the sum of elements of matrix such that their indices are part of the array of size n. Ex: arr = {1, 2, 3, 6} Then we have the sum of elements as matrix [1][2] + matrix [2][3] + matrix [3][6]. In short, we have to find an arrangement of the arr to have the maximum sum of (n-1) elements. We don’t need to return the arr, just the max sum that can be formed. Sol: I can start with the first element from any row. Then I can select any number from that row, let’s say i, j. Then the row of my next element would be j. Hence, I used recursive 2d dp approach to solve the problem. dp[i][n] represent the max sum when we have to select n elements starting from ith row. Given an array server and an integer expected_load, find the minimum number of servers that must be chosen such that the total sum of requests served by all the chosen servers is exactly equal to the expected_load. If there is no combination of servers that can serve exactly expected_load requests, report -1 as the answer Example: n = 4, servers = [1, 1, 2, 4], expected_load = 3 output: 2 it is optimal to choose server[0] and server[2] or server[1] and server[2] My Approach: I took around 7-8 mins to correctly submit it and passed all the test cases. On carefully reading the long question for 2 times, i understood it was a very easy greedy question So I first sort the server array in ascending order and then start iterating from the end of the server array. Used these conditions if(expected_cost>= server[i]) expected_cost-=server[i] countOfServers++ if(expected_cost==0) return countOfServers Question 2 (Easy Difficulty) Given an array, reduce the array to a single element In each operation, pick two indices i and j (where i != j ) and append the value of a[i] + a[j] to the array delete a[i] and a[j] from the array The cost of each operation is a[i] + a[j]. Find the minimum possible cost to reduce the array example array: [25, 10, 20] pick 10 and 20, cost = 30, array = [25,30] pick 25 and 30, cost = 55 array = [55] totalCost = 30 + 55 = 85 My Approach Solved this in 7-8 mins and passed all test cases. Used priority queue to choose & delete 2 smallest elements and inserted their sum to the priority queue. It included multiple sections. Each section had a corresponding timer. You cannot submit answers to any questions of that section if its timer runs out. You can attempt the sections themselves in any order. Section 1 (30 mins) 1. In the first question, we are provided with an array of points (i and j) values and we had to find the sum of the pairwise distance between all of the points. The distance formula was provided and it was |Xi - Yi| + |Xj - Yj|. This question was clearly meant to be solved in O(n2) time so I implemented that solution and it passed 11/12 test cases. After observing the failed test case I realized I had to calculate modulo of the answer with either 109 + 7 or 109 + 9. So I tried the first value and it passed so I did not check it with the other value. 2. We have coordinates of the starting and destination points in a 2D plane. We also have a list of pairs of points where each pair represents a straight line that passes through that pair of points. The task was to find the minimum euclidean distance of the path from start to destination point without crossing over any of the lines. However, you can pass through the endpoints of the line. For example, The starting point is (0,0) destination point is (3,0) and there is a line passing through (1,0) and (2,1) so the shortest path would (0,0) -> (1,0) -> (3,0) with distance 3. I would like to share you my interview experience for Goldman Sachs Internship opportunity (summer analyst).\nI hope my experience is going to help you prepare better for internship and FTE (full time employment). My interview was a little different from others, It might not be the case with you!\nThere were 3 interview rounds and Online assessment. I will share as much as I remember.\n\n2 Online Assesment (30 mins)\nOnline asssesment had 4 sections, here I am listing them in order. Everyone had the same questions in all sections in OA :).\n\n2.1 Coding section\nIt had two problems.\n2.1.1 Maximum sum submatrix of size k x k\nFootball ground is represented by a matrix and each player had a skill on the ground, we had to find a square part of the ground with side k which had highest average skill. This is a matrix problem in 2D, refer this maximum sum submatrix.\nSee the above example, n = 4. if k = 1 then 10.00 will be the answer. if k = 2, 28/4 = 7.00 will be the answer (top right corner 2 x 2 matrix). answer has to be rounded of to two decimal places. I don’t remember if it was told that skill cannot be negative.\nI was able to pass all the test cases 11/11. I wrote the source code in python (I use both c++ and python). question was medium level according to me. It required a thorough understanding of kadane’s algorithm and its appplication in 2D array.\nIt could have been solved by using the concept of prefix sum matrix. and then going through all the submatrix of size k x k to find maximum sum submatrix. refer to this prefix sum matrix. It’s time complexity will be O(n2) (equivalent to time for taking matrix input).\nI would suggest you to solve the problem using this approach because concept of prefix sum matrix can be used to solve many matrix problems.\n\n2.1.2 catch the thief\nThis problem was not similar to standard problems. No one could completely solve it because of time constraint.\nWe were given a threshold(thief’s skill and bike power) as the power of the thief. We were given bikes array and skills array of guards and had to find all combinations of them so that each of the guards have skill greater than or equal to that of theif.\ninput: theif skill = 2, theif bike power = 4, guards skill array = [2, 1, 3], guards bike array = [4, 3, 6]\noutput: 0\nIn the above example there will be zero combinations because guard with 1 skill doesn’t find a bike so that their power crosses the threshold.\ninput: theif skill = 2, theif bike power = 4, guards skill array = [2, 4, 3], guards bike array = [4, 3, 6]\noutput: 4\nIn the above example only the combinations having (2, 3) as a pair will fail the test.\nDo you understand something from examples that I have taken? in both of them answer significantly depends on the smallest element in the array. By this I got the intution to solve this problem similar to what we do in counting inversions using merge sort. basically if (2, 4) satisfies the threshold then we can say that any number greater than 2 in the first place will also satisfy the threshold.\nsort both arrays: skills = [2, 3, 4], bikes = [3, 4, 5]\nkeep a variables answer as = 1, start iterating from start of first array (you can do with second array) and find the point where the threshold is first satisfied (use binary search for better time complexity), in our case when we are at element 2 the first element in second array will be 4, multiply (n - isecond - ifirst) to the multiplier, where ifirst is the index of element in first array, isecond is the index that we found using binary search, (3 - 1 - 0) will be multiplied with the multiplier variable. basically we are finding all possible combinations for the first element in the array, subtracting ifirst is important because one of the possible pair will be taken by the previous element in the first array (all possible pairs of previous element will be subset of next element because next element is greater than previous. It is similar to what we do in permutations), (n - secondindex) is the number of elements that satisfy the combination. for the element 3, ifirst = 1, isecond = 0 so again (3 - 0 - 1) = 2 will be multiplied to the variable. for element 4 in the first array ifirst = 2, isecond = 0 so multiplier will be multiplied by (3 - 0 - 2) = 1. so finally the variable will be 4 which is the correct answer.\nin the first example the multiplier for element 1 will be multiplied with (3 - 0 - 3) = 0 and answer will become zero. binary search will result end pointer which is at 1 + possible index of the array. similarly for any such case the variable will become zero whenever we find a point where there are no possibilities.\nI was able to pass 7/12 test cases, actually I forgot to sort the second array and when I was modifying the code time ended. I don’t think so anyone solved this problem. I was very happy that I was able to intuitively solve the problem. question was medium level but it wasn’t DSA type instead it was CP type.\n\n2.2 Aptitude test: 40-45 mins\nIt had some 12 questions I guess and all of them were math baased JEE questions. You will require pen and paper to model the current position after each condition, Practice those questions because it was also there in morgan stanley test.\na short example:\n1) A is at left of D\n2) B is after D\n3) C is at the start.\nsteps: AD -> ADB -> CADB\n\n2.2.3 Probability with 2 boxes\nThis is also a standard type of aptitude question. 2 boxes will contain 2 types of colored boxes and probability of specific color ball has to be found following the given constraints. focus on the with or without replacement part. refer to Indiabix for aptitude questions.\n\n2.2.4 Probability involving infinite GP\nThere are types of questions which require infinite GP formula to be solved. they are involved in 2 player games. There was a similar question in test.\nthere are two players, player wins if he gets the tail for the first time. what is the probability that player 2 wins the game.\nso HT, HHHT, HHHHHT ... all will be the answers. therefore the answer will be S = (1/2)^2 + (1/2)^4 + (1/2)^6 ...\nso we need to use the formula of infinite GP. S = a / (1 - r)\nYou will get 1/3 as the answer.\n\nSummary\nI don’t think so you will be able to solve all the questions, just make sure you do not mark wrong answers at any cost because this section had negative marking -2 and +5 for positive answer. a wrong answer can be a -7 for you wasting your +5 time and causing you -2.\n\n2.3 HR essay questions; 15 mins\nI will not elaborate a lot about this section it had two HR questions.\n- Your biggest achievement\n- Given a situation(a member is not devoted to his work) in your team, what will you do?\nTry to keep those answers as gentle as possible. The aptitude section consisted of 10 MCQs and we were given 20 minutes. I was not able to solve all the 10 questions and since there was no negative marking, I decided to attempt every question. The debugging section was relatively easier and mainly consisted of questions containing some syntactic and semantic errors. We were given 15 minutes to solve 7 debugging questions. I was able to do 6 but ran out of time. The coding round consisted of 3 questions. One question was based on level order traversal of binary tree and the other two were dynamic programming based. Question 1: In a family hierarchy, there are N family members. Each member has at most two children. Some members may have no children. Each member has a fixed annual income. The head of the family who is at the top of the hierarchy wants to know how much extra money would be required to make the total annual income of each generation of the family equal. Each level of the hierarchy is considered as a generation. The extra money is calculated as the positive value or 0 which should be added to the total income of each generation the same in all generations. The total income of a generation is the sum of income of all the members of the same generation. If a family is not earning then his income is denoted by -1 and this -1 will not get added in the total income of the generation. A simple level order traversal will do. I was able to clear all the test cases. I’m not able to recollect the other 2 questions but they were dynamic programming based questions. I could clear only half of the test cases in both these questions. They gave us an overview of the hackathon, what was expected from our side, timeline, etc. After the meet, we had a team discussion and decided on the tech-stack that we were going to use and then we started developing our project the next day. We were required to give daily updates to the mentor regarding the project, what all things you had accomplished in the last 24 hours, what are the things that you plan on accomplishing in the next 24 hours and so on. Stay as active as you can on the discord server or whatever mode of communication you decide to use. This shows that you have immersed yourself in the project and ultimately generates an impression on the mentor as well. Ask for guidance wherever required, the mentors will always help you. I joined the Zoom meeting 10 minutes prior and then was redirected to a breakout room where my interviewer arrived shortly afterwards. I was asked to introduce myself. You’ll be asked to introduce yourself in every interview round. Prepare a pretty solid introduction beforehand and mention some of the highlights of your resume in the introduction itself. I was then given a situation. Given a number of tasks (string) , what would be the data structure of your choice for storing these tasks? I first asked him if the number of tasks are fixed, to which he replied yes. Since we have a definite number of tasks with us, I said that I would use an array of strings for storing individual tasks. I was then told that there could be duplicate tasks present in the input, how would you keep track of the frequency of each task. I gave him two answers. First one being, instead of maintaining an array of strings, we could keep an array of pairs, where the first entity of the pair would represent the task and the second entity would represent its frequency. This would be disadvantageous as we would need to iterate through the entire array and find out if a particular task exists so as to increase its frequency along and there are several other drawbacks of having a fixed size array. To overcome this, we can use an unordered map and leverage its constant search time complexity to increase the frequency of tasks. He seemed satisfied with my answer and then we moved on to the next question. Given 10 teams numbered from 1 to 10, print the match schedule of all the teams such that the following conditions are satisfied. Only 1 match is scheduled in a day. No team is allowed to play on two consecutive days. If team A plays against team B on one particular day, they cannot play against each other on any other day. I verbally explained my approach. I was then asked to write the code. Basically, you need to keep a track of the teams that have already played against each other and the teams that have played on the previous day. To keep a track of the teams that have played on any given day, I used an unordered map where the integer key (day) is mapped to a pair representing the team that has played on that day. I used the set data structure where every element of the set was a vector of size 2 containing the teams that have played against each other (you can also use a 2D array of size 10x10 for this purpose). After finding a pair of teams that satisfies the given condition, map the current day to this pair, create a vector of size 2 and sort it and then finally store it in the set. Don’t stay silent for more than 7- 10 seconds, it creates a negative impact on the interviewer. Whatever you are writing in your text editor, simultaneously explain the logic to the interviewer. Drop comments wherever relevant, especially the code blocks that provide a critical insight into your code's functionality. I had inserted comments before loops, conditional statements and before performing any critical operation. As a result, when you are constantly adding and deleting lines of code while debugging, the interviewer will get a clear idea of the changes you make and their effects. Always ask clarifying questions to the interviewer, state all the aspects of the problem that you have understood and ask the interviewer to re-explain the parts that you haven’t understood. Always start-off by explaining the most natural approach towards the problem. Explain the drawbacks of the natural process and thereby state the techniques for eliminating the drawbacks. Unfortunately, the code did not give the desired output, I had dropped comments everywhere in my code to make it easier for the interviewer to understand what I had been doing. He gave me a hint and I made the best use of it but to no avail. I then provided a line by line explanation of the entire code and even highlighted the part of the code that should have taken care of the wrong output. I was then given 5 minutes to fix the code, I couldn’t think of anything at that point and started writing some redundant code. 5 minutes passed and then we moved on. Before moving on, he said that he only wanted to know my approach. I was made to choose between Databases and OOPs. I had a really strong grip on OOPs and hence chose OOPs. He then asked me some pretty standard OOPs questions like, difference between Overloading and Overriding, what is a virtual function, etc. He then asked me if I had any questions for him.   "content": "Goldman Sachs Summer Analyst Internship Naman Kothari, B.Tech IT 2021-24 Online Test - 13th August 2022 Students from all branches were allowed to sit for the test. The test was on HackerRank and was divided into four sections. It was a proctored test that required camera and audio permissions. Changing the tab would lead to being flagged. Each section had a separate timer which meant that you could not carry forward the time from any other section and you couldn’t navigate back to a section after submitting it. 4 Sections of Online test : Coding/Programming Questions : (30 mins) There were 2 coding questions of moderate difficulty. Maximum sum square sub-matrix of a given size. The question was not direct it had a long story. There is a football player who wants to score a goal in a square sub-region of the ground. The ground is represented by an n*n 2-d matrix where each element is positive and the value at index(i,j) denotes the score the player gets if the goal is scored at that location. The square region should be of size k*k. Find the square sub-matrix where the player should score a goal to get the maximum average score, where the average is calculated by finding the sum of elements in the square matrix divided by a number of elements in that square matrix. Based on the constraints given, a brute force solution passed all the test cases here. The second question was not standard. Again, it was given in the form of a long story. Given, an array bike where the element at index I, denotes the power of bike[i]. Also, an array of riders is given, where riders[i] denote the riding capacity of the ith rider. Find how the bikes should be allocated to the riders so that the product of bike[i]*rider[j] for every (bike, rider) pair should be greater than a given threshold value. We had to find all possible combinations. Sample Input : bike = [3,2,4] & rider = [7,3,5] threshold k= 8 Output: 4 Here, for 3 bikes and 3 riders, there can be 6 different combinations, but out of these, only 4 combinations will satisfy the given condition. (bike1,rider1) , (bike2,rider2), (bike3,rider3)  → (3*7=21) , (2*3=6) , (4*5=20) The wrong combination as 2nd pair has product 6 which is less than 8 (bike1,rider1) , (bike2,rider3) , (bike3,rider2) → (3*7=21) , (2*5=10) , (4*3=12) The valid combination as all pairs have a product greater than 8. Similarly, 3 more valid combinations exist. Aptitude Questions : (45 mins) 12 Maths-based MCQ questions with +5 and -2 marking schemes were given. It had probability, permutation, and combination, A.P., G.P., matrices, etc. I do not recollect the questions. HR Essay Section : (15 mins) 2 questions were given which were HR-based (Limit 200 Words Per Answer) 1) Describe an incident when you felt that your passion helped you achieve a goal. 2) You and your classmate have been working hard on a challenging team project. You are on track to complete the project on time, but there is still a lot of work to be done, your classmate has a personal situation that requires him to stop working on the project. What would you do in this situation? CS Fundamentals Section : (20 mins) 7 CS-related MCQ questions with +5 and -2 marking schemes. It had OS, OOPs, DBMS, CN, and a few debugging/output-related questions. The questions were fairly easy or moderate, you only needed to worry about the time crunch. Debugging questions are a bit tricky, so solve them carefully. The shortlisted candidates were announced 2 days before the interviews. You could practice questions from here during the period between online assessments and interviews. Revise all the CS Fundamentals during this phase and go through all the previously asked questions from different interview experiences. Also, go through puzzles from here I collected some questions from the interview experiences of our seniors from CoC and revised them thoroughly. OnCampus Interviews - 16th August 2022 All interviews are held on the same day. 36 students were shortlisted for the interviews. The interviews were held offline, on campus. There were 2 or 3 rounds of interviews all were technical rounds depending on the candidate’s performance. Round 1: Technical Interview (30 mins) The interview started with the standard question “Tell me about yourself”. Have some pointers ready in your mind to answer this question as this part is very important. Based on your introduction, the interviewer might ask you certain questions. In my introduction, I highlighted hackathons and social good projects. And as I expected I was asked some questions on the same. One of my projects was discussed for about 5-10 mins. I mentioned the purpose of the project, what problems it solved, some notable features, and highlights of the tech stack used. Then the interviewer asked me to explain to her a data structure of my choice. This was an open-ended question so try to add some things which make your answer special and stand out. I explained stacks using an example of books. Then she asked me about the different functions of stacks. This time I mentioned push(), pop(), top(), and I deliberately mentioned getmin() also as a custom function. This played well and she asked me to explain getmin(). I first told her an approach on how I will maintain a minimum while pushing and told her the problems that will occur if we use this method directly then, I mentioned another method. The method I mentioned was this one. The interviewer seemed very much satisfied with the point that I didn’t do only the bare minimum as I would have only mentioned standard operations, but I would suggest you explain complex use cases also for the same. Another question was about Binary Search Tree. She told me to explain Binary search Trees first. I gave her a gist on the same and some operations. Then she came up with this question. Key Takeaways from this round:- Think loud, and always communicate your approach to the interviewer continuously. For open-ended questions try to tell something extra as the interviewer knows the bare minimum already. This could prove to be a distinguishing point in such cases. I answered him that it is an example of NoSql databases, but I am not familiar with that. I also mentioned some advantages of NoSql Databases as a response to a previous question. Then he moved to an open-ended DSA Problem: Merge 2 sorted Arrays (He didn’t mention anything about space and time but through the discussion, I was able to conclude that he was interested in space optimization. Though he asked me for the most optimized solution, I advise you to discuss different approaches as it shows your thinking process. On every approach, he encouraged me to optimize it more, and finally, I gave him a very unique method to solve the problem. I answered a total of 4 different approaches. Approach 1 - Similar to merge sort Approach 2 - 2 Pointer Approach Approach 3 - Similar to Insertion Sort involving 2 Pointers Approach 4 - Gap Method After this question, he told me that he was done with his questions and asked me if I had any questions for him. I enquired about the culture at Goldman Sachs. Key Takeaways from this round:- The gap method really worked out for me on this question as it was not all intuitive but luckily I knew that method and I mentioned it. So, if you encounter any such questions with multiple approaches in an interview then always discuss multiple approaches for the same. The interviewer also gave a remark that the purpose of such questions is not to test whether you can solve it or not but to examine how deeply you can think and how diversly you can come up with different approaches for a specific problem. You will get a basic idea of what kind of questions you will be asked and what their domain can be. Different questions about your projects can also be asked. Lastly, it’s okay to be nervous. The ground is represented by a n*n 2-d matrix where each element is positive and value at index(i,j) denotes the score the player gets if goal is scored at that location. The square region should be of size k*k. Find the square sub-matrix where the player should score a goal to get the maximum average score, where the average is calculated by finding the sum of elements in square matrix divided by number of elements in that square matrix. Also, an array of riders is given, where riders[i] denotes the riding capacity of the ith rider. Find how should the bikes be allocated to the riders, so that the product of bike[i]*rider[j] for every (bike,rider) pair should be greater than a given threshold value. We had to find all possible combinations. Sample Input: bike = [3,2,4] & rider = [7,3,5] threshold k= 8. Output: 4. Here, for 3 bikes and 3 riders, there can be 6 different combinations, but out of these, only 4 combinations will satisfy the given condition. (bike1,rider1), (bike2,rider2), (bike3,rider3) -> (3*7=21), (2*3=6), (4*5=20). Wrong combination as 2nd pair has product 6 which is less than 8. (bike1,rider1), (bike2,rider3), (bike3,rider2) -> (3*7=21), (2*5=10), (4*3=12). Valid combination as all pairs have product greater than 8. Similarly, 3 more valid combinations exist. There was nothing tricky; we just had to implement what was asked. The three questions were as follows: 1. Three-digit integer problem: Given a three-digit integer N and an integer K, you can perform at most K increments (by +1) on any of the digits so that N becomes the maximum possible number. Example: If N = 285 and K = 20, you can easily increase every digit to 9. So the answer will be 999 (as the total operations required are (9–2) + (9–8) + (9–5) = 12 ≤ 20). 2. Video-based question: The problem was explained in the video with a sample input/output. We had to return true if, at the end, the boy was able to make a complete rectangle following the sequence. Otherwise, return false. 3. Levenshtein distance between two strings is defined as the minimum number of edits required to obtain one string from the other. The cat can walk up/down/left/right by 1 step or jump 2 steps (in the same direction) within the maze. One example maze: (N=4, M=3) GCS GSG EGG GGG The minimum answer is 2 minutes. First, go left, then jump down. The given question did not provide all the information needed to solve it. It is quite normal to encounter such a scenario in an interview. The interviewer tests your understanding quotient of the given problem statement and expects the interviewee to ask questions in order to unravel the underlying details and corner cases. For example, I asked why the unit for the final answer was ‘minutes’. He answered that both a step and a jump require the same amount of time, i.e. 1 minute. Then I asked if it was guaranteed that a solution always exists. After getting a clearer idea of the problem statement, discuss a brute force solution so that you can ensure that you have understood the question. Discuss aspects such as time and space complexity along with each solution you provide. Optimize your solution as much as possible. Think out loud. I provided a solution using Breadth First Search (BFS). After I explained my approach I was asked to code the same on the shared Google Doc. It is recommended to practice writing code without an IDE so that you don't face any problems with the time constraint. Clean code and appropriate naming of functions and variables is something that I would personally recommend. Follow up question: What if the cat could jump at most J times? We discussed a few approaches in the remaining 5-10 minutes of the interview. She explained the problem as follows - There is an introverted child who wants to sit on a bench. Since he was an introvert, he preferred to sit as far as possible from any other child. As we can see, she intentionally left out vital details such as input and output. Similar to the previous round, I asked questions to gather more information regarding the problem statement. After discussing the details, the problem statement then looked as follows - Given a binary array (consisting of only 0’s and 1’s), where 0 represented a vacant seat and 1 represented an occupied seat, the task was to find the index of any vacant seat for the introverted child such that the chosen indexed seat is as far as possible from the occupied seats. Provide time and space complexities of your solution at the end. Question 2: Similar binary trees Given two binary trees, answer whether they are similar or not. Two trees are called similar if one of them can be obtained from the other by a series of flips, i.e. by swapping left and right children of a number of nodes. Any number of nodes at any level can have their children swapped. Two empty trees are similar. For example, the following two trees are similar with the following sub-trees flipped: 2 and 3, NULL and 6, 7 and 8. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/tree-isomorphism-problem/ Results There were no HR rounds or any other interviews conducted after the 2 technical rounds. It has three categories: easy, medium, and hard from which I completed 35%, 61%, and 41%, respectively. Maximum priority should be given to the medium section as questions are most likely to be of that level of difficulty. We are given powers of 2 resources A & B. To execute the software, you must choose one resource from a possible two resources each second. The resource power should be larger than 1 at the moment of choosing. The strength of the chosen resource is reduced by two each second, while the power of the unselected resource is increased by one. When at least one resource is powered down, the programme terminates. Determine how long your software can run for if you choose your resources wisely. Input: int A,B Output: Maximum time for which software runs. Function to Complete: int PowerLimit(int A, int B) { } Approach: For every iteration the power of a resource which is used is decremented by 2 and the power of the unused resource is incremented by 1, hence to run it for maximum amount of time we need to choose the resource having the greater power until any of the resource is depleted. Solution Verdict: All Test cases passed. 2. Auto suggest Difficulty: Medium Topic: DP We are given a vector of strings containing N words and a query word S. We need to auto-suggest the best word from the vector that is closest to S. For comparing the distance between the word from the vector and the query word S we are given a parameter called Levenshtein distance. And if two words have the same Levenshtein distance, then priority is given to the Lexicographically smaller word. Levenshtein Distance is defined as the minimum number of edits required to convert one string to the other. Operations allowed for the edit are insertions,deletions,replacement. Exactly similar to Edit Distance (LeetCode) https://leetcode.com/problems/edit-distance/ Input: vector<string> words string S Output: Closest word from the vector words. Function to Complete: string solve(vector<string> words, string S) { } Approach: This was a straightforward question for me because I had already solved the edit distance problem from leetcode previously. So I just called the editDistance function for every word from the given vector. The word which returns the least distance is our answer. Solution Verdict: All Test cases passed. 3. Note: Backlinks are the links from other web pages to a web page. Input: vector<string> webPage vector<int> backlinks Output: Backlink sorted vector of titles of web pages. B.Tech Computer Engineering 2022-26 Before the Mid-Semester Tests, TPO sent us an email about the recruitment drive by Morgan Stanley. Interview: The interview with Morgan Stanley was conducted online on Zoom and started at 8 AM. Round 1: My interview was scheduled for 10 AM, and there were two panelists for the first round. They began by introducing themselves and then asked me to introduce myself. ● The first question was a DSA problem involving reversing an array using an extra array. I provided a solution with a time complexity of O(n/2). ● The second question was to find the smallest positive number in an array. I explained both the O(n) approach for an unsorted array and the O(log n) approach if the array was sorted. They seemed satisfied with my answers. For both questions they asked to code it in a notepad or gdocs. ● Next, they asked me about my third project, which involved ML. I explained that I collaborated with a teammate proficient in ML, read the documentation, and implemented the backend using FastAPI. They asked why I chose FastAPI over alternatives. I explained that Node.js wasn’t convenient for ML integration due to a lack of frameworks, and I had narrowed my choices to FastAPI and Flask as Python has better compatibility with ML and later chose FastAPI. ● They then moved on to DBMS-related questions: ○ What is SQL and NoSQL? Their full forms and differences? ○ Structured vs. Unstructured data. ○ Platforms offering SQL and NoSQL services. ○ Whether structured data can be stored in NoSQL. ○ Examples of structured and unstructured data. ● The discussion shifted to backend implementation. I explained routing in the backend, and how the database connections work. They asked about common HTTP request protocols so I listed common HTTP request methods: GET, PUT, POST, DELETE. They asked if there were more, and I mentioned PATCH but wasn’t sure about others. ● One question was whether replacing all PUT routes with POST would work. I explained that it would, with some debugging, as the underlying logic could be adjusted, but readability and best practices would be compromised. ● They asked if I knew about idempotence. I wasn’t familiar with the term, so they explained it and then asked which HTTP methods were idempotent. I gave a partially correct answer. ● For the next DSA question, they asked me to implement prime factorization using recursion. My initial implementation failed on a test case, but I debugged it, and it worked. I mentioned the time complexity was logarithmic. They also asked me to code it. ● They then asked about deadlock. I explained it using a cyclic wait diagram and suggested the Banker's Algorithm and Semaphores as a solution. They asked how Banker’s Algorithm works. Next they asked how to handle a deadlock once it has occurred, and I explained options like killing processes or ignoring it, as modern OS often do. ● The final question involved SQL. They gave me two tables and asked for a query to find the student with the highest marks in every subjects. My initial solution displayed only the name of the topper in every subjects. Out of 9 candidates, 8 were selected, and I was fortunate to be among them. Interview Preparation Tips 1. Know every detail on your resume. Use online tools and check the resume’s ATS score. 2. If the value of units becomes surplus after stock replenishment and the value of units out of stock left after stock replenishment is same then output the pair which is still needs to be replenished. Difficulty: Medium Approach: So basically we had to sort the array and find the minimum absolute difference between positive & negative elements. If there is a tie then select the one which has a negative difference. Input: 6 18 -28 -50 -60 58 30 Output: 60 58 Explanation: The pair of outlets whose out of stock units can be nearly replenished from the other outlet are {outlet1,outlet5} i.e. (-28, 30) and (outlet3, outlet4) i.e. (-60, 58). But according to Note, we have to select that pair which still needs stock replenishment because we can't afford to leave the two units surplus (i.e. -28+30= 2) for the outlet because of limited stock. A2: Create an adjacency list and perform traversal using it. I implemented the first approach but due to time constraints I was not able to solve it completely.
