Hours before PwC's online test, a new company made its entry to the on-campus internship drive, which no one had ever heard of. In comes Hilti Technology Solutions India Pvt. Ltd. based in Pune of the parent company - Hilti. Neither had anyone heard of Hilti nor HTSI. They didn't even have a website or a physical office and were visiting any campus in India for the first time, with VJTI being their beginning. We just knew that it is one of the few product-based companies that visit VJTI and offer a great stipend of 80K per month. 2 days later, when TPO sent out the October schedule, we were excited to see HTSI announcing their online test on October 1 with interviews scheduled for the next day. I had no clue what to prepare in particular. There were absolutely no past experiences found on this COC drive, GFG archives, or anywhere on Glassdoor. But I had no time to research the company as I had my interviews for Fiserv on October 1. I was hoping for the wee bit of luck to play its charm with Fiserv not announcing the results on the same day and hence allowing me to sit for HTSI interviews. And that did happen, Fiserv didn't announce their results till 4 days later and I stood a chance for HTSI. After 2 interview rejections, not being shortlisted for interviews with 5 companies, I thought the worst that could have happened, had happened. I only did what I could; do my processes and wait for the results to follow. After attending the Hilti PPT scheduled on October 1, 2021, I wanted to give my best for HTSI. Disclaimer: If you are in a hurry, skip to article 3. I wrote this experience as I would expect it from a senior - the background, about the company, the interviews, the preparation. 01 PREFACE H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A Platform: Microsoft Teams. Attendees: All final and third-year students with CPI 6 or above from all branches. The presentation was taken forward by the technical leads at HTSI and gave the students an overview of Hilti, their products, what is HTSI, and the internship program. About: Hilti is a multi-national company based in Liechtenstein that builds and markets products used in manufacturing and construction works, which includes hardware, services, and software - where HTSI came in. HTSI is the technology center for Hilti based in Pune, India that works on developing one of their major products - ON!Track Asset Management. What I appreciated a lot about the presentation was the HTSI brought in their software and HR team from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia who were going to shift to Pune to work onsite next year. They also shared their experience of working at Hilti Malaysia. 02 THE PPT H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A Some details that were shared regarding the internship program 03 ONLINE TEST H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A In order to implement the Windows screen switch shortcut (WIN + TAB), we need to use a Most Recently Used (MRU) strategy which brings the recently accessed window to the front. However, the question was quite long and many got confused while perceiving the question. Given a list of numbers indicating the window number and a number indicating the window number to be accessed, modify and return the list after applying the MRU strategy. 1 Coding question. Participants: All 290 third-year students who applied for HTSI were shortlisted for the online test. Platform: Mettl - audio, video, and screen proctored. Duration: 90 minutes. Questions: Example: input list - [5, 2, 3, 4, 1], window number to be accessed - 2 output list - [2, 5, 3, 4, 1] Here, as Google Chrome is being accessed at the moment, the next time we use WIN + TAB, it will appear at the front of the list. This was the easiest coding question I had solved in ages. I had to simply find the number and put it in front of the list. There were 10 test cases - 4 Basic, 4 Necessary, 2 Edge cases as listed on Mettl and I passed all of them. There were ample choices for the preferred programming language for the question; I had used C++ 17. There was a pool of questions and few students had slightly tougher questions. H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A 30 questions on Cognitive Ability (timed section - 30 minutes limit). These were basic logical reasoning questions with 7-8 mathematical reasoning questions towards the end. You can practice these on indiabix.com. This was the first section I had attempted and wanted to rush through it thinking that the coding section would be tough given the length of the question so I solved the last 4 questions haphazardly and submitted this section. 6 questions on Data Structures. These were some good questions on the usually asked interview questions such as implementing stack with queue and vice versa, also on merge sort, creating BST, and contiguous memory allocation of arrays. I was able to solve all the questions but stack and queue questions took some time to verify. 5 questions on Database Management Systems. Simple SQL queries and a really good question on the cardinality of relationships of tables in a database. 6 questions on Networking. Questions on the OSI model, transport layer were asked which are the most commonly asked topics in interviews. There was one question on IPv6 which I was not sure of. 7 questions on Object-Oriented Programming. Questions on composition, aggregation were asked based on OOD. Java questions were asked based on OOP. 6 questions on Operating Systems. Questions were asked on deadlock, threads, thrashing and there was one specific question on different methods that could be used to create a thread in Java which I fortunately knew. In a nutshell, all the sections were really easy. And from past experience, when the test is easy, time becomes a deciding factor. Hence, I submitted the test with 17 minutes left on the timer. The shortlist for the interview was declared the day after the online test on October 2 at 11 AM. Out of 290 students, only 30 were shortlisted for technical interviews that were scheduled from the first slot being at 4 PM on the same day to 9:15 PM at night being the last slot. Technical Interview (40 minutes) Situation - I and my peers had the objective of learning natural language processing and knew quite a bit of supervised learning and wanted to make a project in the same. I was the team lead and came up with the idea of predicting prices of cryptocurrencies using sentiment analysis of tweets. Task - We had to first acquire a dataset, study the techniques in various research papers that prove the correlation between cryptocurrency prices and narrative economics (I explained each term as I went on mentioning it). The project deliverables also needed to be decided and since we were all familiar with Django, we decided to run our price prediction model's backend on the same. Since live updates were decided to be shown on the frontend with a visualization of a candle-bar plot, we decided to use ReactJS for the frontend. Action - Here I explained the workflow that was decided, the dataset used, and the prior research that was referred to. Finally, I mentioned the result which was the accuracy of the model with the visualization of the prediction that was created, and all libraries and frameworks that were explored. My interview was scheduled for 5:30 PM. From the online test and the PPT, I had gotten a fair idea that Java will be tested for sure along with DBMS. So, I revised OOP, multithreading, 2 design patterns in Java along with several SQL queries to prepare for the interview. I joined the Microsoft Teams meeting at 5:28 PM and was cordially greeted by their HR from Malaysia who was really sweet and with him was an engineer at HTSI. I was assigned to a breakout room at 5:30 PM. There were 2 interviewers, the female interviewer had her camera off throughout the interview. They both greeted me and said they would introduce themselves first and I should then proceed with mine. The male interviewer had his camera on and was smiling more than me during my introduction. The questions began with my resume. I was asked to explain my latest project, which was CryptoFutureX. I was asked what was it all about and I made use of the STAR method (I had seen seniors mentioning it everywhere but didn't see an example for the same so mentioned it below). H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A 04 INTERVIEW 1 Do you know what is cryptocurrency? When did you first learn about blockchain? Why did you go with the Sentiment140 dataset? Did you use any database for your project? Is the VJCoin blockchain you mentioned based on proof-of-work or proof-of-stake? You need to set a size for the array first before storing these words in it. How will you get the size? Why not use the set data structure? What if the input is online (i.e., the input is a stream of characters), how will you reverse them? Do you know some method in Java that can make the work easy for you? The cross-questions were : I had mentioned VJCoin which I had first seen in our canteen and that helped me gain interest in the domain, but I was unable to answer the last question since I didn't know its implementation. Next, I was given a simple coding question - Find occurrences of 7 in all digits present in the array. Example - input = [7, 17, 20]; output = 2 I was asked to write the pseudocode for the same on a notepad. First I shared what I understood about the question, posed the above example in front of them and asked if this is correct and then proceeded to write the pseudocode and finally did a dry run of 2 examples. They were pleased with the solution and didn't ask any other questions on this. The second coding question was the reverse all the words in a string where the words are delimited by a period ('.'). This was again an easy one. I was given the example 'abc.def.xyz' which is to be reversed as 'xyz.def.abc'. Right away I gave the approach that I will store all the characters in a word till a period is encountered and store the string in an array. Then, I can reconstruct the string with the collected words. I was interrupted and asked: Here there was a discussion on the StringBuilder and String classes in Java. The use of 'split' method of String class. Then how I would do the same in Python (I think they asked me in Python too because my pseudocode was 'pythonic'). Then I was also asked about the mutability of strings in Java. What is dynamic vs. static binding in Java? How is polymorphism in Java different from C++? Always explain OOP concepts with a real-life example. The first query I mentioned was finding the highest salary from a table that excludes the highest salary. The second query used the TOP clause in SQL where the female interviewer tried to confuse me a lot regarding ordering the table twice but in the end, she was convinced with my answer. Finally, I asked the interviewers: I was glad the interview ended on a good note. I thanked both of them and exit the meeting. Then, I was told by the TPO CRs, who were coordinating with Hilti HR to be ready for the next round as students were being called on a rolling basis. A thing I had noticed during the interview was that sometimes both interviewers had their camera off and took some time in getting back with another question. Initially, I thought that there were uninterested in the interview as it was evening and they were working on Gandhi Jayanti but my friend told me they were probably adding remarks for me after each question to submit to HR. 16 students were shortlisted for the HR interview. My interview was scheduled for 6:20 PM and I wasn't told how long it would be. I am an avid learner and inquisitive about learning new things (he nodded his head at this point and started listening more attentively). It was this curiousity that led me to take up science after my school. Though I didn't have computer science as a subject in 11th and 12th, I got acquainted with C programming and later on learned C++ in 12th. Hence, I developed a fond interest in programming and wanted to pursue the same (there was a big smile on his face and I was glad that after all my interviews there was one interviewer who showed genuine interest). In my 2 years at VJTI, I have achieved a CGPA of 9.62 and have developed projects in domains of web development using Django & ReactJS, Android mobile application development using Kotlin, and machine learning. H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A 06 CONCLUSION H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A 07 THE PREP Data Structures & Algorithms Had to unlearn and re-learn DSA in C++ in semester 4 by slowly and steadily solving topic-wise data structures questions on GFG. Began with 450dsa.com in March and to date solved 208 questions. Tried out InterviewBit because everyone was doing it; not for me. Switched to LeetCode in July to start with Top Interview Questions. For DP, Stacks, Sliding Window (MUST), Heap - Aditya Verma. For Graphs - take U forward. Tips - Always revise the sorting algorithms, basic data structure questions because they are frequently asked in interviews such as quick sort, merge sort, stack using a queue, queue using stack, graph traversals, etc. Make notes for each topic that you cover. These could be on some pattern that you identified in such questions such as finding Kth order statistic in an array being related to a heap or some syntax that you find tough to remember such as the declaration of priority queue in C++. Don't hit and trial by submitting your code; it just wastes time. Rather do a dry run of example input and expected output. You won't be asking an interviewer to confirm your code multiple times. so develop the habit of verifying it twice and submitting it once. Sometimes you may be asked to write the driver code, data structure implementation along with the algorithm for the given question - in both online tests and interviews. Do practice writing driver code for linked list, tree, and graph questions. Object-Oriented Programming Always referred to this article from Edureka for quick revision. MUST DO - virtual functions (if you use C++), abstract classes vs. interfaces in Java. Do not ignore Java even if you don't use it as many companies use Java and ask MCQs in their online test on Java. Study Java OOP from Javatpoint. If you mention both C++ & Java in your resume, know their differences well. For low-level design questions, refer to https://crack-oop-system- design.herokuapp.com/. Tips - Don't just study the concepts, implement them in code as well. You may be asked to demonstrate these concepts in C++ or Java. Always back your explanation of OOP concepts with a real-life exmaple. H T S I | H I L T I T E C H N O L O G Y S O L U T I O N S I N D I A Operating Systems Religiously read Silberschatz-Galvin-Gagne. Later realized it was too much :) Simply watch the entire OS playlist of Gate Smashers and make notes! Can't go without GFG commonly asked questions. Tips - Virtual memory is extremely important along with process synchronization techniques such as mutex locks, semaphores. If you know Java, try to practice multithreading in Java. Multitasking vs. multiprogramming, processor vs. core, parallelism vs. concurrency, thread vs. process are common comparison questions so do them well. Database Management Systems Watched Sanchit Jain's playlist on DBMS. If beginner, practice SQL on HackerRank and then move to LeetCode. This covers all the important SQL queries. For indexing, refer to Abdul Bari's video in particular. Not much theory is asked except for ACID properties and normalization. For other theory questions, refer to GFG interview questions. Tips - If you have used a database in any of your projects, be well prepared to talk about the schema and queries done on the database. You should also be able to justify the choice of the database made for the project. Don't be worried about vendor-specific SQL clauses such as DENSE_RANK while practicing SQL queries. There are hundreds of SQL clauses and you are not supposed to know all. Computer Networks Study in brief about each layer of the OSI model, focus on network and transport layers. Study TCP, UDP, and the differences between them along with IP. Only if you have enough time, go through IP addressing from Gate Smashers, 3.1 to 3.13. Last Minute Notes on CN from GFG. System Design (rarely asked, but I was asked a lot on it in my Fiserv interview because of my experience in cloud) If you are really new, refer to sudoCODE's playlist for a System Design Primer. If you have prior exposure to some concepts of cloud, you can directly go to Gaurav Sen's playlist. Rooting for you!! 🎉",

Goldman Sachs came to our college to offer internships to Third Year students, irrespective of branch and pointer. They were offering 75k stipend per month. The company usually seeks to visit as the first company on other renowned campuses and hence it didn’t come to our college for some 2-3 years(as Morgan Stanley always visits us first) until this year. In their presentation which happened before the first round, they seemed to be looking for two roles majorly, one related to Mathematics and Analytics(they’ll ask you permutation and combination and mathematical puzzles to test you on this. Round 1: Online round 4:30 pm-5:30 pm : 15th October, 2018 People from all branches were welcome and there was no pointer restriction for giving the online test. It was held on Hackerrank for a duration of one hour which contained 8 MCQs with -3 negative marking and +10(EDIT: Corrected the marking scheme) I guess for each correct answer. There was a coding question as well for 35 points. MCQs were based on minimum spanning trees(if Tree 1 and Tree 2 and Tree 3 are joined what would be the new minimum cost), probability(expected number), hash table(complexity of building word ladder and related concepts) and graph. The type of questions were a bit unexpected, but that’s how it goes. You can never predict what kind of questions a company will ask. The single coding question was, given a grid containing addresses of houses such that the addresses were sorted in increasing order from west to east and north to south, find the coordinates(row, column) of a given address(pretty pretty basic, O(n^2) solution was getting accepted but I submitted an O(n) solution)). All branches had the same test. Results were declared at 11 PM at night and 25 people from various branches were shortlisted. EDIT: Got to know from other interns that some of them were asked DP based questions on palindromic string as the coding question. Round 2: Personal Interview 1 10:30 am: 16th October, 2018 My interview began with the standard “Tell me about yourself question”. She had printouts of my online test and she asked me how I had solved a particular MCQ(probability one)(This is why try for an optimal approach in the coding round if possible in the coding round, she kept glancing at my code and also read comments which I had written out of habit when solving. Also, always go through the test questions and their possible answers before the interview). I gave an example to explain the same. Then she asked me that probability shouldn’t be greater than one, how is the expected value greater than one. I realized she might be trying to confuse me and explained what expected value meant. She seemed satisfied. Then she drew a tree and asked which tree is this(seriously? :P). I said BST. What is the complexity of searching and element in it? Is it balanced? Balance it. She took away the paper when I had halfway balanced the tree seeing that I knew the concept. Then she proceeded with a permutation and combination question to test my analytical skills. Given 7 couples, how can you pick 2 couples such that no two husband and wife are together in a pair? Then she asked me whether I had any questions(Always ask something, it shows that you’re interested in them). Some of my other friends were asked projects in this round, one guy was asked a bit about system calls and computer networks(this was very unexpected to be asked, but again, everything is unpredictable when it comes to interviews), another person was asked about copy constructors, some DSA questions based on DP/Arrays/Hash tables and were told to code the same, people from other branches were asked some puzzles(triangle in a square of 2 units, find a number that when multiplied by 4 and reversed gives the same number, etc). Round 3: Personal Interview 2 There were some 9-11 of us left I guess It again began with the standard “Tell me about yourself question”. She, too, had printouts of my online test. She told me to write a class Student such that the operation obj1 = obj2 on the objects of this class is invalid. I first told her I’ll override the copy constructor’s definition, but she said doing so won’t throw an error, it’ll still accept that line of code. Then I said I’ll put the method in private. She asked another approach. I said I’ll overload the assignment operator and she seemed satisfied. Then she moved to DBMS. Asked me to construct ER diagram for Student Teacher and Subject tables and what would be the primary keys and stuff. Then she asked me to write a query to find the second highest scorer in a particular subject. Others were asked questions related to their domain in this round. One guy from electronics was asked about gates construction, so I guess they were testing your proficiency in your stream in this round. Round 4: Personal Interview 3 2-3 people were not accepted after the previous round This was taken by the Managing Director for everyone and he asked about projects. Drawbacks, flaws, what can be improved, how I implemented a particular module, he asked a lot of questions. Then he asked me if I had any questions for him(Again, ask something). Round 5: Personal Interview 4 This round happened for just one person. I got to know he was asked puzzles and projects. I guess the company was unsure hence held another round to evaluate this candidate. 4 people were selected in the end. The process wasn’t very draining, the selected ones were free by 2:30 PM. The interviews didn’t last for more than 20 minutes. You need to be prepared with your DSAs, OOPs, DBMS concepts as these are standard in most interviews. Having good projects to elevate your resume helps. They didn’t ask me a single question related to my extracurriculars(fests, committees), but this depends on the interviewer and the company. EDIT: Number of rounds can vary depending on the type of people they shortlist for interviews. Interns from other colleges had 5-6 rounds too, so don’t stick to this format. All the best! :) Remember to stay positive and not worry about things that are not under your control.   "content": "INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE DEUTSCHE BANK Prerna Jagesia, B.Tech Computers (2019 - 23) Round 1 - Online coding round (90 mins) The test was held on the HackerEarth platform. There were 110+ students who gave the coding round. The test consisted of 3 questions, one for 20 marks and the other two for 50 marks each. 1) Find whether the given number is Armstrong or not: (20 marks) https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/program-for-armstrong-numbers/ 2) Given two arrays A [a1,.......,an] and B[b1,.....,bn], you need to make the first array equal to the second(order of elements does not matter) in minimum number of moves such that (50 marks) for 0 <= i,j < n, A[i] = A[i] + 2 & A[j] =A[j] - 2 stands for one move Output the minimum number of moves if it is possible to convert A to B else output -1. Example 1) : Input: A = [2,5,6] , B = [1,2,10] Output: 2 Explanation: Move 1) In array A, we modify (2,3) indices [considering 1-based indexing] So A = [2, 5 -2, 6+2] = [2,3,8] Move 2) In array A, we modify (2,3) indices [considering 1-based indexing] So A = [2, 3 -2, 8+2] = [2,1,10] Example 2) : Input: A = [2,4,6] , B = [1,2,10] Output : -1 Explanation: Not possible to convert A to B because the difference between the elements is not even. Example 3): Input: A = [0,2,8] , B = [2,4,6] Output : -1 3) Consider that you have been given the current state of a parking lot such that numbers > 1 stand for a car, -1 stands for a pillar, and 0 stands for an empty parking space. Find the minimum number of moves required to transform the current state of the parking lot into a given desired state such that each move can be either forward or backward in an empty space. ( 50 marks) Example 1): Input: Current_array = [-1,1,0,2] , Desired_array = [-1,1,2,0] Output: 1 Input: Current_array = [-1,8,0,6,7,4,0,2] , Desired_array = [-1,8,6,7,2,4,0,0] Output: -1 29 people were shortlisted for the interviews. Round 2 - Technical Interview round (~60 mins) 1. Tell me about yourself 2. What was your favourite subject in college? I replied DSA. So he asked me more of DSA problems than other CS fundamentals. 3. Find the lowest common ancestor given two nodes in a BST. 4. What is a threaded binary tree? I was not able to answer this :/ 5. Sort an array consisting of only 0s and 1s - I gave the brute force solution first and then optimized it using two pointers https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/segregate-0s-and-1s-in-an-array-by-traversing-array-once/ 6. Given an array of arbitrary length, find the nth smallest element in the array (without sorting obviously :)) I gave him the approach of using quicksort. When the index returned by the partition method of quicksort is equal to n-1 (because of 0-based indexing), we should break from the function and return the element at that index. He was expecting the approach of using heapsort but looked satisfied with my answer. All the approaches can be found here: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/kth-smallestlargest-element-unsorted-array/ You can use a priority queue instead of building the heap from scratch. 7. Given two numbers, how to find the GCD/HCF of those numbers - https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/c-program-find-gcd-hcf-two-numbers/ 8. What are the disadvantages of recursion? 9. What is dynamic programming? Mention these two very important properties in your answer - optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. He then moved on to simple DBMS questions like: 10. What is normalization in databases and explain the three normal forms? 11. What is indexing in databases? (Just the concept, not the implementation) 12. Given two table structures, what will be the best way to model a one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many relationship. For one to many and many to one, we should add the primary key of the table with one record as the foreign key of the table with many records. For many-to-many relationship, create a separate table with a mapping of the primary keys of the related records. 13. What work did you do during your internship? 14. Explain ACID properties The interview concluded after this and 14 people made it to the third round Round 3 - Technical Interview round (~60 mins) 1. Tell me about yourself. 2. How to build a queue from a linked list? 3. Can there be more than one primary key in a table? NO. 4. Can there be more than one foreign key in a table? YES 5. Can there be more than one unique key in a table? YES 6. Given two tables - employee table (with employee ID, employee name, salary and Dept ID as attributes) and department table (with Dept ID and Dept. Name as attributes) a. Write a query to print the Dept. ID and sum of salaries in each department. b. Write a query to print the employee name and department name of each employee. 7. He then moved to my resume and asked a few basic questions about the projects I had mentioned like what is the role of package.json file in Node.js and what was the structure of my MongoDB database 8. Elaborate on the work done during your internship After these questions, he asked me if I had any questions for him. Always ask questions as it shows your interest in the company. I asked him how projects and teams will be allotted to new joiners. He explained the process and the interview concluded. 12 people were shortlisted for the next round. Round 4 - Professional Fitness Round (~30 mins) This round consisted of simple behavioral and situational questions. Here they evaluate whether you are a fit for their company. 1. Tell me about yourself. (It can get boring ik :/) 2. What is your family background? 3. Consider a scenario where you and your team are having a group discussion and you suggest a solution to some problem. But the senior people in your team dismiss your solution without proper reason. What will you do in this case? 4. Consider a case where you work on a project and deploy it to production. Now a bug arises in the code while in production which is causing some impact on the business of the company. You are called over the weekend to investigate the issue. You find that you can either provide a quick fix for the bug in two days or provide a proper fix for the bug in 3-4 weeks. What will you do in this situation? 5. What are some challenges I encountered in my previous internship experience? She then asked me if I had some questions for her. I asked her about her experience so far at Deutsche bank. Everyone who gave the ProFit round was asked to give the HR round as well. Round 5 - HR Round (~25-30 mins) 1. Tell me about yourself. 2. Since I had to go to the Bangalore office for my internship, I was asked about my experience there. What did I learn in my previous company and similar questions. 3. Explain how does a bank make money? They wanted just the basics of it -Banks generally make money by borrowing money from depositors and compensating them with a certain interest rate. The banks will lend the money out to borrowers, charging the borrowers a higher interest rate and profiting off the interest rate spread. 4. If you see people misusing the money of the company, for example, taking reimbursement for first class tickets while they actually travel in the second class, what will you do? 5. If you see someone be a victim of sexual harassment and is scared to speak up, what will you do? 6. If you see some team member who used to perform very well earlier suddenly underperform and not be able to concentrate on his/her work, what action will you take? 7. How do you keep yourself updated with what’s going on in the world? 8. Do you read? The interview concluded with him explaining to me the different qualities people should have to become a leader at a bank. All the 12 people who gave round 4 and 5 were selected :) Resources used: 1. Apna college YT channel 2. Leetcode 3. Interview bit 4. Gfg (not for questions, but just for solutions to questions I didn't understand) Tips: 1. Keep some hard copies of your resume handy. Since some companies take offline interviews, they do ask for hard copies. 2. Be very thorough with your CS fundamentals. Don’t neglect it and leave it for the end. 3. When you don’t understand a particular problem statement, do ask for clarifications on it. 4. Think out loud. This way the interviewer gets an idea about which direction you are headed and may help you start thinking in the right direction. This also keeps the interview interactive. 5. Make sure to go through all projects on your resume and be prepared for questions that can be asked about them like why did you use this technology/framework instead of that technology/framework, difference between two frameworks, etc. 6. It is alright to tell them that you don’t know a particular thing instead of bluffing about it and getting caught. They don’t expect you to know everything. They are more interested in seeing how you use the knowledge you have and apply your logic to tackle an unseen problem statement. Lastly, keep calm during your interviews and have confidence in yourself. All the best !!👍 If you have any queries, feel free to drop an email at pkjagesia@gmail.com",

Sankhe Final Year B.Tech IT 2020-24 Eligibility:- ●CS, IT, EXTC only ●7+ CPI About the FTE offer:- ●19.63 LPA ●Pune/Bangalore location About the company:- Deutsche Bank has its most banking customers in Europe with it being founded in Germany. (Once check the pronunciation of Detusche especially if you are going for the interview). Deutsche hired for the Graduate Analyst role in the Technology and Data Innovation Department. The entire process includes 1 online coding test and 4 rounds of interviews. (Technical Round 1, Technical Round 2, Professional Fit round, HR round) Online test:- The test was scheduled for 4th August on Hackerearth. It was a standard DSA-based online coding test. Test Duration was 1hr 30 min and the test had 3 questions. Q1) Power generation The problem had a story behind it. But what we had to do was calculate the maximum time required for draining 2 power sources. Now the way this power drains is that if we are currently using say power source A, then its power reduces by 2 units, and the power of the other power source (currently not in use) increases by 1. And we have to stop whenever at least 1 source reaches zero. Eg. We have source A = 3 and B = 5 →So at t=0 we choose B and hence at T = 1, A = 4, B = 3 T = 2, A = 5, B = 1 T = 3, A = 3, B = 2 T = 4, A = 1, B = 3 T = 5, A = 2, B = 1 T = 6, A = 0, B = 2 Here since A reached zero, we stop and the ans is 6. Solution:- I solved it using DP. Some of my friends also solved it iteratively using a while loop. The iterative is also very intuitive. Just maintain 2 variables that contain max and min amongst the two sources and then while none of them are less than or equal to zero, reduce the max values amongst them by 2, increase the min value by 1, and then again update the values of the max and min variable. This was an easy-medium problem. There is also a score associated with these questions. This one had 20 points. Q2 ) Auto suggestions This was a variation of the famous EDIT DISTANCE problem (solved using DP). This question did not require memoization, because I wrote the recursive solution and submitted and it got accepted. There was an array of strings and a query string given, you had to find the word closest to the given query string. There are 2 factors to decide the closeness of a word with the query string: 1) Levenshtein distance:- Minimum number of operations to convert a given string to the query string. Operations allowed are a) Insertion b) Deletion c) Updation 2) If 2 strings have the same Levenshtein distance then the string that is lexicographically smallest will be the closest to the query string. Solution:- Iterate over all the strings in the array. And then calculate the Levenshtein distance(using the edit distance method). Then if 2 strings have the same minimum Levenshtein distance, then choose the lexicographically smaller string. It was a medium problem. Q3) Sorting related something I don't exactly remember the story in the question, but there were 2 arrays given, one was a string array and the second was an int array. You had to sort the string array in descending order using the corresponding values from the int array. And if 2 strings have the same corresponding value in the int array then preserve the natural ordering. Eg. str = [“abc”, “def”, “ghi”], value = [12,12,48] So, the final answer output array will be [“ghi”, ”abc”, ”def”]. Since “abc” and “def” both have the same value, hence maintain the same order as given in the original array. Solution:- You had to write a custom comparator for sorting these string arrays (in Java). In C++ there must be another way to write a custom sorter. Make a pair of strings and their corresponding values and then sort this new array and then create a new array for storing the strings from the sorted array. This was an easy-medium problem if you knew how to write a custom sorter. Note:- The HackerEarth editor had a lot of problems with the Java language. For C++ there were no problems. So be aware and check the input provided to your function if you use Java. I lost a lot of time due to these problems. However, I was able to solve all the problems with 15 minutes left for the test to end. The results were announced on 7th August and we had our offline interviews on 9th August from 9:00 am. Round 1 of Interview:- The interviews started at around 9:30 am and my interview started around 10:00 am. I was first asked to introduce myself. (The only question you can be sure of when preparing). The introduction is one of the most important pieces of preparation as you can easily steer the interview into the zone where you are confident and can leave a good impression on the interviewer. The interviewer asked a few general questions on my introduction. Then the interviewer started asking general computer science questions. There were also some HR questions such as “Tell me about your strengths and weaknesses”. And whether you want to pursue future education. There were many small questions asked throughout the interview. According to me, this interview was just to gauge whether a candidate has a basic understanding of all the core subjects or not. The interview lasted for about 45 to 50 minutes. Around 30 people were shortlisted for the next round. Round 2 of Interview: My second round started around 12:15 pm and this was a 1hr 30 to 45 minute interview. This was a proper technical interview. The interviewer went through my resume at the beginning and questioned me about the details mentioned in the resume. Then the interviewer asked questions about my internships and why I chose some frameworks or language to perform certain tasks during my internship and my projects. Then the interviewer asked me to rate myself in DSA from 0 to 5. I said 3. Then the interviewer asked me the difference between Data Structures and Algorithms. And then asked some basic questions about diff between trees and graphs. And then the interviewer gave me a problem. I don’t remember the question but it was straightforward BFS. However, the interviewer asked me to write the complete code on paper. The interviewer expected me to write everything starting from the Node class to the final output function. Then she also asked me to do the problem using DFS, this time interviewer just asked me to write pseudo code. After this, the interviewer asked me Segregate 0s and 1s in an array - GeeksforGeeks problem. Deutsche always asks some or the other version of Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s | Dutch National Flag problem - GeeksforGeeks. After this, there were some questions on Dynamic programming and she just asked me to explain the benefit of using DP for calculating factorial. Just the pseudo-code for this problem. The test consisted of 5 sections. Suppose for input n = 4, the output goes as follows: Output : 1*2*3*4*17*18*19*20 –5*6*7*14*15*16 —-8*9*12*13 —---10*11 I was able to pass all the test cases (11/11) over here. Tip: Try to solve any Online Assessment as soon as possible, if it contains only Coding Questions then it’s a big plus plus, but if the OA also contains MCQs then please don’t end up giving wrong answers in hurry. 1st Question Prefix XOR Given an Array where each element is XOR of all the previous elements in original array, return the original array. Now I don’t remember their sample examples but solution was somewhat similar to this vector<int> helper(vector<int> pref) { int n = pref.size(); vector<int> ans(n); ans[0] = pref[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { ans[i]=pref[i]^pref[i-1]; } return ans; } Solution: a) A^ B = B ^ A b) A ^ A = 0 c) A ^ 0 = A pref[i] = arr [i] ^ arr[i - 1] ^ … arr [0] pref[i] = arr [i] ^ pref[i – 1] pref[i] ^ pref[i – 1] = arr [i] ^ pref[i – 1] ^ pref[i – 1] pref[i] ^ pref[i – 1] = arr [i] ^ 0 arr[i] = pref[i] ^ pref[i - 1] All test cases were passed. 2nd Question Team Formation The task was to form a team of size k from a given array by following below rules: a) You need to take two windows of size w from front and rear side of the array. b) Take the greatest score from the both windows and add it to the answer variable, at last delete the considered score from the array (so that it is not taken into consideration for next iteration). Solution: I used a max heap and added all the elements that were present in the window of size (w + k), from front and rear side of the array. Now I just needed to pop the max heap k times. int helper(vector<int> score, int k, int w) { int n = score.size(); priority_queue<int> q; int ans = 0; for (int i = 0; i < k + w; i++) { if (i < n) { q.push(score[i]); } } for (int i = n - k - w; i < n; i++) { if (i >= k + w) { q.push(score[i]); } } for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) { ans += q.top(); q.pop(); } return ans; } 10/14 test cases were passed and I submitted with 20 mins remaining on the clock. After this round, 10 students were shortlisted. 13th Sept – 2nd Round (Technical Round + HR Round for 1 hour) The Interviewer directly dived into my projects and started asking questions on them (no tell me about yourself questions were asked).   "content": "Interview Experience\nWarren Jacinto - TY BTech CE, 221070029\nIntroduction\nI am Warren Jacinto, currently in my third year of pursuing a BTech Degree in Computer\nEngineering at Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute, Matunga.\nThis report will serve as a record of my experience interviewing with Goldman Sachs.\n\nPre-Placement Talk\nSomewhere around 12 July 2024, we received an email from TPO informing us that\nGoldman Sachs was visiting the campus for intern hiring. In this email, there were links for\napplying on the official Goldman Sachs Careers page as well as details for a webinar.\nPlatform: Zoom Webinar\nTime: 23 July 2024, 5pm - 6pm\nThe Pre-Placement Talk was engaging and to the point. They started off by explaining what\nGS does, why GS stands out from the rest and what kind of lifestyle you can expect at GS.\nPay close attention to whatever is discussed in this meeting, as it serves as a good way to\nunderstand the kind of people the firm is looking for. Additionally, during your interviews,\nthe interviewers may ask you questions about the firm, and paying attention here, will pay\noff then.\n\nOnline Assessment\nParticipants: Everyone who had applied\nTest Platform: Hackerrank - video, and screen proctored.\nIt's been too long to remember the exact format of the OA, but there were 2 sections, one\nwas coding, and the other was MCQs.\nThe coding questions were easy, even for me who had relatively less experience with DSA\nat that point(~200 LC solved). I can't recall the exact questions, but they were array/maths\nbased.\nThe MCQs were a little harder, they were based on a wide variety of topics studied in our\nsyllabus like: DSA, OOPS, Debugging. The questions were very much doable, it was the time\nthat was an issue. As long as your CS Fundamentals are clear, this won't be hard.\nThroughout this period, your camera and microphone must be on and your screen will be\nshared. Make sure you do not under any circumstances: switch tabs, have another\nperson in your webcam, look away from the screen, speak anything. Your face should\nbe clearly visible and well lit.\nTrust me, the OA is not that difficult and doesn’t even warrant any kind of malpractice, it’s\njust not worth the risk. Instead, prepare well and you’ll do fine.\nResults: 27 people were shortlisted for interviews, and I was one of them. We received the\nresults on 25 July 2024, in the afternoon, and I wasted no time starting my preparation.\n\nInterview Day\nDate: 26 July 2024\nVenue: TPO Seminar Hall\nWe were asked to report at 8.30 am, and the Pre-Interview Talk was scheduled to begin at\n9 am. Additionally we were also asked to bring 3 - 4 printouts of our resumes and dress in\nformal attire. I wore a dark blue full sleeves shirt, along with black trousers, a belt and black\nformal shoes. For financial firms, your attire matters a lot, so dress well.\nGS had sent around 6 -7 people to handle the entire process, of which, ~5 were technical\npeople, engineers at GS, and the remaining were more HR/Manager types.\nDuring the talk, they gave us an overview of the entire process they were conducting and\ntheir roles at GS. They mentioned that there would be technical rounds, followed by HR\nrounds. Then, after the talk concluded, without much further delay, the interview process\ncommenced around 10 am.\nNow, a couple of things to note, before I explain the actual interview experience,\n1. Address them respectfully. I always defaulted to “Sir”/”Ma’am”, but if they ask you\nto use their first names, then do that.\n2. Pay attention to the Pre Interview Talk. Their introductions, their roles at GS,\nmemorise all that you can, you never know which interviewer you may get. Being\nable to recollect all of this about your interviewers will come in handy during the\ninterview.\n3. Try to Answer. If they engage in a Q/A, or just ask any questions in general, try to\nanswer, because mostly none of the other candidates seated beside you will, and\nthis will let you stand out.\n\nRound 1 [Technical]\nEven though interviews commenced at 10 am, I didn’t have my first round until ~3pm!.\nThis was incredibly nerve-wracking as there were people who had finished 3 rounds, and I still\nhadn’t had my first round yet.\nFinally however, I was called for my first technical interview. I sat down across from my\ninterviewer, and he introduced himself and the role he had at GS. Then, he asked for my\nintroduction. I gave him the introduction I had memorised when Ayaan/Raunak took my\nmock interview. You can find it here. Make sure to memorise a good introduction. Keep it\nshort and to the point, and don’t be too technical, include some hobbies too, or maybe an\ninteresting fact. Practise good eye contact and body language.\nThen after asking me which language I was comfortable with(C++), he gave me the first\nquestion and a piece of pen and paper to solve it on.\nFind Length of Maximum Mountain in an array.\nGiven an array, say, 4,5,7,8,9,3,6,8,3\nFind the length of the largest mountain, that is the maximum distance between points\nwhere the array starts increasing and stops decreasing.\nHere the largest mountain would be from i = 0 to 5, length = 5\nNote i = 5 to 8 is also a mountain, but not as big as the previous mountain.\nI don't remember the approach I gave, but it was some kind of two pointer, nothing too\ncomplicated, and after I explained with an example, he was satisfied and asked me to write\ncode for it.\nFind First Duplicate Character in a String.\nGiven a string, s = “abcdefghijkalmnopqrst”\nFind the index of the first repeating character in the string. Here it is i = 11, ‘a’.\nThis question is pretty straightforward and I explained a HashSet / unordered_set approach\nto solving it, and he was satisfied, telling me code was not necessary.\nClient Server Architecture\nThen the DSA part concluded, and he took a look at my resume. I was ready for some\nquestions on the Deep Learning projects I had, or maybe even my GSoC ‘24 project. But I\ndon’t think he had experience with either DL, or was familiar with GSoC. So he chose to ask\nme some questions about Client Server Architecture for Web Applications. He asked quite a\nfew questions, of which I only remember one.\n“Given a client - server web app, the client needs to display the progress of a running job on\nthe server, and the progress must be real time. How would the client fetch the data from\nthe server for this?”\nI proceeded to explain HTTP Requests and why they were a bad fit for this, since you can’t\nhave a client making 100s of requests a second to get real time data from the server.\nThen, I explained what WebSockets were and why WebSockets were a better fit for the\nproblem. He was pretty happy with my explanation.\n\nConclusion of Interview 1\nI’d argue the conclusion of the interview is the most important part, because it’s your last\nchance to improve the interviewer’s opinion of you.\nFrom what I had observed, each interviewer had a copy of our resume that we had\nsubmitted, and were making notes/marking us on the back of our resumes. Then at the\nend, they would give it to the HR person coordinating the process to decide whether to\nsend us for further interviews or to reject us.\nWhat I’m trying to convey is that the interviewers usually don’t have any absolute scale by\nwhich to measure you.\nAs much as possible, try to connect with the interviewer. Whether you’re from the same\nvillage, same school, or have the same shirt. Try to “vibe” with them.\nYou get the chance to do this at the end of the interview, when they ask you, “Do you have\nany questions for me?”.\nNever ask for feedback on your responses. Not only are they not allowed to give that\n(most of the time), it reflects badly on their perception of you.\nAlways ask something though, don’t say “No, I do not” and miss out on this chance. Make\nthat question a good one, it should be unique, and not something generic everyone else\nasks. This is where the attention you paid during the Pre Placement Talk, and the Pre\nInterview Talk pays off.\nI started off by asking him about what his division(memorised from the Pre Interview Talk)\ndid at GS. He went on for 5 minutes explaining what he did and how long he had been\ndoing it. I then followed up with “But, is that the division you always wanted to end up in?\nDidn’t you ever want to switch?” and “How good is the internal mobility at GS, when it\ncomes to switching projects/divisions?”. This conversation continued for like 10 minutes\nand I was able to connect with him, to the point where I guess even he had forgotten it was\nan interview and I was much more relaxed too.\nAfter ending with a thank you, I left the room, at that moment, uncertain of my\nperformance. I then went to grab a snack from the canteen as I hadn’t had lunch and met\nsome friends.\n\nRound 2 [Technical + HR]:\nNow, a lot of people had 3 interviews, 2 Technical followed by 1 HR, but I had only 2\ninterviews, 1 Technical and 1 Technical + HR. I'm not sure how to classify the last round, as I\nhad all kinds of questions.\nBut one thing was certain, all of us had our last round with this person who I'll name “Anish”\nfor anonymity. He seemed to be the person in charge of the entire process and everybody\nhad their final round with him. He was clearly someone who started off as a technical\nperson and graduated to a managerial position, based on the questions he asked us.\nAt ~5pm, I sat down across from Anish and he had a very “chill” vibe to him. We exchanged\nintroductions. He asked me where my interests were, in Computer Engineering. I\nmentioned my love of Operating Systems and Low Level Programming, alongside GPU\nProgramming, and took this as an opportunity to mention my GSoC ‘24 project too.\nAfter hearing this mixture of topics, he asked me a couple of questions:\nI don't remember the exact wording, but he asked me about what the OS does, and more\nimportantly about the device management part. He asked me how so many different kinds\nof devices are able to interface with an OS, what are drivers?, among other questions.\nThen, the conversation went on a tangent towards GPUs and I don't remember exactly\nwhat we talked about, but it was something related to how GPUs are used on a large scale.\nI do know that I was able to answer everything properly, because all of these are my\nfavourite parts of Computer Science.\n“Imagine you have to design a ticketing app like IRCTC’s UTS app. How do you handle 1000s\nof users trying to book the same tickets? Be aware that on UTS, you receive the tickets only\nafter payment, and if for some reason, the booking fails, you are refunded within 7 days.\nCome up with a solution to improve this system.”\nFirst I answered regarding the 1000s of concurrent users on the platform accessing the\nsame resource. I mentioned a kind of “Lock-Out” mechanism, where anyone booking a\nticket had exclusive access to it for, say, 2 minutes, to confirm and complete payment, and\nnobody else could access the same seats in this window. I also came up with some other\nsolutions which I’m unable to recall at the time of writing. We had a long back and forth on\nthis topic and possible solutions, with him constantly poking at my ideas, asking me “How\nwould it work in XYZ situation?”, and “Could it work in ABC case?”.\nAfter this, he seemed pretty happy with my answers, and gave a solution he came up with\non the spot, which was a kind of “Hold Out” mechanism, similar to what Uber/Ola use,\nwhere money is debited from your account and held by the bank, but not credited to IRCTC,\nuntil the booking is confirmed. If for some reason, it is not confirmed, the money goes\nstraight back to your account, without need for a 7 day wait period for IRCTC to refund you.\nIt was at this point I realised, this wasn’t a planned question, but rather something he came\nup with on the spot, and something he wanted us to solve together.\nFinally, he asked me about my background, my family, why I came to VJTI, why I did not try\nfor any NIT/IIT, to which I replied with the truth.\nThere’s a lot of gaps in my memory regarding that round, but from what I remember, he\nwas essentially trying to see how good my communication skills were, alongside my ability\nto think on the spot.\nIt’s one thing to be good at problem solving, but if you can’t explain your ideas to\nothers who are not as knowledgeable as you, then it's absolutely worthless.\nThis is where I got tremendously lucky as I had a ton of practice with my communication\nskills during the Project X meets.\n\nResults\nI went back to the TPO hall, much more relaxed now that the interview was over. I sat and\njoked with friends who had also finished their interviews until somewhere around 6pm.\nThen, the team from GS came into the hall and announced that they were done with\ninterviews and because Swapnil Sir requested, they were declaring the results on the spot.\nOne by one each of the names were called in alphabetical order, and at the very end, my\nname was called too.\nThey selected 6 people:\n1. Alinaa Bharde\n2. Druhi Phutane\n3. Manav Shah\n4. Mohammed Bhadsorawala\n5. Sneha Menat\n6. Warren Jacinto\nInitially I was a bit confused as I thought she meant to say “Varun” who was also a\ncandidate, and not everyone gets my name right on the first try. But nope, she meant me.\nWe all exchanged congratulations and to say I was overjoyed would be an understatement.\nAll of us then left the TPO hall, and the first thing I did, while exiting the Mech Gate was call\nmy Mom and Dad and tell them the news.\nI went home extremely relaxed as the biggest challenge of the Third Year of any BTech\ndegree was over, and I could stop grinding DSA(which I hated doing).\n\nResources and Tips\nThere is no one perfect interview preparation guide, but here’s what I did.\nGet really really good at atleast one core language\nFor me, this was C and C++. When I say good, I mean really good, to the point where you\nknow the ins and outs of the languages. But the other more\nniche stuff, I learnt through practice.\nJava/Python are also good choices, though I’d recommend Java over Python.\nMake sure your CS Fundamentals are super strong\nThis includes OS, OOPS, DBMS, LLD, DSA, etc. I got lucky because my DBMS is atrocious and\nI wasn’t asked a single DBMS question, but if you want to be thoroughly prepared, do\neverything properly. You’ll find resources in CoC’s guide.\nPractise DSA regularly\nI started my DSA prep relatively earlier compared to others, and I used Neetcode 150 as my\nreference, finishing the entire sheet well before GS came to our college.\nBe consistent in your DSA prep, don’t give up quickly and look at the solution, struggle a\nlittle bit, it’s natural and I did it too. Make sure you look at the most optimised solutions\nafter you solve them.\nImprove your English Speaking and Communication skills\nI lucked out in this aspect, because I speak English with my family at home and have done\nso since I was born. I also read quite a lot of crime fiction novels when I was younger. Your\naccent, the way you pronounce words, the intonation you use, the pauses, the uhm’s the\nahh’s, all of it is the first thing the interviewer looks at. Make sure it's proper. The best way\nto improve is by doing, so practise with your friends.\nWhen it comes to communication skills, it helps a lot if you're a part of any club or\ncommunity and have had to organise events in a team with others. Otherwise you can look\nonline on youtube for ways to improve. You should be able to explain an idea you have to\nsomeone with no knowledge of it and have them understand it to the same degree you do.\nBuild a good resume\nMy resume at the time of Goldman Sachs is here. This is hands down the best template for\na LaTeX resume. CoC’s guide for making a good resume should be more than enough. Get\nyour resume reviewed by senior’s as soon as you can and incorporate their feedback. I was\nfortunate enough to get this feedback from Project X seniors pretty early, way before the\ninternship season started.\nBe calm\nI understand how incredibly scary it is when you give your first interview. I was surrounded\nby all these people who were arguably so much better qualified than I was. But it’s\nextremely important you never show this nervousness to anyone. On the outside, you need\nto be cool, calm and collected. Respond with confidence when asked a question. Don't\nbreak under the pressure. Remember, no matter what it may look like, the other\ncandidates are just as terrified, if not more, than you and the interviewers are rooting for\nyou, they want you to succeed, and will never intentionally try to fail you.\nPrepare Well\nMost of the time, TPO receives the interview shortlist by afternoon/evening on the day\nbefore the interviews. So if you proceed with the mentality that “I’ll study OOPS, OS when i\nactually get shortlisted and will do DSA for now, so I can focus on getting shortlisted” Then\nyou’ll be sorely underprepared for the interviews, as one day is not nearly enough to do\neverything well. So alongside DSA, keep doing CS fundamentals as well. Research about the\ncompany visiting, what they do, their rank among similar companies, the role you are\napplying for, the JD associated with it and everything else as soon as you can before going\nfor interviews. Go through CoC’s archive of past interview experiences, for at least the\nprevious 2-3 years to get a good idea about what the company asks in terms of coding and\npuzzles\nGive Mocks\nCoC usually organises mock interviews for those who take an active part in CoC activities\nwhere seniors guide you about how to give interviews. These are extremely important and\nshould be taken seriously, as the feedback you get from your mock interviews will matter a\nlot. If you don’t get seniors to take your mocks, ask your friends to help you out.\nConclusion\nIn conclusion, if there's anything you should take away from this, it is the points in the\nprevious section.\nIf you are not selected, don’t be discouraged. If I had to say, interviews are like 60% luck\nand 40% skill. Everything ranging from the interviewer’s personality and mood, to the other\ncandidates shortlisted, is all out of your hands, so don’t be disheartened if you aren’t\nselected. Take it in your stride and learn from the experience. It will work out eventually.\nFor example, there was someone in my batch who gave interviews for almost 7-8 different\ncompanies, before finally getting selected. So don’t worry.\nIf you do get selected, celebrate! It’s not easy to get selected and requires a lot of effort.\nTake a break from everything and enjoy life for some time. Help out your friends who are\nstill yet to get an offer by taking mock interviews.\nIf you’ve ever got any questions about my GS interview experience, or about interview prep\nin general, feel free to reach out to me at warrenjacinto@gmail.com I will definitely get back\nto you as soon as I can.\nAll the Best!!!",

B.Tech IT 2019-23\nFor 2022 Summer Internship (On-campus)\n04th September 2021\nDE Shaw India (DESIS) visited our campus for Internships for 3rd Year students. A total of\n201 students had applied for this.\nOnline Coding Round (1st Sept, 2021)\nAn online test was conducted on HackerRank. Total time was around 95 minutes and\nconsisted of 3 Coding Questions:\nQ.1) You have been given an N-sized array of product numbers and another N-sized\narray of the product cost for those N elements respectively. There can be multiple\nproducts of the same product number with different costs. You need to find the maximum\ncost we can get by selecting one product of each product number. So you cannot select\nmultiple products of the same product number.\nEg.\nproduct_num = [1,2,3,2,4,4,6,1,1,1]\ncost = [3,6,1,2,8,9,10,4,5,2]\nOutput: 31\nExplanation: We have 4 units of product 1 with the highest cost of 5\n2 units of product 2 with the highest cost of 6\n1 unit of product 3 with the highest cost of 1\n2 units of product 4 with the highest cost of 9\nand 1 unit of product 6 with the highest cost of 10\n5 + 6 + 1 + 9 + 10 = 31\nI made an array of pairs {product number, cost} and sorted this. And for each product\nnumber selected the highest cost and added all.\n(Passed all test cases)\nQ.2) You are given an NxM matrix. The cells contain *(asterisk) or .(dot)\nHere, * means land and . means water.\nYou need to find the maximum one of all the minimum area rectangles that can\ncompletely enclose an island. Neighboring * forms an island (Top, Left, Right, Bottom).\nThe minimum area rectangle can have water in it but should contain an island completely\nwithin itself.\nEg.\n* * * . . .\n* * . * . .\n. . * * . .\n. * * . * *\n. . . . . *\nOutput: 9\nHere, there are 3 islands.\nTopmost island is\n* * *\n* *\nThe minimum area required to cover it will be 3*2 = 6\nThe middle island is\n*\n* *\n* *\nThe minimum area required to cover it will be 3*3 = 9\nThe bottom island is\n* *\n*\nThe minimum area required to cover it will be 2*2 = 4\nThe maximum out of these will be 9.\nThis was similar to the Number of Islands problem, I used DFS on the matrix. For each\nisland, I maintained Top, Left, Right, Bottom boundaries and updated them for each DFS.\nArea will be (Right- Left+1) * (Bottom - Top + 1).\n(Passed all test cases)\nQ.3) You have been given N strings, you need to create a minimum length string such\nthat those N strings are substrings of that output string.\nExtra condition: Let’s consider 2 strings A and B from the given list, if A is before B in the\nlist then in the output string, B should start after the start of A.\nEg.\n[abc, bcfgh, ghtyok, cfghght]\nOutput: abcfghtyokcfghght\nExplanation:\nS = abc\nS = abcfgh\nS = abcfghtyok\nFor the final string cfghght , even though some part of it occurs in S we cannot consider\nthat as it is starting before the start of the previous string in the array (ghtyok)\nS = abcfghtyokcfghght\nSolved this greedily, took one string at a time, and tried to fit it within the main string\nfollowing that extra condition.\n(Passed all test cases)\nI was able to solve all 3 questions with all test cases passed.\nFrom 201 students who applied for the online test from our college, 10 students were\nshortlisted for the next round.\nTechnical Round 1 (4th Sept 2021, 9 AM)\nThis round was conducted on Hackerrank CodePair. So this is like a biased function.\nI started by asking a lot of questions to clarify it as the question was very weirdly framed.\nAfter getting all the info I started coming up with approaches.\nThe first few approaches I thought were completely wrong in the sense of probability, the\ninterviewer directly didn’t point that out but gave hints. Slowly I came to the correct\napproach taking some help from them. Typically this question was super easy, but I took\na lot of time to think about it.\nThe final approach was:\nGenerate random numbers between 0 and 1 using a built-in random function.\nIf it falls between 0 and 0.3 then return 0.\nIf it falls between 0.3 and 0.8 then return 1.   (Why 0.8?   0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8)\nIf it falls between 0.8 and 1.0 then return 2.\nQ.3) Create your own data structure which supports Insertion, Deletion, Search and\nGetRandom each with O(1) time complexity.   (GeeksForGeeks)\nActually, this is a very famous question, but I had somehow never seen this before.\nI started thinking about LinkedList as Insertion, Deletion is O(1).\nTo also support Search, I thought of using Linked List along with Hashmaps. Still, this\ndoesn’t satisfy GetRandom in O(1).\nThought of Queue, Deque, Stack. But none of them fit.\nAlso thought of Array along with HashMaps, but Deletion won’t be O(1). Spent a lot of\ntime thinking about this. The interviewer gave hints that: try to think about Deletion once\nagain.\nAfter spending more time, I came up with the final approach using Arrays + Hashmap.\n(Refer GeeksForGeeks)\nIt was a very easy question if you knew what and how to do it, but I took a lot of time as I\nsaw it for the first time.\nAfter this the other interviewer asked me some OOPs related basic questions:\n-\nDifference between classes and objects\n-\nStatic variables in C++ and real-life use\n-\nInheritance concept\nThen he asked me If I had any questions. An incoming telephone call must be first allocated to a respondent who is free. If the respondent can't handle the call, he or she must escalate the call to a manager. If the manager is not free or not able to handle it, then the call should be escalated to a director. Design the classes and data structures for this problem. Implement a method dispatchCaLL() which assigns a call to the first available employee. SOLUTION All three ranks of employees have different work to be done, so those specific functions are profile specific. We should keep these things within their respective class. There are a few things which are common to them, like address, name, job title, and age. These things can be kept in one class and can be extended or inherited by others. Finally, there should be one CallHandler class which would route the calls to the correct person. Note that on any object-oriented design question, there are many ways to design the objects. Discuss the trade-offs of different solutions with your interviewer. You should usually design for long-term code flexibility and maintenance. We'll go through each of the classes below in detail. CallHandler is implemented as a singleton class. It represents the body of the program, and all calls are funneled first through it. 1 public class CallHandler { 2 private static CallHandler instance; 4 /* 3 levels of employees: respondents, managers, directors. */ 5 private final int LEVELS = 3; 7 /* Initialize 10 respondents, 4 managers, and 2 directors. */ 8 private final int NUM_RESPONDENTS = 10; 9 private final int NUM_MANAGERS = 4; 10 private final int NUM_DIRECTORS = 2; 12 /* List of employees, by level. *employeeLevels[0] = respondents *employeeLevels[1] = managers *employeeLevels[2] = directors */ 17 List<List<Employee>> employeeLevels; 19 */ queues for each call's rank */ 20 List<List<Call>> callQueues; 22 protected CallHandler() { ... } 24 /* Get instance of singleton class. */ 25 public static CallHandler getlnstance() { 26 if (instance == null) instance = new CallHandler(); 27 return instance; 28 } 30 /* Gets the first available employee who can handle this call. */ 31 public Employee getHandlerForCall(Call call) { ... } 33 /* Routes the call to an available employee, or saves in a queue * if no employee available. */ 35 public void dispatchCall(Caller caller) { 36 Call call = new Call(caller); 37 dispatchCall(call); 38 } 40 /* Routes the call to an available employee, or saves in a queue * if no employee available. */ 42 public void dispatchCall(Call call) { 43 /* Try to route the call to an employee with minimal rank. */ 44 Employee emp = getHandlerForCall(call); 45 if (emp != null) { 46 emp.receiveCall(call); 47 call . setHandler (emp) ; 48 } else { 49 /* Place the call into corresponding call queue according * to its rank. */ 51 call.reply (\"Please wait for free employee to reply\"); 52 callQueues.get (call.getRank().getValue()).add(call); 53 } 54 } 56 /* An employee got free. Note that there are many other ways that are equally good. This may seem like an awful lot of code to write in an interview, and it is. We've been much more thorough here than you would need. In a real interview, you would likely be much lighter on some of the details until you have time to fill them in. 8.3 Design a musical jukebox using object-oriented principles. SOLUTION In any object-oriented design question, you first want to start off with asking your interviewer some questions to clarify design constraints. Is this jukebox playing CD? Records? MP3s? Is it a simulation on a computer, or is it supposed to represent a physical jukebox? Does it take money, or is it free? And if it takes money, which currency? And does it deliver change? Unfortunately, we don't have an interviewer here that we can have this dialogue with. Instead, we'll make some assumptions. We'll assume that the jukebox is a computer simulation that closely mirrors physical jukeboxes, and we'll assume that it's free. Now that we have that out of the way, we'll outline the basic system components. • Jukebox • CD • Song • Artist • Playlist • Display (displays details on the screen) Now, let’s break this down further and think about the possible actions. • Playlist creation (includes add, delete, and shuffle) • CD selector • Song selector • Queuing up a song • Get next song from playlist A user also can be introduced: • Adding • Deleting • Credit information Each of the main system components translates roughly to an object, and each action translates to a method. Design the data structures and explain an algorithm to solve the puzzle. You can assume that you have a fitsWith method which, when passed two puzzle pieces, returns true if the two pieces belong together. SOLUTION We will assume that we have a traditional, simple jigsaw puzzle. The puzzle is grid-like, with rows and columns. Each piece is located in a single row and column and has four edges. Each edge comes in one of three types: inner, outer, and flat. A corner piece, for example, will have two flat edges and two other edges, which could be inner or outer. As we solve the jigsaw puzzle (manually or algorithmically), we'll need to store the position of each piece. We could think about the position as absolute or relative: • Absolute Position: \"This piece is located at position (12, 23).\" Absolute position would belong to the Piece class itself and would include an orientation as well. • Relative Position: “I don’t know where this piece is actually located, but I know that it is next to this other piece.” The relative position would belong to the Edge class. For our solution, we will use only the relative position, by adjoining edges to neighboring edges. A potential object-oriented design looks like the following: 1 class Edge { 2 enum Type { inner, outer, flat } 3 Piece parent; 4 Type type; 5 int index; // Index into Piece.edges 6 Edge attached_to; // Relative position 8 /* See Algorithm section. Returns true if the two pieces * should be attached to each other. */ 10 boolean fitswith(Edge edge) { ... }; 11 } 13 class Piece { 14 Edge[ ] edges; 15 boolean isCorner() { ... } 16 } 18 class Puzzle { 19 Piece[ ] pieces; /* Remaining pieces left to put away. */ 20 Piece[ ][ ] solution; 22 /* See algorithm section. */ 23 Edge[ ] inners, outers, flats; 24 Piece[ ] corners; 26 /* See Algorithm section. */ 27 void sort() { ... } 28 void solve() { ... } 29 } AIgorithm to Solve the Puzzle We will sketch this algorithm using a mix of pseudocode and real code. Just as a kid might in solving a puzzle, we'll start with the easiest pieces first: the corners and edges. We can easily search through all the pieces to find just the edges. While we're at it though, it probably makes sense to group all the pieces by their edge types. 1 void sort() { 2 for each Piece p in pieces { ; 3 if (P has two flat edges) then add p to corners 4 for each edge in p.edges { 5 if edge is inner then add to inners 6 if edge is outer then add to outers 7 } 8 } 9 } We now have a quicker way to zero in on potential matches for any given edge. We then go through the puzzle, line by line, to match pieces. The solve method, implemented below, operates by picking an arbitrary start with. It then finds an open edge on the corner and tries to match it to an open piece. When it finds a match, it does the following: 1. Attaches the edge. 2. Removes the edge from the list of open edges. 3. Finds the next open edge. The next open edge is defined to be the one directly opposite the current edge, if it is available. If it is not available, then the next edge can be any other edge. This will cause the puzzle to be solved in a spiral-like fashion, from the outside to the inside. The spiral comes from the fact that the algorithm always moves in a straight line, whenever possible. When we reach the end of the first edge, the algorithm moves to the only available edge on that corner piece—a 90-degree turn. It continues to take 90-degree turns at the end of each side until the entire outer edge of the puzzle is completed. When that last edge piece is in place, that piece only has one exposed edge remaining, which is again a 90-degree turn. The algorithm repeats itself for subsequent rings around the puzzle, until finally all the pieces are in place. This algorithm is implemented below with Java-like pseudocode. 1 public void solve() { 2 /* Pick any corner to start with */ 3 Edge currentEdge = getExposedEdge(corner[0]); 5 /* Loop will iterate in a spiral like fashion until the puzzle * is full. */ 7 while (currentEdge != null) { 8 /* Match with opposite edges. Inners with outers, etc. */ 9 Edge[ ] opposites = currentEdge.type == inner ? outers : inners; 11 for each Edge fittingEdge in opposites { 12 if (currentEdge.fitsWith(fittingEdge)) { 13 attachEdges(currentEdge, fittingEdge); //attach edge 14 removeFromlist(currentEdge); 15 removeFromList(fittingEdge); 17 /* get next edge */ 18 currentEdge = nextExposedEdge(fittingEdge); 19 break; // Break out of inner loop. Continue in outer. 20 } 21 } 22 } 23 } 25 public void removeFromList(Edge edge) { 26 (edge.type == flat) return; 27 Edge[ ] array = currentEdge.type == inner ? inners : outers; 28 array.remove(edge); 29 } 31 /* Return the opposite edge if possible. Else, return any exposed * edge. */ 33 public Edge nextExposedEdge(Edge edge) { 34 int next_index = (edge.index + 2) % 4; // Opposite edge 35 Edge next_edge = edge.parent.edges[next_index]; 36 if isExposed(next_edge) { 37 return next_edge; 38 } 39 return getExposedEdge(edge.parent); 40 } 42 public Edge attachEdges(Edge e1, Edge e2) { 43 el.attached_to = e2; 44 e2.attached_to = e1; 45 } 47 public Edge isExposed(Edge e1) { return edge.type != flat && edge.attached_to == null; 49 } 51 public Edge getExposedEdge(Piece p) { 52 for each Edge edge in p.edges { 53 if (isExposed(edge)) { 54 return edge; 55 } 56 } 57 return null; 58 } For simplicity, we’re represented inners and outers as an Edge array. This is actually not a great choice, since we need to add and removed elements from it frequently. If we were writing a real code, we would probably want to implement these variables as linked lists. Writing the full code for this problem in an interview would be far, far too much work. More likely, you would be asked to just sketch out the code. 8.7 Explain how you would design a chat server. In particular, provide details about the various backend components, classes, and methods. What would be the hardest problems to solve? SOLUTION Designing a chat server is a huge project, and it is certainly far beyond the scope of what could be completed in an interview. After all, teams of many people spend months or years creating a chat server. Part of your job, as a candidate, is to focus on an aspect of the problem that is reasonably broad, but focused enough that you could accomplish it during an interview. It need not match real life exactly, but it should be a fair representation of an actual implementation. For our purposes, we'll focus on the core user management and conversation aspects: adding a user, creating a conversation, updating one's status, and so on. In the interest of time and space, we will not go into the networking aspects of the problem, or how the data actually gets pushed out to the clients. We will assume that \"friending\" is mutual; I am only your contact if you are mine. Our chat system will support both group chat and one-on-one (private) chats. We will not worry about voice chat, video chat, or file transfer. What specific actions does it need to support? This is also something to discuss with your interviewer, but here are some ideas: • Signing online and offline. • Add requests (sending, accepting, and rejecting). • Updating a status message. • Creating private and group chats. • Adding new messages to private and group chats. This is just a partial list. If you have more time, you can add more actions. What can we learn about these requirements? We must have a concept of users, add request status, online status, and messages. What are the core components of the system? The system would likely consist of a database, a set of clients, and a set of servers. We won't include these parts in our object-oriented design, but we can discuss the overall view of the system. The database will be used for more permanent storage, such as the user list or chat archives. A SQL database is a good bet, or, if we need more scalability, we could potentially use BigTable or a similar system. For communication between the client and servers, using XML will work well. Although it’s not the most compressed format (and you should point this out to your interviewer), it’s nice because it's easy for both computers and humans to read. Using XML will make your debugging efforts easier—and that matters a lot. The server will consist of a set of machines. Data will be divided up across machines, requiring us to potentially hop from machine to machine. When possible, we will try to replicate some data across machines to minimize the lookups. One major design constraint here is to prevent having a single point of failure. For instance, if one machine controlled all the user sign-ins, then we'd cut off millions of users potentially if a single machine lost network connectivity. What are the key objects and methods? What problems would be the hardest to solve (or the most interesting)? The following questions may be interesting to discuss with your interviewer further.
