Clients can push data to us—what if they try to DOS (denial of service) us? How do we prevent that? 8.8 Othello is played as follows: Each Othello piece is white on one side and black on the other. When a piece is surrounded by its opponents on both the left and right sides, or both the top and bottom, it is said to be captured and its color is flipped. On your turn, you must capture at least one of your opponent's pieces. The game ends when either user has no more valid moves. The win is assigned to the person with the most pieces. Implement the object-oriented design for Othello. SOLUTION Let’s start with an example. Suppose we have the following moves in an Othello game: 1. Initialize the board with two black and two white pieces in the center. The black pieces are placed at the upper left hand and lower right hand corners. 2. Play a black piece at (row 6, column 4). This flips the piece at (row 5, column 4) from white to black. 3. Play a white piece at (row 4, column 3). This flips the piece at (row 4, column 4) from black to white. This sequence of moves leads to the board below. The core objects in Othello are probably the game, the board, the pieces (black or white), and the players. How do we represent these with elegant object-oriented design? Should BlackPiece and WhitePiece be classes? At first, we might think we want to have a BlackPiece class and a WhitePiece class, which inherit from an abstract Piece. However, this is probably not a great idea. Each piece may flip back and forth between colors frequently, so continuously destroying and creating what is really the same object is probably not wise. It may be better to just have a Piece class, with a flag in it representing the current color. Do we need separate Board and Game classes? Strictly speaking, it may not be necessary to have both a Game object and a Board object. Keeping the objects separate allows us to have a logical separation between the board (which contains just logic involving placing pieces) and the game (which involves times, game flow, etc.). However, the drawback is that we are adding extra layers to our program. A function may call out to a method in Game, only to have it immediately call Board. We have made the choice below to keep Game and Board separate, but you should discuss this with your interviewer. Who keeps score? We know we should probably have some sort of score keeping for the number of black and white pieces. But who should maintain this information? One could make a strong argument for either Game or Board maintaining this information, and possibly even for Piece (in static methods). We have implemented this with Board holding this information, since it can be logically grouped with the board. It is updated by Piece or Board calling colorChanged and colorAdded methods within Board. Should Game be a Singleton class? Implementing Game as a singleton class has the advantage of making it easy for anyone to call a method within Game, without having to pass around references to the Game object. Making Game a singleton though means that it can only be instantiated once. Can we make this assumption? You should discuss this with your interviewer. One possible design for Othello is below. 1 public enum Direction { 2 left, right, up, down 3 } 5 public enum Color { 6 White, Black 7 } 9 public class Game { 10 private Player[ ] players; 11 private static Game instance; 12 private Board board; 13 private final int ROWS = 10; 14 private final int COLUMNS = 10; 16 private Game() { 17 board = new Board(ROWS, COLUMNS); 18 players = new Player[2]; 19 players[0] = new Player(Color.Black); 20 players[1] = new Player(Color.White); 21 } 23 public static Game getlnstance() { 24 if (instance == null) instance = new Game(); 25 return instance; 26 } 28 public Board getBoard() { 29 return board; 30 } 31 } The Board class manages the actual pieces themselves. It does not handle much of the game play, leaving that up to the Game class. 1 public class Board { 2 private int blackCount = 0; 3 private int whiteCount = 0; 4 private Piece[ ][ ] board; 6 public Board(int rows, int columns) { 7 board = new Piece[rows][columns]; 8 } 10 public void initialize() { 11 /* initialize center black and white pieces */ 12 } 14 /* Attempt to place a piece of color color at (row, column). * Return true if we were successful. */ 16 public boolean placeColor(int row, int column, Color color) { … } 20 /* flips pieces starting at (row, column) and proceeding in * direction d. */ 22 private int flipSection(int row, int column, Color color, Direction d) { ... } 25 public int getScoreForColor(Color c) { 26 if (c == Color.Black) return blackCount; 27 else return whiteCount; 28 } 30 /* Update board with additional newPieces pieces of color *newColor. SOLUTION Suppose we are implementing a hash table that looks like Hash<K, V>. That is, the hash table maps from objects of type K to objects of type V. At we might think our data structure would look something like this: 1 public class Hash<K, V> { 2 LinkedList<V>[ ] items; 3 public void put(K key, V value) { ... } 4 public V get(K key) { . . . } 5 } Note that items is an array of linked lists, where items [i] is a linked list of all objects with keys that map to index i (that is, all the objects that collided at i). This would seem to work until we think more deeply about collisions. Suppose we have a very simple hash function that uses the string length. 1 public int hashCodeOfKey(K key) { 2 return key.toString() .length() % items.length; 3 } The keys jim and bob will map to the same index in the array, even though they are different keys. We need to search through the linked list to find the actual object that corresponds to these keys. But how would we do that? All we've stored in the linked list is the value, not the original key. This is why we need to store both the value and the original key. One way to do that is to create another object called Cell which pairs keys and values. With this implementation, our linked list is of type Cell. The code below uses this implementation. 1 public class Hash<K, V> { 2 private final int MAX_SIZE = 10; 3 LinkedList<Cell<K, V>>[ ] items; 5 public Hash() { 6 items = (LinkedList<Cell<K, V>>[ ]) new LinkedList[MAX_SIZE]; 7 } 9 /* Really, really stupid hash. */ 10 public int hashCodeOfKey(K key) { 11 return key.toString().length() % items.length; 12 } 14 public void put(K key, V value) { 15 int x = hashCodeOfKey(key); 16 if (items[x] == null) { 17 items[x] = new LinkedList<Cell<K, V»(); 18 } 20 LinkedList<Cell<K, V>> collided = items[x]; 22 /* Look for items with same key and replace if found */ 23 for (Cell<K, V> c : collided) { 24 if (c.equivalent(key)) { 25 collided.remove( c ) ; 26 break; 27 } 28 } 30 Cell<K, V> cell = new Cell<K, V>(key, value); 31 collided.add(cell); 32 } 34 public V get(K key) { 35 int x = hashCodedOfKey(key); 36 if (items[x] == null) { 37 return null; 38 } 39 LinkedList<Cell<K, V>> collided = items [x]; 40 for (Cell<K, V> c : collided) { 41 if (c.equivalent(key)) { 42 return c.getValue(); 43 } 44 } 46 return null; 47 } 48 } The Cell class pairs the data value and its key. This will allow us to search through the linked list (created by \"colliding,\" but different, keys) and find the object with the exact key value. 1 public class Cell<K, V> { 2 private K key; 3 private V value; 4 public Cell(K k, V v) { 5 key = k; 6 value = v; 7 } 9 public boolean equivalent(Cell<K, V> c) { 10 return equivalence.getKey()); 11 } 13 public boolean equivalent(K k) { 14 return key.equals(k); 15 } 17 public K getKey() { return key; } 18 public V getValue() { return value; } 19 } Another common implementation for a hash table is to use a binary search tree as the underlying data structure. If the 2 strings are unequal and both of even lengths, then we can split them to check for similarity if either of the conditions satisfy: First half of a is similar to second half of b AND second half of a is similar to first half of b. First half of a is similar to first half of b AND second half of a is similar to second half of b. You've been given 2 strings a and b. Offline HR Round Online Assessment The OA consisted of 4 DSA questions which were to be completed within 2 hours. The questions were as follows: 1. An escape game requires that players solve various puzzles to obtain objects that will aid them in escaping. In one such puzzle. Players are given an array of integers and a set of rules to follow in order. Here are the instructions given to the players: \"Given an array of integer values, maximize the points earned using the following method. 1. Choose a value v. Delete all elements of that value and add their sum to the points. 2. Delete all elements equal to v-1 or v-2 for no points 3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 until there are no more elements in the array. Calculate the maximum number of points that can be achieved by following these rules for an array of values. For example, array = [5, 6, 6, 4, 11], delete 11 for 11 points. Since there are no elements equal to 10 or 12, proceed with the remaining elements [5, 6, 6, 4]. Delete the two 6s for 12 more points. Delete any elements equal to 6-1=5 or 6+1=7. Then proceed with the remaining elements: [4]. Finally delete the 4 and add 4 points for total points 11+12+4=27. I solved it by using 2D memoized DP with the states being the current index and previous index, and by using the frequency of each element I calculated the maximum points possible by taking the current element into score only when element-1 is not taken, which can be achieved by sorting the array beforehand. I was able to pass all the testcases. 2. A subarray is a contiguous portion of an array, Given an array of Integers, determine the number of distinct subarrays that can be formed having at most a given number of odd elements. Two subarrays are distinct if they differ at even one position in their contents. Example: Array = [1, 2, 3, 4] The following is a list of the 8 distinct valid subarrays having no more than 1 odd element: [[1], [2], [3], [4], [1,2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [2, 3, 4]]. Since the constraints of the problem were n<=1000, it was easily possible to brute force all possible subarrays in O(n^2) and count the odd elements in that particular subarray. For tougher constraints, a sliding window approach would be the key to go. I was able to pass all the testcases. 3. A subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another string by deleting some or no elements, but without changing the order of the remaining characters.For this puzzle, you need to determine if the second string can be formed from the first string by removing certain characters, and if so, calculate the difference value, which represents the index where the transformation of the second string from the first string occurs. The difference value is the sum of the index differences between the characters of the second string and the matching characters from the first string, where the difference is computed as the maximum index among removed characters in firstString minus the minimum index among the removed characters in secondString. Example: Input:firstString = \"HACKERRANK\" secondString = \"HACKERMAN\" Output:1 Explanation: To form the secondString = \"HACKERMAN\" as a subsequence from firstString = \"HACKERRANK\", you can remove the character 'M' at index 7 in secondString, and the remaining string will still be a valid subsequence of firstString which will be HACKERRAN. The difference value is 7−7+1=0+1=1. Therefore, the function should return 1, indicating the necessary index transformation. This problem was on the tougher side, but still I maintained my calm and started thinking of some approach. I calculated the frequencies of characters in both the strings and ran a loop over the frequency map of the second string. If the frequency of the character in the second string was greater than the first string, I added the difference to the answer else I added the frequency in the second string. I was able to pass 9 test cases out of 15. 4. Given a list of employees where each is assigned a numeric evaluation score, use the selection process below to find the sum of scores of selected employees 1. The employee with the highest score among the first k employees or last & employees in the score list are selected. 2. The selected employee is removed from the score list. 3. The process continues to select the next employee until the team size is achieved. Note: 1. In case multiple employees have the same highest score, the employee with the lowest Index is selected. 2. If there are fewer than k employees, the entire list is available for selection. Example score [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 30, 20] teamSize= 2 k= 3 • For the first selection, choose from the first 3 elements [10, 20, 10] or the last 3 elements: [5, 30, 20] . Score 30 is selected and removed from the list. This makes the score = [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 20] For the second selection, choose from [10, 20, 10] or [15, 5, 20] . Score 20 is selected from the lowest index and removed from the list. This makes score = [10, 10, 15, 5, 20] The sum of the selected employees' scores is 30+20=50. I solved this problem with the help of a max priority_queue of {number,flag}, flag was 1 for first k elements and 0 for last k elements, thus maximum number came to the top and if equal elements were present, the one with flag 1(among the first k elements) became the one we choose. I ran a loop for team size removing the numbers from the priority queue and adding more using two pointers, one for first k elements with flag set and another for last k elements with flag 0. I was able to pass all the testcases. I was able to pass all the test cases for three questions and 9 test cases for the third one. A total of 100 students were shortlisted for this test, which consisted of four sections. You can navigate between the questions. Section 1 : Aptitude (30 Questions in 30 mins) The first 10 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) were based on English Usage covering topics such as antonyms, synonyms and passage-based questions. The next 10 MCQs were focused on Analytical Reasoning including questions related to flowcharts, patterns and statements with conclusions. The final 10 MCQs pertained to Quantitative Aptitude covering topics like profit-loss, missing terms and probability. Section 2 : Machine Learning (20 questions in 20 mins) All 20 MCQs were based on machine learning (ML) algorithms like Random Forest, Hypothesis Testing, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Neural Networks etc. Section 3 : Written English Test (25 mins) In this section we were asked to write reviews on the given topic (Around 250 words) Topic : We should use less plastic in our life. Section 4 : Coding Questions (2 Questions in 60 mins) 1. Longest Substring of Even length Statement : You are given a string s of length n. The string s consists of digits varying from 0-9. Find and print the length of the longest even length substring of string s, such that the length of substring is 2k digits and the sum of left k digits is equal to the sum of right k digits. Note : Print 0 if no such substring is possible with the given condition Input Format : The first line contains an integer denoting n The second line contains a string denoting s Output : The length of the longest even length substring Link : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/longest-even-length-substring-sum-first-second-half/ I was able to solve this completely. 2. Minimum strength to reach destination Statement : You are given a matrix mat of size m*n. Each cell of a matrix contains strength. A robot needs a positive strength to travel from the top left corner of the matrix to the bottom right corner. At any point of the journey, its strength cannot drop to 0 or less. The cells can contain either 0, positive or negative strength. Positive strength increases the robots strength by cell value, negative strength decreases its strength by cell value and no change in strength if the cell value is 0. You are required to calculate the minimum initial strength required by the robot to travel from the source to reach the destination. Note : A robot can only move one cell at a time, either down or right, i.e to cell (i+1,j) or cell (i,j+1) and it cannot move outside the matrix. mat[0][0] = mat[m-1][n-1] = 0 Input Format : The first line contains two space-separated integers i.e no of rows m and columns n The second line contains m*n integers separated by space (Elements of matrix) Output Format : Print the minimum initial strength required by the robot to travel from source to destination. The question was similar to this one : https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/minimum-positive-points-to-reach-destination/ I was successfully able to pass all the test cases for this problem. 12 students were shortlisted for online interviews which were scheduled on MS teams. Round 2 - Technical + HR Since it was an online interview, there was one panel with 3-4 interviewers, including HR. Initially, HR introduced herself, but before we could start the interview, there was a delay on my side. HR then asked me to re-login to the meeting, which took me around 5-8 minutes to join due to my poor network connection. I felt a bit frustrated during this time because of the technical issues. After re-joining the meeting, HR started with a very common question, which you all are familiar with : 'Please introduce yourself.' Typically, in many interviews, technical questions are asked first, followed by HR-related questions. However, in my case, the interview began with HR questions right away. After hearing my introduction, she asked, 'Where are you from?' I replied, 'I'm from Mumbai, Thane.' She then mentioned that most of their branches are located in Chennai, Hyderabad and Bangalore, but since I'm from Mumbai, asked if I would be able to relocate. I assured her that I am flexible with regard to locations. Next, she requested to see my Aadhar card, mostly for verification purposes. Following that, she inquired about my knowledge of NPCI products. I explained this question very thoroughly and she seemed quite impressed with my response. She then proceeded to ask some of the common HR questions: 'Why should we hire you and why NPCI?' After this, she stated that this concludes her portion of the interview and another interviewer will continue from here. However, she remained present in the meeting throughout the entire interview. The next interviewer was very friendly and conducted my technical interview. He started by asking me to explain my projects. Initially, I provided an overview of all the projects. Afterward I asked, Shall I explain each of them one by one or would you like information about a specific one? He then responded, Explain the project you liked the most. I chose a project based on Machine Learning. Since I was well-prepared with that. After I finished explaining, he shifted the focus to questions about data pre-processing. I managed to answer scenario-based questions quite well, except for one that it involved extracting a movie name, for instance, 'ABC___,' and determining how to obtain 'A_B_C' from the dataset. However, before proceeding further into Python-related questions, I made it clear to him that I am proficient in C++ and have limited experience in Python, aside from one ML-based project. I'd like to emphasize a point here: if you encounter a situation in an interview where you're asked about a specific tech stack or subject that you haven't mentioned in your resume and have no knowledge about, it's better to inform the interviewer.   "preview": "Param Parekh shares his placement experience at Axxela Research and Analytics Private Limited for the Trainee Analyst role, detailing the online tests, virtual trading simulation, and technical interview.",
  "content": "Name: Param Parekh\nCourse: BTech (2022-26)\nBranch: Electronics and Telecommunication engineering\nReg. no: 221090049\nCompany: Axxela Research and Analytics Private Limited\nRole: Trainee Analyst\nLocation: Mumbai\n\nEligibility:\nBTech - all branches\nCGPA >= 5\nX and XII >=50%\nNo backlog\n\nHiring Workflow:\n1. PPT\n2. Online Test 1\n3. Online Test 2\n4. Technical Interview\n\nOnline Test 1:\nThere were 4 sections and test was conducted offline on campus\n\nSection 1 - Behavioral questions\nBasic questions about trading in equities, risk-taking psychology, risk management techniques, personal questions like what would you do in this case\n\nSection 2 - Speed Maths\nBasic Algebraic problems\n6-8 algebraic problems combined into 1 question and such 5 questions\nCalculation is easy but very limited time is given so focus on speed and accuracy.\nDo mental math more over here to save time.\n\nSection 3 - Numerical Aptitude\nQuestions on number series, AP, GP, interest calculation, profit/loss calculation, direction-based questions, algebraic equation solving, ratio and proportion, train-crossing questions\n\nSection 4 - Logical Reasoning\nAge-based calculation, pattern-matching, mirror-image, find correct pattern sequence when cube is unfolded given 3 pictures of the cube, find blood relation based on other relations, Circular sitting arrangement on table and who is sitting next to whom, statement and conclusion type-of questions\n\nOnline Test 2:\nAfter clearing Online Test 1, there was a virtual trading simulation round in CCF III. The main objective was to test profit-making skills based on a real-time demand-supply market scenario. Total 38 candidates including me qualified for this round. 4 groups of 8-10 candidates were formed by them (Axxela). Trading simulation was carried-out within the group. There were 9 rounds; in each round a digit from a 9-digit number will be revealed. You have to quickly calculate the minimum and maximum possible number i.e. determine the range based on the already revealed digits and the remaining digits. Each digit from 0 to 9 will appear only once. Within the range you have to predict the most likely value based on the prediction in the previous round. First round will be spontaneous but slowly it will converge to some range of value. You have only 2 options “Buy” and “Sell”. On top right there will be a holdings section and total count section. Total count can only range from -2 to +2. Holdings section will show at what price you purchased. At any moment of time during the gameplay your aim should be to buy at the minimum possible price and sell at the maximum possible price so as to maximize the profit. All this while staying closer to the probable true price or else closer to the most common bidding range within the group. On your trading screen all the group member names and their buy/sell bid with price will be visible on which you have to keep a close eye as well as you have to keep in attention your holdings. A trade gets executed automatically whenever a buy and a sell order gets matched. My strategy was to neither buy more nor sell more so that I have both the options open all the time according to the situation i.e keep holdings count in range (-1 to +1). Buying adds one to the count and selling subtracts one from the count. However if the deal favours profit you can go to +2 or -2. I was not bidding for sell at very high price and waiting for it to be executed, which was done by most of the other candidates. I utilized something called as market momentum i.e. keep less margin but execute more number of trades, following the broader trend visible from available buy/sell bids. Because of this my total profit at the end of 9 rounds was significantly higher than others and I qualified for the Technical Interview round. In this round remember that the final score that will be displayed after 9 rounds will be different from the profit that you’ve made because more points are awarded for trading close to average bidding range and making profit rather than for bidding extraordinarily high or low. So you have to be vigilant all the times and tap quickly for the right trade. An instructional video is available on YouTube\n\nTechnical Interview:\n\nTechnical interview was conducted at their Mumbai office at Lodha Supremus, Powai. I entered the interview room and the interviewer got angry because I was wearing sandals. This immediately made me nervous. I went in sandals because it was the monsoon month of August. He questioned whether it is the correct way to go for an interview. I got clueless here. However I said that during internship also I used to wear sandals because of monsoon and in fact everyone in the office used to wear sandals. There is a concept in corporate settings to carry formal shoes when travelling and wear those on reaching office. I was surprisingly unaware of this and therefore shocked. However the interviewer moved on and asked about my internship - what was my domain of work and what was my role and what was my stipend over there. I was into a data analytics firm where I had worked on structuring raw data using SQL and prepared business reports using Power BI. Later he asked why I did not get PPO there to which I replied stating that the minimum training period over there is 6 months for a full-time role and I worked for 2 months according to our course format. Then he started asking about the stock market and whether have traded previously or not. I have long trading experience in the equity market. I had carried with me my trade logs (trading history) of the past two years. He checked and verified the prices in those. My most of the trades were profitable so I think this impressed the interviewer. He then asked about what technical indicators do I look at while trading. I explained all those namely MA, MACD, RSI, Bollinger bands, DMI, Stochastic oscillator along with how to interpret them for identifying market trends and making buy-sell decision. After this the interviewer asked a psychological question that what would you choose - a trading job or a tech job provided that within trading there will be a filtering and only 40% will survive after 1 year but after that earning prospects would be high and on other hand in tech there will be no filtering but earning prospects would also be limited. To this I answered that I would choose a trading job. I gave reasoning that I have passion for trading, I have a family background in trading and brokerage and I believe that tech jobs are prone to many external factors like geopolitical up-downs and AI developments which are a kind of threat while on the other hand in a trading job only my skills and performance in terms of profit/loss matters. So in this point of view a trading job is more secure than a tech job. However he did not look convinced and started to counter by saying that your resume strongly says that you are a tech enthusiast then how will you perform in the trading industry. I countered by saying that technological tools equip traders in making well-informed decisions so tech background will prove beneficial for a trading role. He countered by saying that it applies to investment banking certainly but this is a prop trading firm so it might not be suitable for you. To this I replied that this role as well as the company are very well suitable for me because I perform well in fast-paced and individualistic environments as demanded by this role. It is evident from my resume also. After that he said checking his laptop that my scores in the test were good and asked what my strategy was in the trading simulation. I explained my thinking as stated in the previous section and I believe it impressed him. Then he asked a mental math question “78*79=?” to which I calculated as 78*80 - 78 without pen/paper and answered 6162. Then he asked an analytical question “what is angle between hour hand and minute hand at 3:15 pm ?”.   "content": "Interview Experience BNY MELLON Stipend:75,000/month ADWAITA PATANE B.Tech Electronics Engineering Procedure 1. Online Assessment(OA) 2. Offline PPT 3. Offline Technical Round 4. Offline HR Round Online Assessment The OA consisted of 4 DSA questions which were to be completed within 2 hours. The questions were as follows: 1. Redundancy Maximizer We have been given a binary string servers where: '1' means a server is working. '0' means a server is redundant (backup). We want to find the number of distinct possible counts of working servers after optimally flipping a contiguous segment of servers (i.e., changing '0' → '1' or '1' → '0'). Example 1 Input: servers = \"1100\" Original working servers = 2. Flip \"0\" → \"1\" → 3 working servers. Flip \"00\" → \"11\" → 4 working servers. Flip \"1\" → \"0\" → 1 working server. Possible counts = {1, 2, 3, 4} → Answer = 4 Example 2 Input: servers = \"111\" Original working = 3. Flipping any subarray decreases count. Possible counts = {1, 2, 3} → Answer = 3 Approach what I did was, I kind of treated this like Kadane’s algorithm (the max subarray sum thing). I thought of every '0' as a +1 (since flipping it gives me one more working server) and every '1' as a -1 (since flipping it means I lose one working server). Then I just looked for the subarray that gives me the biggest gain, and also the one that gives me the biggest loss. Once I had those, I just added them to the original count of working servers to figure out the minimum and maximum I could possibly get. Finally, the answer is just the range of values from that minimum to that maximum. 2. Optimal Team Size We are given n players. For each player, we have: lowerSkill[i]: minimum skill position they can play. higherSkill[i]: maximum skill position they can play. We want to find the largest possible team size we can form, such that for each position from 0 to teamSize-1, some player can fit there (within their skill range). Example 1 Input: lowerSkill = [0, 1, 2] higherSkill = [2, 2, 2] We can form team of size 3 because: Player 1 fits position 0 Player 2 fits position 1 Player 3 fits position 2 Answer = 3 Example 2 Input: lowerSkill = [0, 0, 1] higherSkill = [1, 2, 2] Max possible team size = 2 (cannot place 3 players because constraints won’t match) Answer = 2 Approach just used Binary Search on the possible team size. For each mid value, I checked if it’s actually possible to form a team of that size using a greedy method (I called it canFormTeam). If it worked, then I moved the search to the right (trying for a bigger team). If it didn’t work, I moved left (settling for a smaller team). 3. Cluster Sizes (DSU / Union-Find) Given are a list of integers serverProp. Each number represents a server property (like an ID). Two servers belong to the same cluster if they share any factor greater than 1. Find the size of the cluster each server belongs to. Example 1 Input: serverProp = [5, 10, 15, 20] 10 shares factor 5 with 5. 15 shares factor 5 with 5. 20 shares factor 10 with 10. All are connected. Output = [4, 4, 4, 4] Example 2 Input: serverProp = [7, 11, 13] All are prime, no shared factors. Each cluster size = 1. Output = [1, 1, 1] Approach Use Disjoint Set Union (DSU).For each number, union it with all its factors.After union, count cluster sizes by root.Output cluster size for each element. 4. High Priority Subset We are given n intervals with: start[i]: start time of a task. finish[i]: finish time of a task. We want to find the maximum size of a subset of intervals such that all of them overlap with at least one common task. Example 1 Input: start = [1, 2, 3, 4] finish = [2, 3, 5, 5] Task 3 ([3,5]) overlaps with tasks 2 ([2,3]) and 4 ([4,5]). Max overlapping subset = {2,3,4} size 3. Answer = 3 Example 2 Input: start = [1, 5, 9] finish = [4, 8, 12] No three overlap at once. Max subset size = 1. Answer = 1 Approach For each interval, check how many other intervals overlap with it Take maximum overlap count. I had solved All the testcases for the medium-hard and easy problems and 14/15 for the two medium problems so I was pretty confident about my chances of getting shortlisted for the interview and called my seniors to ask how to prepare for it. This information might be asked later in the HR interviews to check you attentiveness. The PPT also helps you come up with thoughtful questions for the interviewers, which is essential when they ask, \"Do you have any questions for us?\" You should always have a couple of good questions ready for this. The shortlisted students were announced after the PPT. The first round was purely technical for me and the second round was taken by a senior person. Round 1:Technical Interview The interviews had started right after the PPT at around 12:30 pm, but my first interview didn’t begin until 3:30. Always they expect you to be a good learner so frame your replies to give them such an impression. Then she asked me to imagine a situation where I was arranging a party. She then asked me a coding question : Question: Given an array of 0s and 1s. I need to cluster the 1s at specific locations such that I do a minimum no of swaps. (of 0s and 1s) Eg Array [ 0, 1, 0 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 1] Here we hav 3 ones which can v=be clustered as [ 1 , 1, 1 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0] (2 swaps) [ 0, 1 , 1 , 1 , 0 , 0 ,0] (2 swaps) [ 0, 0, 1 , 1 , 1 , 0 , 0] (2 swaps) [ 0, 0, 0 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 0] (2 swaps) [ 0, 0, 0 , 0 , 1 , 1, 1] (1 swap) So the 1s can be clustered anywhere we just need to minimise the swaps. Community of Coders Solution: First I started with the approach of the pointer. Always discuss your solutions with the interviewer. Then while explaining the same I understood that it was a sliding window problem. Here the sum of the array would give the number of 1s and this would act as the length of the window. Check the sum of the first window ⇒ number of 1s in that window. Then the number of zeros would be nothing but the number of swaps for clustering the 1s in that window. Array [ 0, 1, 0 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 1] Sum = 3 (no of 1s) Window size = sum = 3 First window Array [ 0, 1, 0 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 1] ⇒ sum_of win = 1 So the number of swaps for this window ⇒ Sum - sum_of_win = 3 -1 =2 For the next window just check the incoming and outgoing values. Array [ 0, 1, 0 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 1] If same the no changes in sum_of win Else if incoming is 1 and outgoing is 0 ⇒ sum_of win++ Else if incoming is 0 and outgoing is 1 ⇒ sum_of win- - Then store the min Value for each iteration as mn = min (mn, Sum - sum_of_win ) She asked me to write the pseudo-code. Always keep a habit of explaining the code while writing. Explaining each module, time complexity and also dry run on one of the test cases. Then at the end, she asked if I had any questions for her. I asked her to suggest changes in my resume this helped me to understand how an interviewer goes through your resume. Community of Coders INTERVIEW SECOND ROUND (AROUND 1HR) 16/08/2022 Find the starting character of string 1 in string 2 Say you found it at loc (int) If not found then return false Then iterate through each character starting the string 1 from 0 and string2 from the loc. After some time we were sent for the second round of interviews. I was asked purely DSA questions this round. First, the interviewer asked me to introduce myself. I was also provided with coordinates for the same. Solution: I had practised this variety on Leetcode. Using DFS+backtracking I was able to solve this question. I was asked to write the entire code. Explain the modules, and the flow, dry run it on one of the test cases and discuss the time complexity. DSA Question 2 : Given two strings check if one was formed by rotating the other. Solution: Always start with a brute-force approach. Approach 1: Community of Coders Check for equality of each value if not equal at any point return false Return true at the end of the iteration. Append the string2 with itself and find the string1 in the resultant string. If found return true Else return false Here this can be solved using hashing such that given a node as key to the hashmap it would return the parent of that node (immediate ancestor). Use BFS to populate the hashmap For the root node, it would give null as a parent. After this over a while loop checks if node1 exists in the ancestry of node2 if yes then return true Else check again over a while loop check if node2 exists in the ancestry of node1 if yes then return true Else return false Approach 2: Eg string1 = “tree” , string2 =”etre” New_string = string2 +string2 ⇒ “etreetre” DSA Question 3: Given a tree (not a BST) check if the given path is valid. Then he asked me questions on fundamentals of java as java is my preferred language Questions asked : ●Can you overload main function in java - > Yes , but there is only one public static void main others cannot be the same . ●Difference between array and arraylist - > Array has a fixed size while the arraylist is dynamic and the interface that implements them are different . ●What is garbage collector in java - > Garbage collection in Java is the process by which Java programs perform automatic memory management. Java programs compile to bytecode that can be run on a Java Virtual Machine, or JVM for short. When Java programs run on the JVM, objects are created on the heap, which is a portion of memory dedicated to the program. Eventually, some objects will no longer be needed. The garbage collector finds these unused objects and deletes them to free up memory. ●How does garbage collector work in java - > By freeing up heap memory . Java garbage collection is an automatic process. Automatic garbage collection is the process of looking at heap memory, identifying which objects are in use and which are not, and deleting the unused objects. An in-use object, or a referenced object, means that some part of your program still maintains a pointer to that object. An unused or unreferenced object is no longer referenced by any part of your program. ●What are unreachable objects in java wrt to garbage collector -> Unreachable objects are the objects which when deleted cannot be dumped properly because they cannot be accessed directly .   "content": "Deutsche Bank Interview Experience. Technical Analyst Summer Internship. Arvind Mundhe, B.Tech IT’23. Online Coding Round(18 September 2021) HackerEarth coding challenge. The total time was 90 minutes. There were 2 coding questions and some MCQs based on CS fundamentals. Only IT/CS students were allowed to attempt the test. 1st coding question (10 test cases, 20 marks) 2nd coding question (15 test cases, 30 marks) 10 MCQs (40 marks) Total marks 90 I solved both the coding questions (passed all the test cases). And I was sure about 8-9 MCQs. Coding question 1 It was a variation of the 0/1 knapsack problem. I was able to solve it using the greedy approach. Given an array of different unsorted integers, an integer k and an int d(number of available operations) We were supposed to return the number of maximum possible multiples using the d number of operations. Where one operation means you can increment a particular element by one. For example, arr = 4 1 5 7 3 9 8 K = 4 D = 5 I solved this question by making an array of required operations per element to convert it into a multiple. arrReq = 0 3 3 1 1 3 0 Then I sorted this array arrReq = 0 0 1 1 3 3 3 Then I traversed the arrReq and maintained a counter variable (ans). When we came across 0 that means the number is already a multiple of k (in this case 4) So for 0, I incremented ans variable by one (we already have a multiple of 4 without any operation) Then for non zero numbers, I checked if we have the required number of operations left for turning that element into a multiple of 4 If yes, Then I incremented ans by one and updated the remaining available operations. And after traversing I returned the ans. Coding question 2 Given an array representing the chemical reactive powers of different reactants. And an int desired result. We were supposed to choose any 2 reactants such that the difference between their reactive powers should be close to the desired result. That is, we have to select reactants with diff as close as possible to the desired_result and maximum output(maximum summation). I don’t remember how they framed the question but it all boiled down to find the pair that satisfied both of the above conditions. I sorted the array, Traversed the array from the end using 2 for loops. maintained a min difference variable whenever the diff between the pair was closer to the desired result, I updated the answer variable to the summation of the powers. This solution passed 10/15 test cases. Then I changed the code to return the ans whenever the diff between the pair was equal to the desired result. As we are traversing from the end, the summation is going to be maximum. This code passed 15/15 test cases. Then he asked me to explain runtime polymorphism. I explained to him in detail about Dynamic polymorphism and then proceeded to tell him about polymorphism is one of four pillars of the OOPS paradigm. then explained static polymorphism too ;p Then we moved to Java, He asked me if I know java, I said I am aware of the syntactical differences but have no idea of the java collections framework. Each string in the sentence will be separated by a space and each space will be counted as one character.\nInput: N = 4, Array = [“priorityqueue”, “linkedlist”, “binarytree”, “adjacencymatrix”], Values = [5, 6, 9, 10]\nOutput: 19\nExplanation: When the last two strings from the array are selected, the sentence formed will be of length 10+1+15 = 26.\nTip: Although I didn't realise it at the moment, it was a standard 01 knapsack question. Section 3 (Advanced)\nGiven a graph, we can apply the operation an arbitrary number of times (possibly 0) to transform the given graph into a Complete Graph . An operation is defined as follows.\n1. Pick any vertex from the graph.\n2. Remove all pre existing edges from the vertex to other vertices.\n3. Add edges to all other vertices except the ones we removed in the previous step.\nWe have to figure out whether it's possible to obtain a complete graph from the given graph by applying the operation an arbitrary number of times.\nInput Graph:\nOutput: Complete Graph Possible\nExplanation: We have 3 nodes (1, 2 and 3) and have only 1 edge between nodes 1 and 2. We choose node 1, so the existing edge is removed, and the remaining edges are added. Then we finally select node 2, and the 2 remaining edges are added and we have a complete graph.\nTip: Go through the questions that you weren’t able to solve or think of an optimal approach for a question that you had solved in the online test. Given an array containing weights of stones, and an integer K representing maximum weight a box can contain (All boxes are uniform). Each box carries at most 2 stones at the same time, provided the sum of the weight of those stones is at the most limit of the box. All levels LinkedList from the given tree. Given two integers min and max denoting lowest and highest level of a tree and a tree was given. You need to return the head of the LinkedList of nodes that are within the given level of the tree. Example: Low = 2 High = 4 The output should be: 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> NULL Firstly I gathered all the nodes which are within the given level using level order traversal of the tree then I created a LinkedList from it. While creating the LinkedList from the gathered nodes I used the sentinel node technique so that for hidden TC’s I don't get TLE. 3. Overlap Binary Tree Given two binary trees tree1 and tree2. We need to overlap tree2 to tree1. The overlap rule was defined as follows: If two nodes overlap, then the node value will be of tree2 otherwise, the non-null node will be used as the node of the new tree. Example: Given two trees. The output tree should be: (You need to return the root of the new tree.) I used DFS to solve this problem. Basically traverse both the trees in the same order and if we have the node for tree2 then the output node would contain the same value as tree2 else will attach the non-null node to the tree. My recursive solution: TreeNode* overlap(TreeNode* tree1, TreeNode* tree2){ if(!tree1)return tree2; if(!tree2)return tree1; tree2->left = overlap(tree1->left,tree2->left); tree2->right = overlap(tree1->right,tree2->right); return tree2; } After 2 days results came and 2 students were shortlisted for the next round. It shows that you do have interest in the company. ● Keep some hard copies of your resume handy. They have a relatively easy process of selection and familiarity with basic coding is sufficient to clear it successfully. Following were the rounds conducted for hiring interns. Round 1: Online Test The online test consisted of 3 sections: 1. Quantitative: Basic math and logical ability questions which you regularly encounter in olympiads. The level of math is not above 10th grade and is very easy but the number of questions is high which makes it slightly harder. (30 mins) 2. Verbal: Basic English questions like “fill in the blanks”, comprehension etc. (typical AMCAT questions) (30 mins) 3. Coding: 2 questions of beginner level but everyone has a different set of questions. 1 of my question was to find the last digit of a^b for large values of a and b. The other one was easy as well. Everyone who had basic experience in coding did not take more than 10 minutes to solve both the questions. Round 2: Technical Interview After the online test around 30-35 people were shortlisted for the interviews. My interview began with a small introduction. After this the interviewer asked me to walk him through my resume. I explained all the projects I had mentioned in my resume and my extra-curricular activities. The interviewer also posed some technical queries to me relating to my project. After this he asked me to write a few simple codes in Java/C++(choice was given). After this he started asking situational questions designed to introduce some difficult choices and test how I would react. Banks usually conduct this round to gauge the professional fitness of the candidate. There is no right answer to these questions, just try to give ethically and morally sound responses and you should be good to go. Barclays, as is the case with most banks, was looking for students with sound knowledge in Database management systems, as well as a good foundation in any major programming language, preferably Java. They did not focus much on data structures or complex programming skills as most of their profiles relate to development and testing. Round 3: HR interview Barclays expects the candidates to know a bit about the company and they ask you questions about the values of Barclays. You can look up the full form of RISES on the Barclays website and prepare for questions on the same. The interviewer might ask you about examples of RISES in your life. You just have to convince the interviewer that you understand the meaning of every word in the acronym, and that you try to apply it in your personal/professional life. After these questions end the interviewer will inquire whether you have any queries. Make it a point to ask a question so as to show your interest towards joining the company. This leaves a lasting impression on your interviewer. Result: After this round the results were declared and a total of 12 people were selected from CS and IT. The results were skewed in favour of IT branch (8 from IT, 4 from comps). Internship Experience: The internship began on 20th May, a few days after my end semester exams. However only 10 out of the 12 people selected had received their offer letters. This was highly unprofessional from Barclays and the 2 remaining people had joined almost 5 weeks after I did. Also the old office did not have enough space and most of us were not allotted a permanent desk. Instead there was a rotation schedule where in the full time employees would take turns to work from home one day of the week and we would sit in their places for the day. However this should not be a problem anymore since they have shifted to a new office building. I had been assigned an interesting project related to Optical Character Recognition (OCR). But I was very lucky in this. Many of my friends were stuck on testing projects and were asking to be shifted to other teams. This is the harsh truth about working in a bank. If you are lucky, you will get to work on a challenging and engaging project. It is also possible that you might have to work in testing which in comparison is not as fun. Also the desktops I had to work on came with Windows 7 which is again a pretty big disadvantage of working at banks. Banks are reluctant when it comes to accepting new technologies before their security has been proven. This is why it is hard to get work on modern operating systems and technology stacks and there is a tedious procedure for installation of necessary software which eats up a lot of valuable time. We were also encouraged to meet with Directors and Managing Directors (MDs) of various departments as part of their overall intern development. We set up meetings with them, asked them about their roles and career paths and gained insightful information. We were also lucky to have a meeting with the BX India co-CEO, Mr. Praveen Kumar and the Chief Security Officer Mr. Tim McNulty, and leave with the inspirational session in mind. In addition to this, we also took part in one of the regular social drives that take place in the company. The office location is in Kharadi, Pune and Barclays provides transport to and from your residence. Travelling in Pune otherwise is very costly owing to the traffic and poor public transport. Apart from the large stipend they offered an additional 25k a month as a relocation benefit which makes it easy to find comfortable accommodation like OYO rooms (Hostels and PGs are horrible and squalid in Pune). Pre-Placement Offer: Barclays conducts two reviews with your line-manager and here is your chance to discuss your position on the pre-placement offer. Problem Maximum index a pointer can reach in N steps by avoiding a given index B - GeeksforGeeks There is an infinite array of integers numbered consecutively from 0. At each step, a pointer can move from index i to index i+j, or remain where it is. The value of i begins at 0. The value of j begins at 1 and at each step, j increments by 1. There is one known index that must be avoided. Determine the highest index that can be reached in a given number of steps. Example steps = 4 badElement = 6 The pointer is limited to 4 steps and should avoid the bad item 6. ● Scenario 1: ○ In the first step, j starts at 1. ○ Move 1 unit to index 0+1=1 and j=2. ○ At step 2, move 2 units to index 1+2-3, and j=3. ○ At step 3, do not move. Now j=2. ○ At step 2, move 2 units to index 0+2-2 and j=3. ○ At step 3, move 3 units to index 2+3=5 and j=4 ○ At step 4, move 4 units to index 5+4=9 The maximum index that can be reached is 9. >> First line of input shows the number of steps. At step 2, move 2 units to step 1+2=3. Sidenote: Maximum Index - My approach Okay, so if you did find an approach, great! But don’t worry if you did not… Let’s look at my observations and approach. Observation I looked at the examples and figured out 2 things: 1. The aim is to maximize the final index. 2. A step means either to “stay” at the same index or “move on”. 3. The leap I can take increases with each step. (At the 5th step my leap is of 5 indexes) 4. I cannot take a leap in which I encounter the bad index/bad element. Approach Let’s forget about the bad index for a second and just focus on the step choice. I figured that I should aim to always choose to “move on” when at a higher index, otherwise I will miss out on the opportunity of taking a giant leap. What this means is, IF I want to “stay” I should prefer to “stay” early on in the game rather than later, otherwise I will miss out on a giant leap later on. Example: Initially i=0, j=1 (according to problem statement) ● I choose to stay at 0, and j counter increases to 2 now. ● I choose to stay at 0, and the j counter increases to 3 now. ● I choose to stay at 0 again and the j counter increases to 4 now. Observe that with each choice/step, the value of j increases, and I am missing out on an opportunity to jump ‘j’ number of steps. So I should choose to “stay” only at the initial stage of the game where the stakes are low and my leap value is least (this happens when i=0, j=1). We want to keep leaping in order to maximize the final landing index. Okay so one major thing out of the way, I should “stay” ONLY IF i=0, j=1. Otherwise I won’t be maximizing the final index. So what about the bad index/bad element? I want to avoid leaping onto the bad index at any step. I can avoid this easily. Notice in the example: steps = 4 badElement = 6 The pointer is limited to 4 steps and should avoid the bad item 6. ● Scenario 1: ○ In the first step, j starts at 1. ○ Move 1 unit to index 0+1=1 and j=2. ○ At step 2, move 2 units to index 1+2-3, and j=3. ○ At step 3, do not move. Otherwise point moves 3 units to bad item 6. Now j=4. ○ At step 4, move 4 units to item 3+4=7. ● Scenario 2: ○ At step 1, remain at index 0. Now j=2. ○ At step 2, move 2 units to index 0+2-2 and j=3. ○ At step 3, move 3 units to index 2+3=5 and j=4 ○ At step 4, move 4 units to index 5+4=9 The maximum index that can be reached is 9. In scenario 1: We chose to move at step 1 itself. Then we choose to not move at step 3 since we’ll encounter the bad element, thus missing out on a leap of 3 units. 0->1->3->(stay)->3->7 In scenario 2: What if we chose to not move at step 1 itself? Now j=2. Obviously we won’t encounter the bad index=6 now, because the leap distance has changed by 1 for each step and thus we will be off by one unit. So now if we keep leaping: 0->(stay)->2->5->9. So all you have to do is, find out: max ( final index when leap at step 1, final index when stay at step 1 ) ( Final index when stay at step 1 will be ) > ( Final index when leap at step 1 ) ONLY if the bad index lies in the path of ( Final index when leap at step 1 ) and the reverse is also true.",

But here’s the catch: given\nan integer k, each character in the second string can be increased or decreased ci times, such that\nsum(ci) over all i is less than k, to get the LCS.\nEg:\nString 1:  a x d a j\nString 2: a c b y l\nAnd k = 6,\nSo my second string will be changed as follows:\na\nc\nb -> c -> d  (c2 = 2), moving ahead by two alphabets\ny -> z -> a (c4 = 2), ‘z’ can move to ‘a’ and ‘a’ can move back to ‘a’\nl -> k -> j   (c5 = 2), moving behind my two alphabets\nString 2 becomes: a c d a j\nd a j is the LCS\nThis is a problem I(or anyone of the other candidates I asked later) had never seen before. The only\nsaving grace was that at its core it was still LCS. So, I started by describing the DP approach to LCS and\nhow the tabulation for the same will be done. And as I kept talking, I realized that we can use recursion\nfor each cell in the table. At each char where we have a choice to increase or decrease it, we make two\nrecursive calls, where each call will lead to a different table and choose the one which leads to the max\nLCS.\nFurther, I mentioned we can use memoization to eliminate the tables which were already generated. I\neven mentioned more fine grained tabulation for each cell in each table. If it had already been calculated\nfor a previous tabulation, then using appropriate data structure, we can use those values from memory.\nHonestly speaking, I have no idea how I managed to come up with such a good solution in the first go.\nBut the interviewer was quite impressed, and asked me to immediately start coding it midway through my\nexplanation. I used multidim lists for all the data structures and while the code was quite convoluted in its\nfirst draft, I managed to make it quite clean, presentable and working by the end\nFollow Up\nSince my coding question ran upwards of 45 mins, I was relieved to realize that I wasn’t going to be asked\nany further coding questions. The second interviewer then asked me a few basic questions on OS and C,\nwhich I managed to answer.\nAt the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions for them. Always ask a question, it shows you are\ninterested. I asked them what the actual work is like in an Internship at D.E. Shaw and what the past experiences\nof them as mentors have been like. They happily answered both questions.\nThe results for this final round came at about 9:40 PM and 2 students were\nselected. I was fortunate to be one of them!\nTips\nRelated to DSA:\nI personally had never delved too deep into either Competitive Programming or regularly practicing DSA.\nThe only resource I relied on were my DSA notes I had made for Computer Engineering Sem 3 while\nwatching Abdul Bari’s Algorithms Playlist. I would highly recommend referring to Sarvagnya’s experience\nfor some actually good resources.\nRelated to Core CS (OS, DBMS, OOPS):\nGeeksForGeeks, Gate Smashers, Neso Academy are your best friends for college courses or otherwise.\nTry to understand the core concepts instead of mugging up the material. I personally make notes on\nGDocs or on a Note making app on my Tab, but a simple notebook and pen to roughly note down\nconcepts while reading or watching these resources should be more than enough.\nRelated to Interviews:\n1.\nBe very cool, calm, collected and confident.\n2.\nSpeak up without hesitation. Be a good communicator and listener. Go on clearing any doubts\nyou have throughout the interview.\n3.\nBe friendly and easy to talk to. The more nervous you are, the more serious the mood will be.\nThere were points where I laughed or acknowledged my own stupidity during the interview and\nthe interviewers were quite in for it.\n4.\nThe interviewers are the only other humans besides you in that call. And they are there to help\nyou. Use this to its maximum advantage.\n5.\nStay hydrated and isolated during the interview. Take short walks or breaks in between.\nMost importantly, this isn’t the end all be all. There are many great companies out there, and many\ninternships to be had. Take it as it comes!\nAll the best!",

There are two programming questions in this 100-point test, both worth 50 marks. This test has a 60-minute time limit. The questions I was asked during the coding round were as follows: 1. Minimum servers with maximum load: It took me ten to fifteen minutes to figure out the solution. I was able to complete every test case. To be honest, it was a greedy problem that could be solved with some observation and insight rather than any knowledge of DSA. Try it out before reading my method. I was given the projected load and vector capacity of 'n' servers. I have to find out how many servers are needed to handle the anticipated load. The bare minimum of severs should be used. My Approach: The question was quite simple, but in an attempt to mislead the candidate, a very long description was provided. However, based on my observations, I discovered that it is really just a greed issue, similar to the knapsack dilemma. So I first sort the severs array in ascending order and then start the loop from the back of the array. Each time I check if current server capacity is smaller than or equal to current expected load or if expected load - current server capacity is >= 0 to ensure we are choosing correct server. If any of these conditions are met then we decrement that server capacity from the expected load & increment the counter to keep track of the servers used. Explanation with Eg: Input: servers = [4, 12, 10, 14, 6] expected_load = 32 Output: 3 In this case, after sorting, the array will look like: [4, 6, 10, 12, 14] Now we start from the last element of array so first we take 14, hence 32 - 14 = 18 Then we take 12 as it is <= 18, 18 - 12 = 6 Now we skip 10 as it is > 6 At last we take 6. Hence count = 3 2. Parsing the HTTP request: I don’t remember this problem exactly. The problem involves parsing an array of HTTP requests (URLs) and extracting tokens and other parameters. The goal is to validate the \"token\" parameter against a set of known valid tokens and, for non-GET requests, check the \"csrf\" parameter for a minimum length of 8 characters. If both conditions are met, the request is considered \"VALID.\" Otherwise, it is marked \"INVALID.\" Since it was heavily based on strings, I coded it in Python. Video Interview (10 minutes): The next step of the recruiting process is a video interview, powered by HireVue. In this HireVue interview, you will be asked to record video responses to 2 interview questions. What made it successful? Pretty standard questions. I chose to talk about my recent hackathon experience in questions related to my experiences and communication approach . You can google or search on YouTube ‘HireVue questions’ and you’ll get a list of questions and good answers for the same. Also,, there is an option to re-record your response once for each question.   "content": "Tracelink Interview Experience Name: Shaunak Raiker Branch:Computer Engineering Company:Tracelink Role: Software Engineering Intern Details: CPI criteria:8 Stipend:₹35,000 per month. Location:Mumbai/Pune About the Company: Tracelink is a USA based company which manages pharmaceutical supply chains. Every medicine has a unique number which is generated on the basis of some rules and there are a lot of strict regulations related to handling medicines. After the medicines are manufactured and number is given they travel from manufacturer to different warehouses and different countries where it further goes to wholesalers and finally to customers. In this process it is necessary to track and trace each medicine as some of them can expire/get damaged/spoiled etc. So Tracelink helps managing its clients’ supply chains by maintaining the registry of whole process and creating serial numbers and helping in the tracking and tracing. Also there are a set of rules to be followed which vary from country to country so Tracelink also helps in abiding the rules and regulations. Apart from these major functions tracelink also helps to connect manufacturers to distributors and wholesalers so that all the medicines are tracked and necessary medicines can be sent to places where they are needed. Coding Questions - 3 Questions 1) Modest Number The problem is to identify modest numbers within a given range (inclusive of start and end). A number is considered modest if it can be split into two parts (left and right), such that dividing the number by the right part gives a remainder equal to the left part. The program should check all possible combinations of left and right partitions of a number to verify this condition. Solution Approach 1. Splitting Numbers: Iterate over all digits of a number to partition it into left and right parts. 2. Validation: Check if the right part is non-zero and if the condition number % right == left holds. 3. Iterate Over Range: For every number in the given range, apply the above check. 4. Output: Collect and print all numbers that satisfy the modest number property. This approach ensures all possible partitions are tested for each number within the range. 2) Identifying Unique Colors on Painting Sheets Problem: You are given N rectangular painting sheets and M shots. Each sheet is defined by four integers representing the bottom-left and top-right corners of the rectangle, i.e., (x1, y1) and (x2, y2). Each shot has a set of coordinates (x, y) and a color. The goal is to determine, for each sheet, how many unique colors have been shot within the boundaries of that sheet. For each shot, you need to check if the shot's coordinates lie within the bounds of each painting sheet. If the shot is within a sheet, the color of that shot should be considered for that sheet. Input: N (number of painting sheets) and M (number of shots). N rectangles, each defined by four integers (x1, y1, x2, y2), representing the coordinates of the bottom-left and top-right corners. M shots, each defined by three integers: (x, y) for the coordinates and color for the color of the shot. Output: For each sheet, output the number of unique colors that have been shot within the sheet's bounds. Solution Approach: 1. Store Sheet Data: Each sheet is represented by a rectangle with four coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2). 2. Track Unique Colors: For each shot, check if the shot’s coordinates fall within the bounds of each sheet. If they do, add the color of the shot to the respective sheet's set. 3. Output: After processing all shots, the size of each sheet’s set will give the number of unique colors associated with that sheet. This approach efficiently uses sets to ensure that only unique colors are counted for each sheet. 3) Card The problem involved using a greedy approach and working with arrays. I suggested using an unordered set to store the unique characters from the string and returning the size of the set. This approach would take time complexity of O(n) and a space complexity of O(n). When they told me to optimize further, I explained using a fixed-size array of 26 elements (for the English alphabet). I traversed the string and incremented the corresponding index in the array for each character. I maintained a counter variable. After processing the string, I iterated through the array and increased the counter when indices with values were greater than zero just once. This reduced the space complexity to constant. Follow Up : Count only those characters in the string whose occurrences are greater than equal to k in the string For this part, I stuck to the optimized approach using the fixed-size array of 26 elements. I added a simple condition to check if the value at a specific index was greater than or equal to k. Only in such cases, I increment the counter variable. The goal of the first part was to determine whether it was possible to reach the end of the array. The second part asked for the minimum number of jumps required to reach the end of the array. I suggested that we could use dynamic programming to solve this. Although I couldn’t derive the formula in time, they seemed satisfied, and we moved on to the next questions.   "content": "SAP Labs Interview Experience 2022 Amogh Prabhu, B. Tech IT’24. Online Test: An online test for 45 mins was conducted on the SHL platform. The test had 2 simple questions. 1. We are given a string which should contain only English alphabetical characters, spaces, and numbers. If the string contains some other character then we need to find the total occurrence of such characters. E.g., If the given string is “Hello World, 1 + 2 = 3” then the output will be 3 (‘,’ ,’+’, ‘=’ ). I iterated through each character in the string and incremented the count when a character was not an English alphabetical character, space, or number. (Passed all test cases) 2. Martin’s father goes for a jog every morning. Martin follows him several minutes later. His father starts at a position that is X1 meters away from their home and runs rectilinearly at a constant speed of V1 meters per step for N steps. Martin is standing at X2 meters away from his home. He wonders how fast he must run at some constant speed of V2 meters per step to maximize F, where F equals the number of his father's footsteps that Martin will land on during his run. It is given that the first step that Martin will land on, from his starting position, will have been landed on by his father. Note that if more than one prospective velocity results in the same number of maximum common steps, output the highest prospective velocity as V2. Calculate F and V2. E.g., Input: Martin’s initial position: 0 Martin’s father’s initial position: 3 N = 5 V1 = 2 So, output should be F = 2 and V2 = 7. Explanation: When Martin starts walking, his dad would have walked 5 steps (5,7,9,11,13) starting from position 3 with speed 2m/steps. Since his first step should land on his father’s past steps, the possible values of V2 are 3,5,7,9,11,13 i.e., the total distance of the steps from Martin’s initial position, For V2 = 3,5,7 we get F = 2 and for V2 = 9,11,13 we get F = 1. Hence output is V2 = 7 and F = 2 (As highest value of F is 2 and for F = 2 highest value of V2 is 7). For all possible values of V2 I calculated the F value. (Passed 9/10 test cases). (Yes) Longest Palindromic Substring Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s. The interviewer asked me to present my screen and code in any text editor. I used VS code. My Solution: Expand Around Centre There are two cases in a palindrome: Case 1: Palindrome has odd length. In the given string find the character with maximum number of equal characters on both the sides. Example: For string “abbabbaad”, ‘a’ at index 3 has 3 equal characters on both the sides. Hence the centre of palindrome will be ‘a’ at index 3. (Solution will be s.substring(idx-length, idx+length)) Case 2: Palindrome has even length. In the given string find the index with maximum number of equal characters. Example: For string “abbaabbaad”, At index 3 there are 4 equal characters. (Solution will be s.substring(idx-length+1, idx+length)). 4. Logical Question: How do you measure 4 Litres of water using a 3 Litre and a 5 Litre bucket? It \nstarted off with a resume screening round, after which about 70 students were \nshortlisted and invited for the HireVue interview.\nResume guide:\n1. Be sure to add only relevant things in your resume and follow the latex \noverleaf template provided by TPO, which parses well with the ATS. I thought the brought force would \ndefinitely give TLE, so I went for the optimized approach using \ntwo-pointers. \nThe code looked something like this:\nWe had to parse the input carefully. Each line was of the format:\n2,3,4,12,19,22:36 -> Here the target and array are separated by \nthe colon, so we first split using “:” and then we split using “,” \nand map it to an integer array. Since the list was already sorted, \nwe start checking for sums of each pair and if the current sum is \ngreater than the target, move the right pointer to the left and vice \nversa.
