Group discussion\nAll subsequent rounds were held offline. There were around 40 students, and we \nwere divided into 4 groups with 10 students each. I was in group 4.\nIt was my first GD and I didn’t know what else to do apart from watching YouTube \nvideos and reading articles regarding GD. It is also helpful to practice speaking as \nif you’re in a real GD - randomly take a topic and try to speak for an argument for \nat least one minute.\n Since the time taken was only 10-12 minutes per group, I only had one thing in \nmind - that it’s ok to speak only once or twice but I will make a unique point, or \nprovide a counter perspective to someone else’s point. Speaking just for the heck \nof it is not useful at all and will probably get me negative judgment, so it’s best to \nformulate a point before speaking.\nThe topics are often general knowledge-based. The two topics I remember \nwere “Cashless Economy”, “WFO vs WFH”, and “Role of AI in Finance”. Mine \nwas simpler, “Social Media - a Boon or a Curse”.\nThere were six senior panelists and we were seated around benches facing them. \nThey revealed the topic and told us that we may start the discussion now. \nSuddenly, 4-5 people, including me started to speak (intro ke points 🍭). \nEventually, everyone went quiet and one girl gave the intro (I felt a bit dejected, \nbut I’m not the end of the world. There’s plenty of time to make your mark). 2-3 \nspeakers later, I realized they were mostly negative, so when I got the chance I \nmentioned how social media has allowed many people like David Goggins to \ninspire others. I said something along the lines of social media is a double-edged \nsword, that it depends on the user whether it will be beneficial or not, and that \nsocial media is not to be blamed. A few minutes later I got irked when someone \nsaid that even young kids are so addicted to social media that they won’t even \nhave food without it, start to cry, lose focus, it’s a drug etc etc 👹. So I tried to \nspeak 4-5 times about that point (listening skill ke points 😋) and kept my hand \nraised. Finally, I said something like (with extensive hand gestures) “If one wants \nto waste time, one will find a way to waste time. A few years earlier, we would be \ndiscussing whether magazines are a nuisance or not. The instrument changes, \nbut human behavior remains the same, hence that is to be blamed. Also, the kid \nbeing addicted is just an example of bad parenting and not social media being \naddictive”. Few of the panelists smiled as I spoke and I felt more confident (¬‿¬). \nThat’s it, I only spoke twice.\nRoughly 5 students were selected for the next round, and I was one of them 😎.\nPrefer quality over quantity. There are examples where someone spoke 3-4 times \nbut didn’t proceed, and where someone spoke only once but moved ahead. \nRemember, they aren’t here to see who can speak English the loudest.\n\n3. Interview round\nAbout 20 students had proceeded. Three interviews were conducted in parallel, \nby a pair of interviewers each (two for GPM, and one for GPT). I was feeling \nextremely nervous and underprepared. You would probably feel so too. It was my \nfirst, so I accepted it. Took a few deep breaths, rehearsed my intro one last time, \nand went in.\nAs I sat, they asked me how my day was and how I was feeling. I said that it was \na wonderful morning, that I was feeling nervous but I like to tell myself that it’s \nexciting. They smiled and told me to introduce myself. After the intro, in which I \nmentioned at the end that I enjoy football, he asked me for my favorite club. I said \nReal Madrid. He said “Oh, a Real Madrid fan. Favorite player?” I said Cristiano \nRonaldo and they laughed while saying “Of course”. \nThen, they took a look at my resume. The sir then said “I see you’ve been part of a \nfew leadership positions at Pratibimb. What according to you makes a good \nleader?” This question threw me off a little because I was mostly expecting \ntechnical questions. I said, after a bit of fumbling, that a good leader makes the \nteam “own” the project. The team has to understand that they’re not just \norganizing an event or completing their project, they are actually showcasing \nthemselves. A good leader also makes sure to give personal attention to \nunderperforming members, and also be polite yet firm regarding things. I \nexpanded something along these lines.\nHe then asked me which language was my strongest among the ones I \nmentioned on my resume. I said Java. He told me to rate it, to which I gave an 8. \nIt is better not to go above 8 I think, no matter how confident you feel.\nHe quickly withdrew a blank sheet of paper and started writing something. As \nhe was writing, he asked if I was aware of error handling in Java to which I \nreplied yes. Then he showed me the code he’d written: \nTry {\nSystem.out.println(“In first block”);\nThrow A;\n} catch ( ExceptionTypeA e) {\nSystem.out.println(e.getMessage());\nThrow B;\n} catch (ExceptionTypeB e) {\nSystem.out.println(e.getMessage());\nThrow C;\n} finally {\nSystem.out.println(“In finally block”);\nThrow Z;\n}\nFirst, he asked me what would be the output of this, and what if ExceptionTypeB \nwas a subclass of ExceptionTypeA 😳. I said that we wouldn’t get any output but \nrather a compiler error if we’re catching errors that are subclasses of some other \nerror. I gave an example of first having a catch Exception block and second with a \ncatch ArithmeticException block, how it would give an error since the Exception \nblock would already catch exceptions of type ArithmeticException.\nThen I looked at the code and said directly that Error Z would be thrown since \nthe final block is always executed at the end. He then told me to go step by \nstep and tell what happens with error C. I got very confused in between. A and B \nwere caught so their statements were printed, but there was nothing for C, hence \nwe should get a runtime error for C. But isn't the finally block the one that is \nalways executed at the end? So what about Z? After thinking I said that I was not \nsure, but “In finally block” would be printed and Z would be thrown at the end. I do \nnot know whether C will be thrown or not.\nAfter this, he asked me to give some real-life use cases of try-catch blocks. I \nmentioned we may use the try block to make a request to our server, catch any \nnetwork errors, and display them to the user, or do whatever we want. The finally \nblock is generally used to free resources like database connections, so that \nwhether or not the request was successful we make sure to free up the \nresources. He asked me, “What if I return some value in the try or exception \nblock? Will it still be executed?” I replied yes. “What will be returned if all blocks \nare returning different values?” I said the value sent by the finally block will only \nbe returned. “In what cases will the finally block not be executed?” I said we can \nuse System.exit(), or if the JVM itself crashes only then will it not be executed.\nThen he asked me if I was aware of multithreading. I gave a basic definition. He \nthen asked me to implement it in Java. I was a bit taken aback, but I vaguely \nremembered an example I did while learning mergesort and wrote it down. It was \nsomething like this: \nclass MergeSortThread extends Thread {\nprivate int[] array;\npublic MergeSortThread(int[] array) {\n        this.array = array;\n}\n    public void run() {\n        mergeSort(array);\n    }\nThread leftThread = new MergeSortThread(leftArray);\nThread rightThread = new MergeSortThread(rightArray);\nleftThread.start();\nrightThread.start();\nleftThread.join();\nrightThread.join();\nI said that the Threads class in Java allows us to implement multithreading. He \nseemed satisfied with it, and just said that we usually put the join part in try catch \nfor error handling.\nHe then asked me what type of algorithm is mergesort. I said it’s a sorting \nalgorithm that uses the divide and conquer technique. He asked me if it was \nstable. I replied with yes since it doesn’t change the relative order of two entities \nif they have the same value. He asked me what algorithm is called if I use \nArrays.sort(). I said that in Java, if the array is made of primitives then a double \npivot quicksort is called. It’s unstable but doesn’t matter for primitives and is \nfaster. For objects it uses “TimSort”, a combination of merge sort and insertion \nsort (I got really lucky with this question because I had done it just the night \nbefore). He seemed impressed and then asked me if I was aware of spring \nboot. I said that it’s used to develop web applications using Java, after which he \ntold me to write a REST controller that exposes an endpoint /hello to return a \ngreeting message. I said that I had never made something with spring boot. I only \nknow its purpose. He said it’s fine. Looking back, I should’ve mentioned this the \nfirst time itself. But anyway, spring is quite uncommon amongst college students.\nHe then asked me if Java was a purely OOP language. I replied no, stating that for \na pure OOP language, every data type must be user-defined and every method \nmust be called through objects only. This is not the case because: \n1. The static keyword in Java allows us to access data or methods belonging \nto the class i.e. without the need of an object.\n2. Primitives are not user-defined objects.\nHe then asked me, “But we use Integer as a class right? So doesn’t that make it \nan object?” I said that Integer, Double, Float, etc are wrapper classes that still use \na primitive int, double, or float underneath. They are used to invoke certain \nfunctions like Integer.parseInt() etc that can’t be called via primitives like int. He \nthen asked whether strings are primitive, to which I replied no. He asked if strings \nare mutable or not and to explain why. I said that strings are immutable in Java \nmainly due to storage optimization and safety. He then wrote this on the paper: \nString a = “abc”;\nString b = new String(“abc”);\nString c = “abc”;\nprintln(a==b); print(a==c);\nHe asked me to explain the output. I said false for first and true for second, \nand drew this diagram: \nBut with “abc”. I mentioned that we are saving memory by not creating new \nobjects to store a string like “abc” but rather pointing to the same object in the \npool. Using the “new” keyword normally allocates memory to the heap like any \nother object. I had watched this video previously.\nAfter this, he asked me what I knew about equity derivatives. I was caught off \nguard and felt stupid for not reading about these things, considering I’m \ninterviewing for a bank. I anxiously mumbled something about stocks and mutual \nfunds. Then he asked me what is the process of buying a stock. I said that the \nexchange where the stocks are listed handles the transactions. To which he \nreplied “No, what is the exact process? What happens when someone buys a \nstock?” I admitted I wasn’t aware of the underlying details. Next, she asked me \nwhat good coding practices one should follow. I gave examples of my project,\nand said something along the lines of keeping your directory structure clean, \ngiving descriptive variable/function names, keeping a simple and clean flow of \ndata, etc.\nHe then asked me if I had any questions. I asked him the answer to the first \nquestion, and he explained that I was going in the correct direction - that the \nuncaught error would simply be ignored and only the final block error would be \nprinted, after which the interview was over.\nI wasn’t feeling too confident since I gave terrible responses to finance-related \nquestions and many times they didn’t seem satisfied with my answers. But it was \ndone, so I took a break and relaxed.\nOnce all the interviews were over, 9 students were shortlisted and luckily I was \none of them.\n\n4. HR round\nThere were six panelists for this interview. They told me to introduce myself and \nasked me a few basic questions regarding my family, what role my father has at \nhis work, any hobbies, etc. Then, one of the senior panelists asked me why I \nwanted to work for a bank instead of some tech-specific company like TCS or \nInfosys. I said that banks require as much coding expertise as any other tech \nfirm, if not more, as they have to handle data of millions of users, their \ntransactions and need to have high levels of security as they deal with sensitive \ndata. I mentioned some products like Bofa Mercury, Bofa electronic trading \nplatform that I had read on their website, and said that these definitely require a \nlot of developers to maintain.\nNow, I should’ve stopped here but I got carried away and said that firms like \nTCS are mainly involved in the outsourcing business, and banks probably \noutsource some projects to them for cheap labor (❁´◡`❁). They looked at each \nother and started laughing. Then he read my resume and said that you seem to \nhave done a lot in Pratibimb, so give us your experience and what you learned \nfrom it. I said something about learning how to speak properly, managing \nextracurricular with academics (I said this only because I had a decent cgpa of \n8.9, otherwise you need to be careful with these statements😝), and working in a \nteam. I asked, “I had read that people generally switch within a few years to get \nmuch larger salary hikes, so what made you stay at Bank of America for more \nthan 35 years? If you had switched a few times, maybe you would’ve been at a \nhigher compensation”. He started off by saying that there’s no right or wrong \nanswer to whether you should stay or switch. He said that he did switch when he \nwas younger, but he found more meaning in working and contributing to this \nplace. He also mentioned that you get yearly raises at every company, and \nsometimes it’s okay to not want to leave a place where you enjoy working. With \nthis, the interview ended. \nAfter an hour, the results were announced and I was one of the four selects \n(⌐■_■).\n\n5. Conclusion\nHere are certain things that might help you with your preparation: \nTechnical\n1) Pick a language and become a master at it, preferably the language you \nuse DSA. \n2) Don’t focus too much on the quantity but the quality of your projects. Add \nnew and unique features with time, so that it becomes really impressive at \nthe end.\n3) Always start DSA from the basics. I have wasted huge amounts of time \ntrying to do tough problems, thinking that I am developing my \n“Problem-solving skills” which were clearly above my level. Certain \nproblems cannot be solved by you without knowing the solution first. Your \njob is to comfortably understand basic algorithms like binary search, tree \ntraversals, recursion, etc. Only then move on to tougher problems. \n4) It helped me a lot to perform a dry run on paper to understand the solution. \nI also tried to watch videos since the written explanations took a lot of time \nto understand.\n5) You’ll have an easier time if you follow an order of doing topics. You may \nfollow something like this:\nResources: Aditya Verma’s binary search and DP playlist, Striver’s array \npisplaylist, and Love Babbar for trees and recursion. DSA 450 is a good collection \nof questions arranged in increasing difficulty. I liked Kunal Kushwaha’s videos for \nJava and oops.\nNon-technical\n1) Focus on making habits. Do the leetcode daily challenge, work and push \nchanges to your project daily on github, and regularly google any new \nthings you find. The only reason I knew about what function was used in \nArrays.sort() was because I googled it out of curiosity. Same with many \nother concepts. You won’t get all the things perfectly placed in some \nplaylist or article, so make this habit of learning anything new you find. You \nfeel much less burdened if you immerse yourself in the learning process \nrather than always thinking about whether this will help you for internships \nor not.\n2) Don’t be disheartened by failures. This was the first time ever that I could \nclear the online assessment and actually give an interview ;) No matter \nhow well you do, there is always a factor of luck. So focus on what you can \ncontrol - your preparation. Rest will be taken care of. Quoting James Clear \nhere: “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of \nyour systems.”",

I’m super excited to share my interview experience with Wells Fargo, and I hope it helps you in your placement journey too. So, a little about the company first — Wells Fargo is one of the top 4 banks in the United States, and trust me, it’s a big name in the finance and tech world. When we heard that Wells Fargo was finally coming for intern analyst roles, there was a wave of excitement across campus. It came a bit late in the placement season, and we were honestly starting to get worried that it might not show up at all. But once the registration link dropped, there was this collective “Finally!” feeling among all of us. The registration process was simple, and the selection process had a clear structure: one Online Assessment (OA) round followed by three interviews – two technical and one HR. It felt a bit intense seeing three rounds lined up, but since it was Wells Fargo, we were all geared up. This interview experience turned out to be a mix of challenges, surprises, and some really cool learning moments. So, if you're someone looking to land an internship at a major firm, I hope my story gives you some insights (and maybe a little confidence boost too!). Online Assessment (OA) Now let’s talk about the Online Assessment — honestly, it was quite a mix of everything! Wells Fargo didn’t want to leave any area untouched. This OA was conducted offline on 22nd April 2025, which honestly added its own kind of pressure. You know that feeling when you're not just competing with logic but also with the silence in the room? Yep, that one. The assessment had English comprehension, aptitude, a graph-based stock analysis section, a few basic Gen AI questions (which I really didn’t expect!), and three coding questions. Quite the combo platter, right? The English section was mostly standard stuff — comprehension, synonyms, arranging the sentences in correct order, sentence correction, paragraph related questions — you know, the usual suspects. But at one point, the options were so close that I started second-guessing my entire understanding of grammar. I'm pretty sure I stared at one sentence for a solid minute trying to decide if it sounded right or was actually right. Then came the stock-based graph analysis section, and boy, that felt like I was suddenly working at Bloomberg. They gave a stock price chart and threw questions like, “When was the price highest?”, “Which day had the steepest drop?”, and I was like — Wait, am I giving an OA or preparing to become a stock trader?? It was interesting, though, and definitely different from the usual aptitude rounds. Oh, and just when I thought I had seen it all — a few simple Gen AI questions popped up! Things like identifying AI applications, understanding basic AI logic, and I was like “Umm... okay, didn’t study for this but let’s go!” And then... the coding part arrived — with its own twist. Three coding questions, but one of them was sitting mysteriously under a different heading: “FTE Wellness.” Still not sure what was \"well\" about it, but okay Wells Fargo, we trust your vibes. Coding Questions – The Real Deal Okay, now let’s dive into the coding section — probably the part everyone’s most curious about! Like I mentioned earlier, there were three coding questions, and for some reason, one of them was tucked away in a completely different section called “FTE Wellness”. Still no idea why they put it there — maybe solving it was supposed to make us feel “well”? Anyway, here’s how it went down: ● Question 1 – The Warmup The first question was honestly a breeze. I can’t recall the exact problem (classic moment, right?), but I do remember solving it within 5–7 minutes. It was very easy, probably something basic with arrays or strings. Definitely a good confidence booster to start off with. ● Question 2 – Frequency Sort This one was more interesting. We were given a list of numbers with multiple occurrences, and the task was to arrange them in decreasing order of their frequency. If two numbers had the same frequency, we had to maintain their original order of appearance in the list. The moment I read the problem, I was like \"Ohhh okay, this looks fancy but not too bad.\" I quickly thought of using a hashmap to store frequencies and then sorting based on that, with a touch of stable sorting to maintain order. Solved it without much trouble and was feeling pretty good about it. ● Question 3 – Cryptarithmetic Chaos Ah yes, the final boss of the OA – a cryptarithmetic puzzle. And not the cute ones with SEND + MORE = MONEY. This one meant business. The logic was okay to grasp, but it involved a lot of permutations and backtracking. I tried optimizing as much as I could, but sadly, the last two test cases kept failing due to time limits. Not gonna lie, it was a little frustrating because I knew the logic was right — it was just the execution speed that wasn’t keeping up. Still, I was proud I gave it a solid shot. And considering the rest of the OA had gone well, I was hopeful. Technical Interview 1 This round happened on 29th April 2025, in online mode, and went on for about 30–35 minutes. It was one of those interviews that started off like a regular technical round but slowly turned into a fun blend of technical + HR — like the interviewer was trying to see how I think and who I am as a person. As expected, we began with the classic: “Tell me about yourself as I go through your resume.” I had practiced this part, so I was comfortable. But what really made me smile was what came next. He looked at my project and said: “This TradeSphere looks catchy. What is it?” And that was my moment! I explained what the project was, why I built it, and why such an application is actually needed. He seemed genuinely interested and started giving me scenario-based questions like: ● “Suppose your scraper fails because the website now asks for a captcha. What would you do?” ● “If your data source crashes unexpectedly, how would you handle it?” To be honest, I was able to answer all the scenarios confidently, because yep — I actually built the project myself and didn’t just copy it off GitHub or some random blog (That’s why you should always know what’s on your resume!) Then came the surprise twist. He suddenly said: “Since you’ve worked with MongoDB, let me give you a Mongo query.” I was like — \"Wait what? MongoDB query in an interview?\" People usually ask SQL, right? (BTW, till now, all my Mongo queries were mostly written by ChatGPT) But I gave it a shot, wrote something that made sense logically. Just to go the extra mile, I even wrote the SQL version of the same query right after — wanted to show that I understood both. He then moved to some OOPs basics — asked me to explain: ● The 4 pillars of OOP ● What’s an abstract class ● What’s an interface That part was pretty chill, and I handled it well. But the real highlight was toward the end. He suddenly said: “What is Naman?” And I, totally confused, replied: “Naman means Namaskaar...” He burst out laughing and said: “No no, I meant — who is Naman? What kind of person are you?” I laughed along thinking what have I even done, but I gathered myself and answered genuinely. He wrapped it up by asking: “What’s your motivation behind what you do?” Overall, it felt like more than just a tech grilling — it was a conversation where he tried to understand me technically and personally. A really refreshing experience, to be honest. Out of 25 people I got selected for the next round. Technical Interview 2 This interview took place on 10th May 2025, again in online mode, and lasted for about 30 minutes. But this one started off with a surprise. Some person joined the call and casually said: “Naman, please wait for 5 minutes, the Executive Director will be joining soon.” And I was like — \"Whaaaaat? Executive Director??\" Cue mini heart attack. I mean, it’s not every day you casually chat with someone that high up, so yes, I was a little nervous... but I quickly told myself: “You’ve got this.” He joined and started just like the previous round — “Tell me about yourself.” After that, he asked me basic questions like: “What is Operating System?”, “What is Computer Networks?” All good till here. But then he goes: “Let’s make things a little more interesting…” That line is never not scary in an interview. He said, “If you had a superpower, and you could keep only one subject — OS or CN — which one would you keep?” I took a second to think and replied OS. I explained that the OS acts like the heart of the system, managing processes, memory, threads, and acting as the foundation layer between hardware and software. Without an OS, nothing really \"runs\" — it's the base that keeps everything ticking. He smiled and jumped in: “But CN has enabled global communication, the internet, cloud... don’t you think CN has revolutionized everything?” And I totally agreed with him — CN has taken us from isolated machines to a connected world. But I stood my ground and said: “Even with all the advancements in CN, without a stable OS underneath, those systems wouldn't even function. OS is what lets CN happen in the first place.” That seemed to satisfy him, and the nervousness started fading away. Then he asked about the projects I had worked on. I walked him through all three on my resume. And no surprise — his attention locked onto TradeSphere again (of course, it's a bank — so anything with stocks is like magnet). He asked: “There are so many existing applications for stock analysis. Why did you make another one?” I said, “Because unless we build something ourselves, we never truly understand how it works underneath. I wanted to learn by doing — not just by reading or using apps built by others.” That hit the mark. Then came the wildest question of all: “If you were to make a Naman Indicator, how would you design it?” I blinked. Literally sat there like for a second. But then the creativity kicked in. I said something like: “First, I’d identify what kind of investor Naman is — short-term, long-term, or intraday. Based on that, I’d adjust the weights on technical indicators like the 50-day and 200-day EMAs, maybe even add RSI or MACD. For example, if he’s a long-term investor, I’d put more weight on the 200-day EMA and trends over months. If he’s into short-term trading, I’d factor in volatility-based indicators. So basically, I’d design a custom weighted moving average system that adapts to the person’s behavior.” He nodded with a satisfied smile, and I was really happy with that answer. I could tell it made a solid impression. Finally, he asked some behavioral questions: “Can you work in a team?” “What if you have to work alone?” I answered both honestly, giving examples of both scenarios. And with that, we wrapped up. To be honest — this round was unexpected, slightly intimidating, but also really enjoyable. I walked away feeling happy and confident with how it went. Out of 12 people I was lucky to be selected for the next round. HR Interview The final round — the HR interview — came with a mini jump scare of its own. It was 12th May 2025, around 3:30 PM, when I received a call from someone from the HR Talent Acquisition team. They said: “Hi Naman, can we schedule your HR interview today at 6 PM?” And I was like — “Of course, yes!” (I mean, come on, who says no to HR?) The interview happened online and lasted about 20 minutes, but it was a nice, chill conversation — more about getting to know me than grilling me. He started with a casual tone: “How are you? And tell me honestly — were you free or just said yes out of fear?” I laughed and said I was actually free — no fake bravado needed! Then he asked for my CGPA, about my 12th and 10th marks, and I could hear the keyboard sounds in the background — so pretty sure he was noting things down. The next few questions were classic HR stuff: ● “Why do you want to join Wells Fargo?” ● “What are your weaknesses?” ● “How can you contribute to Wells Fargo?” I answered them honestly, connecting my skills, interest in finance-tech, and what I hoped to learn from such a big company. Then he suddenly asked: “Have you ever lived outside Maharashtra?” I said I hadn’t, just traveled outside a few times. So he told me, “Since our offices are in Bangalore and Hyderabad, you’d have to move — would you be okay with that?” I confidently said yes, and told him I was open to exploring new places and was confident in my ability to adapt to different environments. Toward the end, he said something that lit up my day: “We’re planning to start the internship from 9th June. Would you be okay with that?” That’s when I felt like — this might actually be happening. I had a huge smile and said yes without hesitation. But then came the waiting game. The results didn’t come for days, and honestly, everyone was super tensed. We kept checking, hoping, overthinking… Finally, on 19th May, the results were out — and guess what? I was one of the 5 people selected for the internship! Felt like all the effort, prep, and genuine answers had finally paid off. Tips (That Aren’t Really “Tips”) To be honest, tips are just things people say based on their experiences — but I genuinely believe everyone should develop their own will and way of doing things. What works for me might not work for you, and that’s completely okay! So nope, I’m not gonna throw a list of “Top 10 ways to crack an interview” at you. I believe in keeping things simple — that’s exactly how I approached all my interviews, and trust me, it helped. The moment you start overcomplicating things, you’ll confuse yourself more than the interviewer ever could. Here are just a few thoughts from someone who’s been through it: ● Know your resume — like really, really know it. Please don’t put things just to make it look good. That random “blockchain certification” from 2022? If you don’t remember what it even means now, maybe leave it off. Put stuff you can speak about confidently. Trust me, it matters. ● Know your projects in and out. As you saw in my case, both technical interviews circled back to my project, and since I actually built it myself, I could answer everything easily. So, whatever you’ve built — own it. Debug it. Break it. Fix it. Repeat. ● Be confident and don’t be scared. It’s not just what you say — it’s how you say it. Speak clearly, be honest, and don’t get thrown off if the interviewer laughs or goes off-script. (Looking at you, \"What is Naman?\" guy) ● Keep learning and keep improving. If you get rejected, don’t get sad. Okay fine, get sad for 15 minutes, eat some chocolate, and then get up and figure out what went wrong. Every interview is a step closer to the one that’s meant for you. Just don’t stop. In the end, all I want to say is — All the best !! Keep working hard, keep it real, and success will follow.",

It can be seen that to collect 7 coins you will have to travel through at least 2 houses. \n \ntypedef long long ll; \n \nint main(){\n4 \n    ll n; \n    cin >> n; \n    ll arr[n]; \n \n    for(ll i=0; i < n; i++) \n        cin >> arr[i]; \n     \n    ll k; \n    cin >> k; \n     \n    ll pre[n + 1]; \n    pre[0] = 0; \n     \n    for(ll i=1; i<=n; i++) \n        pre[i] = pre[i-1] + arr[i - 1]; \n     \n    if(pre[n] < k) \n        cout << -1 << endl; \n     \n    else{ \n        ll ans = INT_MAX; Coding section (2 Questions in 60 minutes) a. Consecutive Gray Code Numbers. A gray code sequence is one in which two successive terms differ by only one bit. Print 1 if binary representation of given numbers can be placed successively in a gray code sequence else print 0. Example: ●areGrayNeighbors(9,11) --> 1 (since (1001, 1011) differ in only one bit and are neighbors) ●areGrayNeighbors(9,10) --> 0 (since (1001, 1010) differ in two bits) ●areGrayNeighbors(14,10) --> 1 (since (1110, 1010) differ in only one bit and are neighbors) If you want to know whether two Gray codes a and b are neighbors, you have to check whether previous(a) = b OR next(a) = b. For a given Gray code, you get one neighbor by flipping the rightmost bit and the other neighbor bit by flipping the bit at the left of the rightmost set bit. For the Gray code 1010, the neighbors are 1011 and 1110. In the question the definition of successive terms and neighbors wasn’t explicitly mentioned. Passed 25/25 test cases b. Maximum Toll Revenue There are N cities with unique city codes from 1 to N and are connected by N-1 roads.The road network is in the form of a tree which connects two cities.A path is a road,combination of roads,connecting two cities.Each road has a toll booth that collects toll equal to maximum number of paths of which that particular road is a part.We need to identify the road which 3 collects maximum toll revenue(output is pair of cities connected by road).If two or more toll booths collect same total revenue,then we have to print the pair of cities with lexicographically smaller city codes. The inputs to the tree were taken like a graph (adjacency list) unlike a node based tree.The way of taking input did confuse a lot of people,this had also happened in a previous test.   "content": "Sagar Dholakia, CE B.Tech, 2018-2022\nssdholakia_b18@ce.vjti.ac.in\nGOLDMAN SACHS INTERVIEW EXPERIENCE (FTE 2021)\nRound 0 (Online Assessment):\nThe online assessment was held on HackerRank and there were a total of five sections. It\nlasted for 135 minutes.\nSection 1: Basic Programming (30 mins)\nThe first section consisted of two programming questions of easy to moderate difficulty.\nFor the first question, we were given an array of length 2^N (misprinted as 2N). Each element\nin the array represents the strength of a player, and each consecutive player competes with the\nother. The player with more strength wins, and if the strengths are equal, the second player wins\nand proceeds to the next round. Then the winners compete with each other, till there is only\none player left. We had to print the maximum level each player could reach.\nFor example, arr = {1, 2, 4, 3}.\nAfter the first round matches conclude, elements 2 and 4 proceed to the next round.\nAfter the second round, element 4 is the winner of the tournament.\nAs we can see, elements 1 and 3 reach a maximum level of 0, 2 reaches a maximum level of 1,\nand 4 reaches 2. The expected output is {0, 1, 2, 0}.\nThe second question was a 01 Knapsack based question, where we were given an array of\nstrings, and each string had some value to it. The total weight of the knapsack was predefined\nas 30. We had to maximise the value by choosing some strings from the array, and appending\nthem to an empty string. We had to add spaces in between adjacent strings that we chose\nand had to account for the length of the extra spaces as well.\nFor example, N=4, arr={“priorityqueue”, “linkedlist”, “binarytree”, “adjacencymatrix”},\nval={5, 6, 9, 10}\nThe answer here would be 19, as we select the last two strings from the array. The total length\nwhich we have used out of the given weight of 30 would be 10+1+15 = 26.\nI was able to fully solve the first question and partially solve the second question.\nSection 2: Problem Solving (25 mins)\nThe second section consisted of multiple-choice questions based on aptitude and maths\n(topics like trigonometry, probability were included). There were a total of 8 questions, and\neach question had a +5/-2 scoring scheme (+5 for correct answer, -2 for wrong answer). So it’s\nbetter to leave a question if you’re unsure about it rather than making a guess.\nSection 3: Advanced Programming (45 mins)\nThis section had one advanced programming question.\nGiven a graph, we can apply the operation an arbitrary number of times (possibly 0) to\ntransform the given graph into a complete graph. An operation is defined as follows -\n1.\nPick any vertex from the graph.\n2.\nRemove all pre existing edges from the vertex to other vertices.\n3.\nAdd edges to all other vertices except the ones we removed in the previous step.\nFor example, if we have 3 nodes (1, 2 and 3) and have only 1 edge between nodes 1 and 2. We\nchoose node 1, so the existing edge is removed, and the remaining edges are added. Then we\nfinally select node 2, and the 2 remaining edges are added and we have a complete graph.\nI was able to solve this question partially.\nSection 4: Subjective (15 mins)\nThe fourth section consisted of two subjective questions which were based on your behaviour\nand instances of motivation in your life.\nThe first question described a situation in which your classmate drops out of a project at a\ncritical time, and the deadline is near. How would you handle this situation?\nThe second question asked about a time where you were so motivated to do a project that you\nwent over and above to complete the project that you’re working on, and achieved better\nresults.\nBoth these questions are very frequently asked in the online assessment of Goldman Sachs,\nfor Internship as well as for FTE, so you can prepare for them beforehand.\nSection 5: Computer Science (20 mins)\nThe last section again had multiple choice questions, but questions in this section were based\non topics including OOPs, Operating Systems, and Computer Networks. There were a total\nof 7 questions which followed the same scoring pattern as before, i.e. +5/-2 for each question.\nRound 1 (Technical Interview):\n11 candidates were shortlisted for the interview process.\nThe interview was conducted on Zoom, and we were provided with a link to HackerRank\nCodePair, which is a shared IDE and Whiteboard.\nI was first asked to introduce myself. After the introduction, I was asked about LCA (Lowest\nCommon Ancestor) of a Binary Tree. I explained what it was, then we discussed my approach\nto find the LCA of 2 nodes whose values were given to us. After explaining my approach, I was\nasked to write a pseudo code for the same and had to dry run the code with the input my\ninterviewer provided. She was satisfied with my code and explanation.\nShe then asked me a second question. Given one way connections of flight, I had to find the\nstarting airport which connects (directly or indirectly) all other airports.\nFor example, B → C, A → B, C → D, then the answer here is A, as we can reach every airport if\nwe start from airport A in the following order A →B → C → D.\nWe only discussed an approach to the problem; due to time constraints, I wasn’t asked to code\nmy approach. I gave a solution to check the indegree of each airport, and there should exist\nexactly 1 airport having an indegree of 0. This should be our starting airport. It was guaranteed\nthat there are no loops, no disconnected components, and only one possible starting airport.\nI was then asked if I had any questions for my interviewer. This round lasted for around 45\nminutes.\nRound 2 (Technical Interview):\nAfter the first round, 6 candidates qualified for further rounds.\nMy second interview started with a puzzle. Given three bags containing only red balls, only\nwhite balls, and a mix of red and white balls, respectively, all of them are initially unlabelled. I\nwas asked to find the minimum number of balls to be taken out in order to correctly label each\nof the three bags.\nFor the second question, I was asked to Sort a Linked List. I came up with a solution of O(N^2)\nwhich was based on Selection Sort, but my interviewer was expecting the optimal solution\nwhich is based on Merge Sort. I was then asked different sorting methods, and had to explain a\nfew of them.\nLastly, I was asked whether or not I had any questions for my interviewer. This round too lasted\nfor 45 minutes.\nRound 3 (HR + Technical Round):\nOnly 3 candidates reached the final round of the interview process.\nIn this round, I was again asked to introduce myself. The interviewer asked me how the\nprevious rounds were and which type of questions were asked. Then he started asking me\nquestions about where I live, and how I commuted to college before the pandemic struck. After\nabout 10 minutes, he gave me a puzzle to solve.\nGiven a robot at position (0,0) and facing north, it is given a sequence of instructions.\nThere were 3 specific commands -\nR → Rotate the direction of the robot 90° clockwise,\nL → Rotate the direction of the robot 90° anti clockwise,\nG → Move the robot by 1 unit in whichever direction it is currently pointing at.\nNow, if the given sequence of commands is repeated infinitely many times, whether the robot\nwill move outside a given bound or not.\nWe discussed the solution on a Whiteboard, and I was not asked to code my approach. Finally,\nmy interviewer asked if I had any questions for him. This round lasted for 30 minutes.\nVerdict:\n2 of the 3 candidates were offered FTE roles; I was one of them.\nPreparation:\n- For questions based on Data Structures and Algorithms, GeeksForGeeks and\nInterviewBit are more than enough.\n- Prepare for topics like DBMS, OS and OOPs, don’t leave them for the last minute.\nSystem Design questions can also be expected in interviews.\n- Be thorough with what you have mentioned in your resume.\n- Polish your oratory skills. Sometimes you may know the answer, but may not be able to\narticulate it into words.\nTips:\n- Whenever discussing an approach to a question with your interviewer, don’t jump to the\noptimal solution straightaway (even if you do know the optimal solution). The\ninterviewers want to see your ability to think and come up with solutions.\n- Think out loud. For each index, check the relevant neighbours\nand collect the index if the condition holds.\n• Time Complexity: O(n)\n• Space Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of peak indices returned.\nSolution:\n1 #include <bits/stdc ++.h>\n2\nusing\nnamespace std;\n3\n4\nint main () {\n5\nint n;\n6\ncin >> n;\n7\n8\nvector <int > arr(n);\n9\nfor(auto &x : arr) cin >> x;\n10\n11\nvector <int > result;\n12\n13\nfor(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n14\nbool leftOk\n= (i == 0)\n|| (arr[i] > arr[i - 1]);\n15\nbool rightOk = (i == n - 1) || (arr[i] > arr[i + 1]);\n16\n17\nif(leftOk && rightOk)\n18\nresult.push_back(i);\n19\n}\n20\n21\nfor(auto idx : result) cout << idx << \" \";\n22\ncout << \"\\n\";\n23\nreturn 0;\n24 }\nResult: Passed all 20 test cases.\n3\n\nVISA Inc. Also there was a negative marking scheme for MCQs, so read the instructions well. 3. MCQs again, based on CS related subjects Computer Networks LRU from OS Programming language related, OOPS Time complexity, recursive functions, dynamic programming 4. Advanced Coding Question (45 mins) 5. 2 Essay type situation based questions Describe a time where your passion and energy led to a team victory. You are in a team of two members, and your co-team member cannot work on the project that needs to be completed within a certain deadline. What will you do in this situation? Tip: Generally no one takes this section seriously, but I would suggest attempting it honestly if you have time for this section. Coding Questions The coding questions were of medium to hard difficulty level. The difficulty of the questions may vary drastically each year. a. Section 1 1. First question was related to finding distance. I don’t remember the question, but it was easily solvable. I passed 11/12 test cases in the first go, and the last test case required us to apply modular arithmetic operation (1e9+7) though it wasn’t mentioned anywhere. Tip: If you fail only a few of the test cases, it might be because of mod. Also in some cases you need to do (ans+mod)%mod instead of ans%mod, these are the cases of overflow. 2. There were two friends Alice and Bob. Bob goes to Alice’s house to play, but one fine day there were trees that fell on his path. Now he has to find the length of shortest path(consider euclidean distance) to reach Alice’s house avoiding the trees. Alice’s and Bob’s house coordinates are given on the XY plane. The coordinates of a tree are given by two points on the XY plane representing the start and the end of the tree. Assume trees to be of the form of line segments on the XY plane and their houses to be like points on the plane. I was able to pass 4/12 test cases. b. Section 4 (Advanced) We were given a n*m matrix with each cell containing a number i, representing i th type of flowers in that cell. We had to find the size of the largest connected component (any cell in the connected component has at least one of its sides common with any other cell of the component ) having at most two different types of flowers. Input: 3 4 1 2 3 1 1 1 2 1 4 2 1 1 Output: 10 The question is similar to the link I have mentioned below. It can be solved using DFS, however I wasn’t able to solve this question in the test. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/find-number-of-islands/ Tip: Go through questions that you weren’t able to solve or think of an optimal approach for a question that you had solved in the online test. Many times you get a similar question in technical interviews. Also sometimes, the interviewers have a copy of your answers to the online test, and may ask you to explain your approach. Part 2: Technical Interview There were 2 technical interviews which consisted mainly of DSA questions (at least in my case). The interviews were held on a zoom video call, and we were asked to code on Hackerrank Codepair during the interviews. 29 people had been shortlisted for this round. Round 1: Technical My interview started with the basic tell-me-about-yourself question. Tip: This is always going to be the first question in all the interviews you give, so prepare a crisp introduction that you will use everywhere. The things you say can guide your interview from here on. For example, if you say you are more into development, you can expect follow up questions on your projects. Also you can mention your internships, hackathons and positions of responsibility. He then moved to asking me DSA questions: (i) https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/search-an-element-in-a-sorted-and-pivoted-array/ (ii) https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/lexicographical-maximum-substring-string/ I was asked to code the second question. My code was compiled, and he tested it on multiple test cases. Luckily I didn't get any errors, but even if you get some you can always debug those with a calm mind. The links that I gave above were not the exact same questions but the logic was the same as used to solve the above questions. After this he asked me if I had any questions for him. I asked him questions about the work culture at Goldman, the projects that they work on, and what will be my role as an intern. Also I asked him, is there anything in my resume that is a matter of concern. It was beneficial for me as it turned out he had not seen my resume, so after this question he checked my resume as well. Out of 29, 15 were shortlisted for the next round. Round 2: Technical The round as always began with the tell-me-about-yourself question. She asked me to describe any project of my choice. I had done a summer internship, so I described that project. From my resume she also asked me about a hackathon that I had mentioned in achievements. After that we moved to DSA questions: 1. Find the minimum depth of the binary tree. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/find-minimum-depth-of-a-binary-tree/ 2. Given a source and a destination coordinate on a chessboard, find the minimum number of moves a knight will have to make to reach from the source to the destination. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/minimum-steps-reach-target-knight/ Till here, I was asked to code for both the questions. As the interview was on a zoom call, I had used the whiteboard to explain the logic. Tip: Think out loud. Explain your logic, before you move on to the code. Even if you are stuck on a question, build up your approach and explain as you think. Listen carefully to the interviewer, generally they give you hints when you are stuck somewhere. Having said that, don’t ask for help from your side, tell your approach and work on that. 3. I was given the list of friends of two users on Facebook and was asked to find their mutual friends. As the question didn’t mention the way the data is formatted I asked this, to which she replied that I could use any data structure of my choice. I gave one solution that was using intersection of sets. Another approach I gave was merging of both the lists into a single array of objects. Mutual friends will appear twice, can be found using hashing or sorting and checking consecutive elements. When I gave two to three different solutions, she was satisfied. With this ended my second round. Part 3: Technical + HR Round This round was taken only for 5 people out of the 15. Interview began with introduce-yourself question. This round was conducted by two interviewers, one took the technical section for the first half, followed by the HR interview. In the technical section, I was asked DSA questions as I mentioned in my introduction that I do competitive programming. 1. Given an n*m matrix of 1s and 0s only, where a group of connected 1s forms an island, find the number of islands. https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/find-number-of-islands/ 2. I was given a string s. A rotated string of s is defined as any string r that is made by concatenating two non empty substrings(s1,s2) of s such that s=s1+s2 and r=s2+s1; I gave an O(n^2) solution. More optimal would have been using https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/kmp-algorithm-for-pattern-searching/ After this question, the HR round began. In the beginning, I was asked a few questions on core CS subjects. Questions were based on Computer Networks, Operating Systems, and System Design (the basic scalability question). 1. How familiar are you with Computer Networks ? I said I know only the basics, as we have this course in our current semester. https://medium.com/@maneesha.wijesinghe1/what-happens-when-you-type-an-url-in-the-browser-and-press-enter-bb0aa2449c1a Luckily I had read this article, and I included everything mentioned in this article in my answer. 2. What is memory management in operating systems? Do you know the concept of virtual memory? Explain. 3. Suppose you deploy your website, and the users increase 500x, how would you scale it up? In the end, they asked me if I had any questions for them. Tip: Always ask questions, it shows your interest in the company as well as your communication skills and confidence. I asked a few questions, to which the interviewer gave detailed answers. With that ended the third round. Results The way they selected candidates for the internship was confusing. They selected 2 applicants directly, from 15 who gave the second round (technical), and 4 applicants out of 5 who gave third round (technical + HR). So in total 6 of us (2 girls, 4 boys) were offered the internship. Tip: The key point is to always be prepared for anything and stay calm in between the rounds. You may be called at any moment for your next round, or it may so happen that you get selected without giving the third round. In my case, one hour after my third round, 3 of us were asked to join the zoom call together. It was kind of a prank round, and all three of us were offered the internship. So be patient (or not xD) and enjoy the process. Preparation I used interviewbit.com (one question from each bucket) and geeksforgeeks.com articles for DSA preparation. If you are starting late, it's the best platform. Whenever you are preparing for an interview, reading company specific archives from geeksforgeeks.com and about interview experiences helps a lot. You will get the basic idea of what kind of questions you will be asked and what their domain can be. Different questions about your projects can be asked. You can also be asked many questions on core subjects apart from DSA like OS, DBMS, CN, etc. I was just lucky in that case, because in the majority of rounds I was asked DSA questions. This totally depends on your interviewer and your luck. Lastly, it’s okay to be nervous. It’s okay to not stay calm. But don’t let it affect your interview. Be confident about yourself, and everything shall go well. All the Best!",

The grid comprises nrows\nand m columns of cells, where the content of each memory cell (0, j) is denoted by mem[i][j].\nwhere 0 <= i < n 0 <= j < m This memory management system operates as follows:\n\n3\n• Memory Access: Memory access begins from the top-left cell (0, 0). For every memory cell (t,\nj) there is an option to either access the data in the current cell (i, j) or proceed to the next cell\nby moving one cell right (1, j + 1 ) or one cell down (t + 1, j) provided that such cells exist within\nthe grid.\nThe objective is to reach the bottom-right cell (n - 1, m - 1 ) to complete the data retrieval.\nData Retrieval: During memory access, data stored in a cell can be read or skipped.\nMemory Usage Limitation: No more than k data items can be read from a row.\nDetermine the maximum sum of data that can be retrieved considering the per row read limit.\nExample It is given that mem =[ [3, 4, 10] , [2, 8, 1] ], and k = 2 Only 2 cells can be read in a row.\nIn row 0, for instance, cell pairs are (3, 4), (3, 10), (4, 10).\nThe optimal way to move will be from (0, 0) -> (0, 1) -> (1, 1) (1, . 2), reading the data from\nevery cell visited The sum of data retrieved is 3 + 4 + 8 + 1 = 16 .\nNo path exists from (0, 0) ^ + to (1, 2) to collect a greater sum of data .\nThe PPT\nThe results were announced on the interview day after their ppt, which everyone had to\nattend compulsorily. It's very important to attend the ppt and try to note down points\nwhich might be important for the interview.\nParticipate in the ppt if possible give answers ask questions when given a chance\nThis really did help me but again not being able to do this doesn't mean you will not get\nthe internship but if you can grab the opportunity go for it.\nThe names of every interviewer is really important to remember when you enter the\ninterview room and greet them with their name like hello Tvisha.\nInterviews\nThere were 2 interviews one was a pure tech based round the second was conducted by\na senior person which involved questions related to projects on your resume and general\nHR questions\n\n4\nInterview1(Pure Tech)\nI greeted her as hello Asha! smiled and took a seat.\nShe started with asking with are you excited to which I replied yes and\nI wasn't asked to introduce myself\nBut it's very important to have a good introduction ready as it's asked in most interviews.\nAlso the points you collect for the introduction can always be used for the HR round later.\nThen she moved on to ask me about my language of preference to which I replied cpp\nfor DSA and that I am familiar with python as I have used it in my projects\nShe asked me why I preferred cpp\nFirst I told her that it is a very fast language\nAnd I told her that it's a lower level language compared to python and the industry works\non the basis of time. There are cases where instruments like ATM machines use\nassembly to increase speed by milliseconds .\nI then paused for a second as I thought that this is one of the most important point\nin my opinion she then asked if is that it??\nThen I added that it is also a language that supports OOPs.\nSo she then asked me to explain OOPs\nI immediately started with explanation of the 4 pillars first naming them all\n(I would suggest not to do this) We should explain what it really means and then move\non to the 4 pillars.\nI explained her encapsulation and polymorphism for polymorphism I explained about\nruntime and compile time polymorphism by mentioning static and dynamic allocation and\nthen abstraction upon completion of the explanation of abstraction.   "content": "HTSI Interview Experience\nSumit Mhaske\nThird Year\nInformation Technology\nLocation: Pune\nStipend: 80,000 INR.\nTimeline\nOnline Test\nThe test had 61 questions for 90 mins in total and was held on Mettl, we had to allow camera and microphone access.\nCoding Section\nMr. Myers and the Exam -\nA mathematics question paper has a certain number of questions and each question is assigned some random maximum marks. Mr. Myers wants to edit the marks assigned to the questions such that:\n1. All questions in the paper should have distinct maximum marks.\n2. The total marks of all the questions should be as low as possible.\nMr. Myers wants to achieve this by making minimal changes in the original format, assigning the question at least as much marks as it originally had. Find the minimum total marks that he can set the paper for.\nInput Specification:\nInput1: The number of questions in the paper\nInput2: The array representing the original marks assigned to every question.\nOutput Specification:\nThe minimum total marks Mr. Myers can set the paper for.\nSolution: We simply need to maintain an unordered_set to check if an element has already occurred and then run a for loop. If the element is not present in the set, insert it. If it is present, increment the element by 1, decrement i (because the for loop will increment it, and we’ll decrement it so that it remains at the same index to check if the incremented value is present in the set or not).\nAptitude Section\nThis section had a 30-minute timer. The questions were quite easy; you just needed to think quickly and solve them fast, as there were 30 questions to complete in 30 minutes. Some were mental ability questions, while others required math (probability and statistics). The math questions were a bit challenging, so it's better to solve the non-math questions first.\nComputer Fundamentals\nThis section had questions based on -\nDSA -6\nOS -6\nOOPs -7\nCN -6\nDBMS -5\nI finished my online assessment with around 10 minutes remaining. I submitted the test quickly because sometimes, when people get the same scores, they might judge you based on the time taken to finish. I had already checked my answers, so I didn't need to double-check them. You should double-check if you haven't.\nAround 27 students were shortlisted for interviews. We received the shortlist between 3-4 PM on the next day (1st August), and the interviews were scheduled for 9 AM on 2nd August. I had already started preparing for the interview because I was confident about the questions I solved. On the day of the online assessment itself, I informed my senior, who had been guiding me throughout my preparation, that I was confident about the test and expected to be shortlisted, with my interview scheduled for the day after tomorrow. She arranged a mock interview for me in the morning so she could give feedback on certain topics, allowing me to prepare accordingly that day.\nNote: Always verify your resume and seek preparation guidance from your seniors.\nINTERVIEWS (Offline)\nTechnical Round\nWe were seated in the TPO hall and introduced to the panelists who came to interview us, consisting of six people, one of whom was from HR. The technical rounds ran simultaneously, with one interviewer assigned to each candidate. We were called in batches of five, and those deemed capable were sent directly for the HR round after 15 minutes to an hour of technical interviews (so be prepared for the HR round as well). I was 16th or 17th in the serial order, and my turn came just after the lunch break, around 1:45 PM. Don't forget to ask those who go for the interview before you about the questions they were asked, as sometimes the questions get repeated.\nFinally, I was called in and greeted warmly by the interviewer. Always greet the interviewer with a smile and be confident. He took my resume and asked if I knew how much I scored in my online assessment. I replied that we weren't informed about the marks (at this point, you might feel a bit anxious, but remember—never doubt yourself in an interview). He then asked me to introduce myself and share some background information. Always have a brief introduction ready, about 1 to 2 minutes long.\nThe flow should be:\n1. Name\n2. Branch\n3. Technical stacks/domains you've worked on (I focused on web development)\n4. Achievements (hackathon wins, competitive programming awards)\n5. Positions in clubs/internship experience\n6. Hobbies\nAfter this, he introduced himself and mentioned that he would share more about his career at the end of the interview (which I asked about at the end, making a good impression by showing curiosity and attentiveness).\nHe went through my resume and started with technical questions. He began with, \"So you do C++, right?\" and then asked me about the differences between C++ and languages like C, COBOL, and Pascal. I told him that I had never worked with COBOL or Pascal but that I was familiar with C, and I explained the differences between C and C++ (always be honest with your answers, and don’t hesitate to mention things you haven't done—they won't focus on those areas).\nHe then expanded on my explanation and asked about inheritance, specifically whether we can inherit everything from a parent class (the answer is no—private members cannot be inherited), and asked me to explain it with code. Another question from OOP was to explain function and operator overloading, also with code examples.\nHe then asked about my projects and requested that I explain one of them. Always follow the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) pattern when explaining your projects.\nHe went on to ask what exactly I did in this project, how I did it, the flow of data, and how we implemented it (make sure to remember the libraries you used in your projects). He was interested in the concepts and didn’t ask for any code.\nNote: Be clear about the objectives of your projects, what you did to achieve them, and the technical details involved.\nAfter this, he moved on to data structures and algorithms (DSA). He gave me a sequence of numbers written on a paper and asked me to implement a stack and a queue, then push this sequence into both and predict the output sequence when we pop all the elements. After that, he asked me to consider this as a depth-first search (DFS) of a tree and construct the tree, telling me that 54 (which was somewhere in the middle of the sequence) is the root.\nThe trick here is that since the root isn’t at the start or end of the sequence, it can’t be a preorder or postorder traversal—it must be an inorder traversal. This means all the elements on the left of the root are part of the left subtree, and those on the right are part of the right subtree. I constructed the tree and explained that the left and right subtrees of the root can be arranged in multiple ways because we don’t have further information.\nThen he asked me to consider this as a breadth-first search (BFS) and construct the tree again. I pointed out that this can't be BFS because, in BFS, the root is always at the start, representing the top level of the tree.\nThis experience highlights that it’s not always about your coding skills; sometimes, you’re presented with trick questions where you need to act smart and think rationally.\nThen he moved on to operating systems (OS) and asked me what paging is. The follow-up question was whether I knew how the Windows setting for 'changing page size' works. He then asked about race conditions and how to prevent them. When I mentioned locks along with other techniques, he asked what the similar concept is in DBMS. He was referring to Two-Phase Locking (2PL), so I explained transactions, concurrency, and 2PL. He also asked about normalization.\nHe then drew a table on paper, and I knew it was time for SQL. He asked me to write a simple query to retrieve data based on certain conditions (essentially using the WHERE clause). However, the follow-up was tricky. He drew another table and asked me to retrieve some attributes that were from both the first and second tables. Now, if I had mentioned joins, I would have been wrong because there were no common attributes between the tables. I pointed out this observation, and he smiled before adding a ‘serial_no’ column to the second table to create a common attribute. He then explained his requirements and asked me to write the query. It required the use of a nested loop, and after some thinking, I figured out the answer.\nHe then presented a quiz: We have three jars with capacities of 12 liters, 8 liters, and 5 liters. None of the jars have any markings on the inside. You can fill, empty, or transfer water between the jars. The task is to measure exactly 6 liters of water, meaning you need to have exactly 6 liters in one of the jars by following the given steps.\nHe gave me ample time, and I used paper to draw the transitions. After around 10 or more transitions, I managed to get 6 liters in one jar. (Hint: In these types of questions, focus on what extra amount you need to reach the target, compared to the capacity of the jar that is just smaller than the target, and try to achieve that by leveraging the differences in the jar capacities). You can find similar puzzles on GeeksforGeeks (GFG).\nHe then asked me if I had any questions about the work or the company. It's important to always scroll through the company's website and gather information from seniors and other sources. Be sure to prepare your questions based on this research (always ask questions—it shows that you're genuinely interested in the company). Make sure to ask relevant questions and try to come up with something unique, rather than just the common questions you find on the internet.\nWe talked about this for a while, and he explained everything in great detail, as he seemed interested in me. I also reminded him that he mentioned earlier that he would tell me about his career path, and he shared it with me.\nAt the end, he said, \"I liked you pretty much. Power Limit Given 2 resources with powers A and B respectively. At each second, you have to select one resource out of 2 to run the software. The power of the resource at the time of selection should be greater than 1. Every second, the power of the selected resource gets reduced by 2 and the power of the unselected resource gets charged by 1. The software stops when at least one resource has 0 power. You are given integers A and B. Print the maximum number of seconds your software can run if you select the resources optimally. Function Description Complete the function PowerLimit(). This function takes the following 2 parameters A represents the power of the first resource and B represents the power of the second resource. I passed 9/10 test cases. 2.Auto Suggest Given a dictionary consisting of N words and a query word S. You need to auto suggest the best word from the dictionary that is closest to S. Two words are first compared by their Levenshtein distance to the word S. If two words have the same Levenshtein distance, then the lexicographically smaller word is given priority. Notes Levenshtein distance between two strings is defined as the minimum number of edits required to obtain one string from the other. An \"edit\" is defined by either an insertion of a character, a deletion of a character, or a replacement of a character. All the words and the query word S consist of lowercase alphabets only. I passed all the test cases of this question. 3.Backlink Sorting Backlinks are links from other websites to a particular web resource, and they play a crucial role in the SEO of pages. You are given N web page titles and corresponding arrays that contain the number of backlinks for each web page. The objective is to rank the web pages in descending order based on the number of backlinks they have. Note: If two or more web pages have the same number of backlinks, maintain their original order. Function description Complete the function Sorter. This function takes 2 parameters as arguments and returns the strings: WebPage: Represents an array of strings that contains the webpage titles Backlinks: Represents an array of integers that contains the backlink count. Don’t stress yourself too much. Don’t beat yourself up if you don’t get selected. There will be many more opportunities. Do not lie on your resume or try to cheat in the interview. Write only those things in your resume which you are confident about. Explain to the interviewer every detail of the code, and keep conversing. Think out loud and let them know your thought process. They might encourage you by saying that you are on the right track. During interviews, keep yourself calm, hydrated, and be confident. Make a document where you can add answers for those questions which you think the interviewer can ask you about your resume. Like your introduction, Descriptions of your projects, Why do you want to join XYZ company, What are your strengths and weaknesses, etc Most of the HR questions didn’t require any preparation but the recollection of your past journey would be a nice option because if you can co-relate the question asked in the interview to the real-life situation which has occurred before, there are decent chances of yours getting selected. Sometimes try giving mock interviews, it will help you to boost your confidence. During interviews always have a smile on your face. Don’t let interviewers think that you are nervous or under stress. Do good research about the company and recruiters. Research the company you are interviewing for thoroughly. Also, if you know your interviewer beforehand then go follow on LinkedIn to know more about their work. Try contacting a senior who works there/ has worked there. We were free to make any assumptions regarding the use of STL, library functions and format of input data. However, whatever assumptions we made, we were supposed to be written. In a football tournament having 20 teams, each team plays every other team twice – once on their home ground and once away. Find the team having the highest points. 3. Given the fate of a ball, find the runs scored in one legitimate over. 'N' and 'W' stand for no ball and wide ball respectively Input represents the kind of ball and the runs scored on that ball. Eg: ['N', 4] implies 4 runs are scored on a no ball. We were free to make further assumptions about the input that would be provided. We received an email at around 2:15 wherein they gave a schedule for the 'technical' and 'personality' rounds of all candidates. All those selected for the coding round were required to appear for these two rounds as well. These two rounds were at a gap of one hour from each other. Personality round The interviewer started by asking me about myself and my family. Then he asked me about how I liked to spend my free time. At the end, he asked me if I had any questions. I asked some questions regarding the company and the culture and he answered them. HR round At around 6:30PM, we got a message from our TPO CR that Yash and I had been called for the HR round. I joined the meet. I was asked about how my day was and my experience regarding the interview process. After that, one of the interviewers said that they would be sharing the screen and showing me the compensation breakdown. This is your salary discussion.” And that is when I realised that my job hunt was finally over. At the end they said that I was assigned the Mumbai office and they would mail us the final offer by night. It was a long day, but it was worth it.
