Information Technology Batch 2027 Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute (VJTI) The Morgan Stanley Experience Overview During our 2025 TY internship drive, the company that arrived near the beginning of August was Morgan Stanley. The online assessment (OA) was scheduled for the 10th of August, while the pre-placement talk (PPT) was scheduled on the 11th of August. The process from the arrival of the company to the final shortlists took almost an entire week. Eligibility Criteria The eligibility criteria for Morgan Stanley is, 1. Circuital Branch (Computer Engineering, Information Technology, E-branches) 2. CGPA ≥7.5 3. No active backlogs Online Assessment Date: 10th August, 2025 Platform: SHL AMCAT (No Proctoring) Duration: 2 hours The online assessment was held on the SHL AMCAT platform. It had an overall duration of 120 minutes (lasting from 14:00 to 16:00) and consisted of three sections: Debugging, Aptitude and Programming. Each section was separately timed; you had to complete one section for the entire stipulated duration before moving onto the next. This also meant that once the duration of a section was over, it was not possible to return to a previous section. Below are the descriptions of the individual sections. Section 1: Debugging Duration: ∼20 minutes Allowed Programming Languages: Only C++ or Java This sections consisted of a lightning round of simple programming problems where an implementation of the code was already given, albeit intentionally buggy. The objective of the round was to “assess the candidate’s ability to diagnose and identify any bugs in the code and fix them”. The round consisted of around 7 or so problems, all very introductory programming programs such as sorting, searching or if-else problems. An example I recall from memory is: for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++); System.out.print(\"*\"); System.out.println(); } In the above problem, not only is there an off-by-one error (j <= i), but also the inner loop body ends early because of the stray semicolon (for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++);). Another example was a case where an implementation of selection sort was provided, but it was returning the contents in the reverse order than what was expected. A bit of digging around with the comparisons allowed fixing of this one. What is worth noting is that the only languages allowed in this section are C++ or Java. I reckon this is because of their universal curly brace and semicolon syntax. I personally had better experience with Java, so I solved all problems in that. Section 2: Aptitude Duration: ∼40 minutes This was probably the meat and potatoes of the entire assessment. This section had a mixed set of interactive and MCQ-style problems. The theme of the questions was logical reasoning and data interpretation. While the exact questions themselves are lost to time, here is a gist of the kind of problems asked: • Logical scheduling: Meeting schedules given for a bunch of employees, and a map of an office consisting of multiple departments. Each employee and department have their own availability windows and conflicts, and our objective was to align the employees to have a non-conflicting schedule. The interaction to this problem was also fun, as we had to literally drag-and-drop the employee to the correct department using the mouse on the map. • Logical ordering: Some riddle-like clues such as “A is faster than B with one in between” and “C is slower than D” are provided; we have to drag-and-drop the entities to rank them in the correct order. • Pattern recognition: A very typical olympiad-style problem where three esoteric images are provided, and you gotta pick the next likely image in the sequence. • Data interpretation: A description of some companies’ finances is provided, and we had to interactively resize a pie chart or reorder a bar chart to match the exact percentages of the finances in the correct categories. This section had the most problems, which was around 15 to 20 of them. I personally could not finish some of the last few problems in time, but as we shall see later, it still worked out. Section 3: Programming Duration: ∼60 minutes Allowed Programming Languages: Any This section is the typical programming round, where three DSA problems were asked, not dissimilar to a CodeChef or Codeforces contest. Unlike the debugging round, all well-known programming languages were allowed here predictably, and I chose to go with Python; being the language I had the most experience with in Competitive Programming. Here are the descriptions of the three problems, best recalled from memory: 1. Given an array of order sizes, which is intended to be sorted in ascending order, find the number of orders which are currently in their incorrect positions. The approach was very simple, as it only required a comparison of the given array with its sorted version. 2. An array of 𝑁 numeric IDs are given of the same digit length. The problem essentially asked to count the sum of the number of distinct digits in the same position across all pairs of the IDs array. While this seems daunting, and some optimized approaches may come to mind, a brute-force solution was actually accepted by the judge. 3. There are 𝑀 sprints and 𝑁 events. Each sprint is essentially an interval with a start and end time, and each event should occur at a certain time. The question asked for the number of events that were not covered by any sprint. Sorting the sprints chronologically and performing a prefix calculation allowed counting all events that do not get covered by any sprint. As it can be observed, the judge focused on correctness over optimization. Most brute-force solutions were acceptable, and thus did not ask too much of the candidates. I was able to get all three problems cleared with a good 15 minutes still remaining, so I was able to complete the assessment early. The OA happened on Sunday, and with no results out I was just shopping groceries on Monday evening, only to be surprised by a congratulatory notification, finding out I was actually shortlisted for the interview that would occur... the next day. Well that was unexpected. Not only me, but a grand total of 17 shortlists and 3 waitlists were selected; me being a part of the 17 shortlists. Interview The interviews were conducted on the 12th of August, on Zoom. Since the interviews were online, we did not need the commute to college. The interviews conducted of two rounds: Technical and Human Resources (HR). Interview 1: Technical Round The interviews started at 09:00 in the morning and lasted till 16:30, each interview lasting one hour long. My position in the queue was #13, and my interview slot itself was at 13:00. This meant that I had to essentially wait in anticipation from the start of the first interview, frequently revising all topics I could recall. Now while this section is about the interview itself, I would like to mention my last-day preparation method, which is outlined in the last section of this document. Coming to the interview itself, I joined a Zoom waiting call and the first step to begin the interview for a candidate was to just present a valid government ID via the camera to prove their identity. After that, the candidate is redirected to the call with their interviewer. As the interview began, I gave a short introduction of myself, simply stating my current academic and programming background. The interviewer requested me to open an IDE or code editor without autocomplete to begin the DSA round. However, I myself elected to perform the technical round in Google Docs or Word instead, which was also fine with the interviewer. My rationale was to mitigate any contemporary issues in the dev environment on my machine, which could mess up code execution. Other than that I could also showcase programming without intellisense or autocomplete, which was possible only due to my proficiency in Java, and also dodge the event of subtle bugs or errors if the code were to be executed. Although I would like to confirm that this is not a required step (or even a possible step given the interviewer), and if you are comfortable with an IDE, then do so. First Problem: Left Side View of a Binary Tree The interviewer properly began the technical round by asking me whether I “had the knowledge of tree data structures”. I affirmed and she was able to provide the first DSA problem: Left Side View of a Binary Tree. The problem presented a rooted binary tree which if were to be looked from the left side, would produce a list of vertices that are visible. This is a variation on the LeetCode problem 199. I solved all DSA problems in Java, as it was the language I had the most confidence with. I explained the method leftSideView(...) that would input the root of the tree as an argument, and verbally constructed my logic as I coded along the solution. I opted for a recursive solution (DFS), as is the case for binary tree-based problems. An interesting quirk of that approach was me wanting an initial condition on the first call, because of which I opted to overload the above method with an additional height parameter. This very decision prompted the interviewer to ask what I understood by “overloading”, starting a tangent of OOP/Java questions in the midst of the DSA problem. The questions best recalled from memory were: • What is method overloading? • What is the difference between ‘overloading’ and ‘overriding’? • What is an interface? • How can you implement a default method from an interface? Note: I actually was unable to correctly answer this question, and communicated that to the interviewer, who clarified that this question was post Java 8, which is likely why I did not possess knowledge of it. Thankfully having a good grasp on OOP principles, I was able to answer most of the problems. Returning to the DSA problem, while I may not have had the most elegant solution, this is what I constructed: class TreeNode { public int x; TreeNode(int x) { this.x = x; } } public class Main { private int max_height = 0; public void leftSideView(TreeNode root) { leftSideView(root, 1); } private void leftSideView(TreeNode root, int height) { if (root == null) return; if (height > max_height) { max_height = height; System.out.println(root.x); } leftSideView(root.left, height + 1); leftSideView(root.right, height + 1); } } While typing the solution, I also drew some test cases (perks of using Docs) to dry-run my logic and prove the correctness and complexity of my implementation. After my justification, the interviewer was convinced and moved on to the next problem. Second Problem: “Merge” Sorted Arrays This was another variation on a well-known problem, this time being on the LeetCode problem 88. The setup was simple: Given two long arrays, the elements within which were already sorted in non-decreasing order, I had to perform some swaps in-place such that the minimum elements are held in the first array, and the maximum in the second, while preserving the non-decreasing order across both arrays. An example test case used was as follows: a = [1, 2, 8, 10], b = [5, 6, 9, 11]. After running the algorithm, the arrays should have been: a = [1, 2, 5, 6], b = [8, 9, 10, 11]. There was also this other spanner thrown in by the interviewer that if a[0] < b[0], then a should be treated as the “minimum” array, else b. I initially picked a to be the “minimum” array, and ran a two-pointer nested loop across both arrays, swapping bigger elements out to b in favor of smaller ones in a, while also correcting any internal inversions. My implementation was certainly convoluted, but I justified every decision I took and explained the logic aloud with test cases. This is the code I presented: public class Main { public void merge(int[] a, int[] b) { if (a.length == 0 || b.length == 0) return; if (a[0] <= b[0]) { mergeArrays(a, b); } else { mergeArrays(b, a); } } public void mergeArrays(int[] a, int[] b) { int m = a.length; int n = b.length; for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) { if (b[j] < a[i]) { int ptr = j; swap(a[i], b[j]); while (ptr < n && b[ptr] > b[ptr + 1]) { swap(b[ptr], b[ptr + 1]); ptr++; } } else { break; } } } } } Do note that swap(...) is not a standard Java function; swapping typically requires three lines of additional code. However, I communicated with the interviewer if I could use some psuedocode, and I was allowed to do so. This is why constantly communicating with the interviewer is really important. I was very much stuck while coding up this solution, but the interviewer always nudged me by providing more test cases so that I could define the logic first and write it down later. I justified the correctness and the 𝒪(𝑚𝑛) complexity of the solution and the interviewer moved onto the next topic. Third Problem: Querying non-retired employees The next topic was of databases and SQL. The setup was two tables: employees and retired_employees in a relational database with the same schema: first_name TEXT, last_name TEXT, age INTEGER, salary REAL, dept TEXT. The problem was to obtain the full names of the non-retired employees with salary greater than 50,000, age less than 20, and dept of ‘XYZ’. Simply obtaining the first and last names given the condition in either table is trivial. The curveball was to exclude all the employees that existed in the retired table from the employees queried from the first table. I personally first constructed the trivial query to fetch the employee names with the given specifications, and then used the set MINUS operator. The other nitpick was to have a single column full_name derived from first_name and last_name. I pretty much threw the CONCAT operator at the end of my query, and the interviewer accepted the result. This was the query I had presented: ( SELECT CONCAT(first_name , last_name) AS full_name FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 AND age < 20 AND dept = 'XYZ' ) MINUS ( SELECT CONCAT(first_name , last_name) AS full_name FROM retired_employees WHERE salary > 50000 AND age < 20 AND dept = 'XYZ' ); Note that the CONCAT operator may be used incorrectly here. This should reinforce that the objective of an interview is not to always be 100% correct in terms of code; it is to be able to present your logic and thinking clearly. Apart from the SQL problem the interviewer also transitioned into some DBMS questions, which were as follows: • What are joins? • What is the difference between a LEFT JOIN and a LEFT OUTER JOIN? Note: I was unable to answer this question, as this was a trick question: there is no semantic difference between the two. Interview 2: HR Round My initial interview had ended by 14:00, and by the next hour the shortlists for the next round had arrived: 3 shortlists from the original 17 and the 3 waitlists were also revealed for their first round, who were unknown so far. As the technical rounds continued in parallel, few more people were eligible for the HR round. My HR interview was due in the next 30 minutes from the time of the update. I did not have much to prepare as such, and opted to surf through commonly asked questions. The interview began with my introduction, and I pretty much explained my academic and programming background the same way as the first time, but the outcome was different. First of all, the interviewer was simply curious about VJTI and the relation of its autonomy with Mumbai University. I explained the history of the institute off the top of my head. Another attribute I had mentioned in my intro was my CGPA, which was over 9 at the time. This prompted a question by the interviewer: “If people like Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman are dropouts, then why would you feel the need to mention your CGPA?” This was a tough question, as one of the pillars to hold in an on-campus internship is a high GPA. I tackled it by justifying that while people may succeed regardless of GPA, being able to actually maintain a high GPA over all the semesters does prove a candidate’s consistency and effort. I also pointed out Morgan Stanley’s own 7.5+ CGPA criteria, which existed to prove a candidate had put in the effort to maintain that score. Another description I mentioned about me was my participation in student clubs, primarily Project X and the CP Club. The interviewer was intrigued by the CP Club and asked what it is and what role I played in it. This provided me an opportunity to praise the mentoring culture of VJTI and its application in the CP Club. Continuing on with the CP Club, I also described the ICPC as it was related. Not only that, I also mentioned about me participating in the ICPC of 2025, which helped me make a stronger impression on the interviewer. This was technically true, as I did appear for the ICPC prelims later that year. After the introduction was over, the interviewer asked me about AI-assisted coding, and if I used any tools for those myself at the time. I mentioned the name of an LLM-based IDE I had used, and the interviewer was impressed, as the company behind that software had good relations with Morgan Stanley. This was completely unintentional though, but it sure was a pleasant surprise. Continuing on with the topic, the interviewer presented the first proper question: “Where would you see yourself in five years if LLMs generate all code?” Since I had used LLMs for coding myself, I was somewhat prepared for the question. My answer in a gist was explaining the fact that engineers are problem solvers; not code writers. Not only that, the imaginative skills of humans can fundamentally not be replaced with AI, or at least not in those next five years. Ultimately I presented my own independent views on the topic, which is what is expected of a candidate in an HR interview. Thus, there is no need to consider any of these answers as templates; treat them more as guidelines to think of your answer. Always remember the only person the interviewer wants to see is ‘you’. Having said that, I will now list down the remaining questions that were asked to me upon which I presented my own thoughts. • What are you planning to do after your four years of engineering? • What are three of your non-negotiables? • How would you handle a conflict within a team? Circling back to the discussion on GPAs, here was another fun question asked: • If someone with a lower grade is in conflict with you, how would you win the argument? This is another kind of a trick question, as there is no real correlation between a person’s academic grade and the matter of a conflict. After all these questions, the HR round was pretty much over. The interviewer asked me for any questions I had for the firm, and I connected a research experience I had in my profile to the question and inquired of Research and Development (RnD) in the firm. The interviewer explained a lot about the firm and what many of its sectors do. It was a pleasant conversation. And that word is important: Conversation. Never did I feel I was necessarily getting ‘tested’, as I was simply responding instinctively with the answers and opinions I already had. I felt genuinely confident that I had performed well. Results Unlike other company experiences, there was actually some waiting for the Morgan Stanley results. This was because 2 of the waitlisted candidates were actually eligible for the second interview round, but the time of the day had run out. This induced a second set of interviews only for the two remaining candidates the next day (Wednesday), and the day after that (Thursday) was when the results got announced within college hours itself: 4 people were accepted, of which I was one! Resources Here are a few resources I personally used during my preparation, although the list is very flexible: Youtube Java Full Course by Bro Code, LeetCode Top 150, Interviewbit — Technical Interview Questions, CodeHelp Core CS Notes, CodeChef Starters, Codeforces Rounds, My peers. Do practice coding problems under time constraints; contests like those of CodeChef and Codeforces provide very similar environments to OAs which can help preparation. Researching and preparing using LLMs is also recommended, as for the most part one can get accurate information about core CS and also tailor the chat according to their preferences. Behind the Scenes This was surely a whole lot of a process for one internship. But the reality is that none of this existed in a vacuum: Everyone who had to wait till Morgan Stanley on-campus had essentially “failed” six or so companies already, including JPMorgan Chase & Co., D. E. Shaw & Co., Goldman Sachs, Bank of New York Mellon and others. It is easy to read this experience and assume things went hunky-dory, while in reality it was a very stressful and meticulous process. While I personally do not like labeling companies as ‘good’ or ‘bad’, one metric a lot of people use is the pay. Higher-paying companies, on average, are expected to arrive early, while lower-paying companies tend to arrive on-campus later, although there is no guarantee to this rule. Keeping this in mind, imagine a student not making into any company early on and they observe their opportunities gradually thinning out. I was a victim of this very scenario. I personally could not clear the OAs for any of the first few companies. The first company I did succeed in was Pattern, an e-commerce accelerator. I was a waitlist interviewee, which induced my slot of the first round to the very end, making me wait till late evening inside the campus. It was all for naught, as I butchered the interview. The next company in-line before Morgan Stanley was BNY Mellon. I had an okayish experience with its OA, and carried some expectations for the shortlists. However, that too ended in disappointment, as I was not selected. While the process was depressing, I did not have much to control apart from my own preparation. I opted to isolate myself from distractions and revisit some fundamentals and LeetCode problems in the one week between the BNY rejection and the Morgan Stanley OA. Being notified about my interview shortlist at the night of Monday was surely a pleasant surprise, but I pretty much had only 12 hours to prepare before the interviews formally began. I hopped on a call with some of my colleagues who had collaborated on one of my résumé projects to help me explain the project in the event an interviewer wished to see. While this did not happen in my interviews, other candidates did experience questions on their résumé and their projects, even going as far as presenting and explaining the codebase within the interview. The colleagues were kind and also helped me revise CS fundamentals and common HR questions in the same call, providing a sort of crash-course. I am still grateful of Kartikay and Tanish for that. After the call, I spent some time midnight solving the top interview LeetCode problems. Turns out the first question in the problemset is Merge Sorted Array itself, which was yet another pleasant surprise the next day. The final rush, combined with the advice of colleagues who had cracked internships earlier, was what put me at my best for the two rounds I appeared in. Now one peculiarity observed in Morgan Stanley’s results was that they were the first company so far last season to fully interview all waitlisted candidates. Typically waitlisted candidates are assumed to be kept at the tail end of the interviews and are expected nine times out of ten to not receive the offer. However, the trend a lot of companies had been noticing at the time was the inability of candidates to answer programming and development-based problems that they should be expected to solve given they cleared the online assessment. This lackluster performance was probably the reason Morgan Stanley chose to not only fully interview the waitlisted candidates, but also one of the 4 interns they did select was indeed one of the original 3 waitlists. This theory is further bolstered by the statistic of them hiring 8 interns in 2024, but only 4 in 2025. A possible explanation for this situation well-known unaddressed elephant for online assessments was the rampant cheating that could be happening at the homes of some candidates, regardless of the proctoring severity. OA cheating is nasty and cannot really be avoided. It was one of the supporting factors for why clearing the OA is a much more difficult task than clearing the interview. Since the alleged cheaters are unable to clear the interviews, them losing one company and immediately claiming the interview seat of the next causes a perpetual wastage of a few seats that could have been claimed by an honest candidate. Other than that, getting selected also requires a lot of fortune. It is practically impossible to predict your success regardless of how much effort you may have put in. You could literally count the number of ‘pleasant surprises’ I had this entire experience, and it would demonstrate the power of luck, while every OA failed in the past would be an example otherwise. Remember that companies hire with no prior knowledge about the candidates, so if CGPA, OA performance, Résumé ATS, vibe-check-by-the-assigned-interviewer or any other metric helps them gauge by their preferences, they may opt for it. Since this is not only out of our knowledge but also our control, attempting to predict the offer is no better than rolling a dice. What I would ultimately suggest is to not obsess over any companies, as there is no guarantee of achieving the offer. However, this should not stop you from practising and revising your skills, as they still improve the chances of survival. Keep improving yourself until the only way the dice can roll is in your victory. The End.",

The OAs for both were held together on 5th November on campus. Out of all the students that had applied, 60 were selected for each role to sit for the OA. Online Assessment (OA) The OA was the same for both roles — 22 questions with a time limit of 1 hour. 20 were MCQs and 2 were coding questions, they were not separated into distinct sections. You need to keep a close eye on the timer while solving the MCQs so you leave adequate time for the coding questions. MCQ Breakdown The MCQs fell broadly into three categories: • Code Snippets: These were relatively straightforward — pseudo code was given and you either had to complete the code or identify possible outputs. • Financial Maths: Compound interest, pattern finding, rate of return, P/E ratio, and some probability questions. • Financial Knowledge: Portfolio risk assessment, hypothesis testing, covariance testing, and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF). Coding Questions The 2 coding questions were relatively manageable: • Candy distribution problem: Two siblings (older sister and younger brother) had to be given candies such that the sister always got more than the brother, based on the formula k×(a+x) = b×y, where a = candies to sister, b = candies to brother, and (x + y) = minimum total candies. • Stock market max profit: Find the day where the stock earned maximum profit. I didn't get time to attempt this one, but something similar is available on LeetCode — worth a look. There were 2 panels for each role. Don't skip this — firstly because this sets an expectation for what they expect out of you and secondly this gives you an opportunity to ask questions to the company as a whole – the right question can give you the edge so chose your questions wisely, my advise would be to centre them around the current affairs. Interview Round 1 This was my first interview ever, and I was first on the list — so naturally the anxiety was through the roof. My panel had just one interviewer, and I think he sensed the nerves and actively tried to ease the environment before we got started. Here's roughly how it went: • Why this role? — What attracted you to Asset Allocation / Risk Investment. • Resume walkthrough — He went through my resume and asked me to explain my main project and give a demo. • Financial concepts — Terms like the Sharpe ratio came up. • OA reflection — He asked which questions I liked in the OA. • HR questions — Strengths, weaknesses, the usual. • Puzzle at the end — 100 hens sitting in a circle. Each hen will peck at least once, either the hen to its right or left. Find the maximum number of hens that remain unpecked. The Hen Puzzle — Solution A hen remains unpecked only when both neighbours peck away from it. So think in groups of 3 — the unpecked hen sits in the middle with the two on either side pecking outward. 100 ÷ 3 = 33. I didn't get it immediately, and the interviewer did help me through it — don't be afraid to think out loud and ask help. One important thing to note was that the interview was actually built around my OA performance; they had a full analysis showing strengths and weaknesses, and my maths and financials clearly outshone my coding which shaped the direction of questions. Personal Interest & Beyond the Resume They asked about something that wasn't on my resume and about my personal interests. Finance Case Question This was the hardest part. They presented different individuals with varying backgrounds and asked me to classify how each would invest across three categories — equities, savings, and bonds. I honestly had very little idea. I gave an answer based on whatever I knew, I'm fairly sure it was wrong, and I'm fairly sure the panel knew that too. I thought it was over for me — but we continued. There's no right answer to this — just be honest. Final Outcome Then came the stressful waiting time — and then the announcement on the spot. Quite a relieving moment. Key Takeaways Preparation For the OA, don't just focus on one area — cover everything. On the coding side, Striver's A2Z sheet and LeetCode are your best friends. Beyond the OA itself, take some time to read about the company and understand what the roles actually involve. This would also help you out in the OA Time Management This goes beyond just pacing yourself in the OA. Be early — not on time, early. Carry a pen and a notebook to every stage of the process, from the pre-placement talk through to your interviews. Jotting things down during the pre-placement talk helps you pick up useful details that can feed directly into your interview answers. In the interview itself, using a notebook to work through a problem lets the interviewer see how you think, not just what you conclude — and that visibility into your process can make a real difference. Communication I can’t emphasize enough about this one. Judge the scenario of the interview and go with the flow – don’t restrict yourself to a question-and-answer vibe. And also be open to small talk – this helps them gauge your personality. One thing that genuinely makes a difference is thinking out loud. Don't rush straight to an answer — interviewers want to follow your reasoning. This matters even more when you're wrong. And before you even walk into the room, spend 10 minutes talking to whoever came out before you. Once you're in there, be upfront about where you're strong and where you're stuck as they will genuinely try to help you out. Be Yourself It sounds obvious, but don't script yourself. The moment you start reciting a rehearsed answer, the panel can tell — and it closes you off from the moments that actually land. Let your real interests come through, even the unexpected ones. In my Round 2, mentioning motorsport genuinely seemed to work in my favour — not because it was impressive, but because it was real. By the second round especially, they're not just assessing whether you can answer questions. They want to know if they'd enjoy working with you. Readability is just as important as correctness, especially in Google interviews. ● Listen to the interviewer: Consistently listen to what the interviewer is saying. He/She might drop some hints where you are stuck. ● Be quick but not hurried: The interviewer may expect you to solve follow up questions. In interviews, the interviewer won’t help you identify edge cases, it’s your responsibility. Given an array, count the number of elements which occur more than once. Example: arr = [1,3,3,4,4], should return 2 Constraint: Size of array <= 10^5 2. In this question, we were given a number in the form of a string. What we had to do was swap adjacent elements if their parity (odd/even) was the same and then form the largest number possible using these swaps. We could do any number of swaps. Example: 1. 7956801 gives 9758601 We can swap 9 with 7 which gives 9756801 We can swap 6 with 8 which gives 9758601 2. 1806579 gives 1860975 We can swap 6 with 0 We can swap 9 and 7, then 9 and 5 Constraints: Number of digits <= 10^5 OA Solution & Experience: 1. For the first question, I used the Counter data structure available in python. I also used a variable 'count' to store the count of the duplicates. I iterated over all the keys of the Counter and checked if its corresponding value is > 1. If yes, increment 'count'. Time and space complexity: O(n), where n is the number of digits. 2. It took me a while to get the second question right. First I tried the brute force approach, but it did not pass all testcases. In the end, I grouped the array into contiguous sequences of elements with the same parity, sorted them in reversed order, then joined them back and returned it. Why this works: Sorting can be represented as swapping adjacent elements until some order is achieved (Bubble sort). So instead of actually swapping adjacent just group them and sort using inbuilt sorting, which then reduces the time complexity. Time and space complexity: O(nlogn) , O(n) resp. OA Results: Around 13 people got selected from the OA. Video Interview The next step of the recruiting process is a video interview on HireVue. In this HireVue interview, you will be asked to record video responses to 2 interview questions. My questions were something along the lines of: 1. Talk about an instance where you have worked on a group project. Describe your tasks and the outcome. 2. What steps have you taken to learn about this program? A question appears on the screen for which, 1. You are initially given 30 seconds to prepare your response 2. The recording starts automatically after that 3. After recording the first response (maximum 3 minutes limit), you click done and it gives you an option to retry or submit the recording. You can also preview the recording just made. 4. After your first recording, there is no time limit to choose between retry and submit. 5. But once you click retry and record your response, the next response is submitted automatically, and you can't preview it. Video Interview results: 4 students were selected from the video interview. JPMC allows you to choose your tech stack preference before the hackathon itself - frontend/backend/fullstack. At this point you should be well versed with one of these. If you don't know the tech stack chosen, you can pick up some part of it before the hackathon. 7. Regularly track the progress of the project as it's easy to lose track. Mentors see all this and the company offers you an internship based on these parameters. 8. Some companies tend to ask extremely hard OA questions, so I’d recommend trying later questions also, and to at least have some knowledge about advanced data structures used in competitive programming. Examples would include STL for C++, collections for python and java etc. You should mainly know how to sort, how to use arrays/vectors (depending on your language), HashMaps and HashSets. 3. import { Routes, Route } from "react-router-dom";
import SignUpPage from './pages/SignUpPage'
import AdminDashboardPage from './pages/AdminDashboardPage'
import LoginPage from './pages/LoginPage'
import UploadPage from './pages/UploadPage'
import ExperienceDetailsPage from './pages/ExperienceDetailsPage'
import NavBar from "./components/NavBar";
import HomePage from "./pages/HomePage";
import MyExperiencesPage from './pages/MyExperiencesPage'
import ContactUsPage from './pages/ContactUsPage'
import AiSearchTestPage from './pages/AiSearchTestPage'

function App() {
  
  return (
    <>
      <NavBar />
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<HomePage />} />
        <Route path="/signup" element={<SignUpPage />} />
        <Route path="/admindashboard" element={<AdminDashboardPage />} />
        <Route path="/loginpage" element={<LoginPage />} />
        <Route path="/uploadpage" element={<UploadPage />} />
        <Route path="/experiencedetailspage" element={<ExperienceDetailsPage />} />
        <Route path="/myexperiencespage" element={<MyExperiencesPage />} />
        <Route path="/experience/:id" element={<ExperienceDetailsPage />} />
        <Route path="/contactuspage" element={<ContactUsPage />} />
        <Route path="/aisearchtest" element={<AiSearchTestPage />} />
      </Routes>
    </>
  );
}

export default App

import { io } from "socket.io-client";

export const createSocket = (token) => {
	return io(import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL, {
		withCredentials: true,
		auth: {
			token
		}
	});
}

import api from "./axios";

export const onApprove = (id, accessToken) => {
	return api.patch(`/api/experiences/${id}/status`, { status: 'approved'}, {
		headers: {
			Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}`
		}
	});
}

export const onReject = (id, accessToken, reason, remark) => {
	return api.patch(`/api/experiences/${id}/status`, { status: 'rejected', reason, remark }, {
		headers: {
			Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}`
		}
	});
}

// ✅ FIX: Decodes HTML entities (e.g. &lt;p&gt; → <p>) before rendering
function decodeHTMLEntities(str) {
  if (!str) return '';
  const txt = document.createElement('textarea');
  txt.innerHTML = str;
  return txt.value;
}

// ✅ FIX: Strips all HTML tags and returns plain text (safe for preview snippets)
function stripHTML(str) {
  if (!str) return '';
  const decoded = decodeHTMLEntities(str);
  const div = document.createElement('div');
  div.innerHTML = decoded;
  return div.textContent || div.innerText || '';
}

import { NavLink } from "react-router-dom";
import { useAuth } from "../context/AuthContext";
import { useState, useEffect } from "react";

export default function NavBar() {
  const { isLoggedIn, role } = useAuth();
  const [menuOpen, setMenuOpen] = useState(false);
  const [scrolled, setScrolled] = useState(false);

  const navLinks = [
    { to: "/", label: "Home", show: true },
    { to: "/admindashboard", label: "Admin Dashboard", show: role === "admin" },
    { to: "/loginpage", label: "Login", show: !isLoggedIn },
    { to: "/signup", label: "Sign Up", show: !isLoggedIn, cta: true },
    { to: "/myexperiencespage", label: "My Experiences", show: isLoggedIn && role === "student" },
    { to: "/uploadpage", label: "Upload", show: isLoggedIn, cta: true },
    { to: "/contactuspage", label: "Contact Us", show:role !== true },
  ];

  useEffect(() => {
    const onScroll = () => setScrolled(window.scrollY > 12);
    window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });
    return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
  }, []);

  const handleLinkClick = () => setMenuOpen(false);

  const visible = navLinks.filter((l) => l.show);
  const normal = visible.filter((l) => !l.cta);
  const ctas = visible.filter((l) => l.cta);

  return (
    <>
      <style>{`
        @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Syne:wght@400;600;700;800&family=Outfit:wght@300;400;500;600&display=swap');

        :root {
          --ink: #0d0d12;
          --surface: #f5f4f0;
          --accent: #e8521a;

                key={link.to}
                to={link.to}
                className="nb-mobile-cta"
                onClick={handleLinkClick}
              >
                {link.label}
              </NavLink>
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      </nav>
    </>
  );
}

    <path d={d} />
  </svg>
);

const ToolBtn = ({ onClick, active, disabled, title, children }) => (
  <button
    type="button"
    onMouseDown={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); onClick(); }}
    disabled={disabled}
    title={title}
    className={`rte-tool-btn${active ? ' rte-active' : ''}${disabled ? ' rte-disabled' : ''}`}
  >
    {children}
  </button>
);

const Divider = () => <span className="rte-divider" />;

const RichTextEditor = ({ content, onChange }) => {
  const editor = useEditor({
    extensions: [StarterKit],
    content: content || "",
    editorProps: {
      attributes: {
        class: "rte-content",
        spellcheck: "true",
      }
    },
    onUpdate: ({ editor }) => {
      onChange(editor.getHTML());
    }
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!editor) return;
    if (content !== editor.getHTML()) {
      editor.commands.setContent(content, false);
    }
  }, [content, editor]);

  if (!editor) return null;

  const charCount = editor.getText().length;
  const wordCount = editor.getText().trim() === '' ? 0 : editor.getText().trim().split(/\s+/).length;

        {/* ── BUBBLE MENU (selection toolbar) ── */}
        <BubbleMenu editor={editor} tippyOptions={{ duration: 150 }}>
          <div className="rte-bubble">
            <ToolBtn title="Bold" active={editor.isActive('bold')} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleBold().run()}>
              <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="3" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M6 4h8a4 4 0 0 1 4 4 4 4 0 0 1-4 4H6z"/><path d="M6 12h9a4 4 0 0 1 4 4 4 4 0 0 1-4 4H6z"/></svg>
            </ToolBtn>
            <ToolBtn title="Italic" active={editor.isActive('italic')} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleItalic().run()}>
              <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><line x1="19" y1="4" x2="10" y2="4"/><line x1="14" y1="20" x2="5" y2="20"/><line x1="15" y1="4" x2="9" y2="20"/></svg>
            </ToolBtn>
            <ToolBtn title="Strikethrough" active={editor.isActive('strike')} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleStrike().run()}>
              <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><line x1="5" y1="12" x2="19" y2="12"/><path d="M16 6C16 6 14.5 4 12 4s-5 1.5-5 4c0 5 9 4 9 8s-2.5 4-4 4-4-1.5-4-4"/></svg>
            </ToolBtn>
            <ToolBtn title="Code" active={editor.isActive('code')} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleCode().run()}>
              <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><polyline points="16 18 22 12 16 6"/><polyline points="8 6 2 12 8 18"/></svg>
            </ToolBtn>
            <Divider />
            <ToolBtn title="H2" active={editor.isActive('heading', { level: 2 })} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleHeading({ level: 2 }).run()}>H2</ToolBtn>
            <ToolBtn title="Quote" active={editor.isActive('blockquote')} onClick={() => editor.chain().focus().toggleBlockquote().run()}>
              <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M3 21c3 0 7-1 7-8V5c0-1.25-.756-2.017-2-2H4c-1.25 0-2 .75-2 1.972V11c0 1.25.75 2 2 2 1 0 1 0 1 1v1c0 1-1 2-2 2s-1 .008-1 1.031V20c0 1 0 1 1 1z"/><path d="M15 21c3 0 7-1 7-8V5c0-1.25-.757-2.017-2-2h-4c-1.25 0-2 .75-2 1.972V11c0 1.25.75 2 2 2h.75c0 2.25.25 4-2.75 4v3c0 1 0 1 1 1z"/></svg>
            </ToolBtn>
          </div>
        </BubbleMenu>

        {/* ── EDITOR ── */}
        <EditorContent editor={editor} />

        {/* ── FOOTER ── */}
        <div className="rte-footer">
          <span className="rte-count"><span>{wordCount}</span> words</span>
          <span className="rte-count"><span>{charCount}</span> chars</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
};

export default RichTextEditor;

FILE: client\src\context\AuthContext.jsx
============================================================
import { createContext, useState, useContext } from "react";
import { useEffect } from "react";
import { jwtDecode } from "jwt-decode";
import api from "../api/axios";

const AuthContext = createContext();

export const AuthProvider = ({ children }) => {
	const [accessToken, setAccessToken] = useState(null);
	const [isLoggedIn, setIsLoggedIn] = useState(false);
	const [role, setRole] = useState(null);
	const refreshAccessToken = async() => {
		try {
			const response = await api.post(
				'/api/auth/refresh',
				{},
				{withCredentials:true}
			);
			setAccessToken(response.data.accessToken);
			const decoded = jwtDecode(response.data.accessToken);
			setRole(decoded.role);
			setIsLoggedIn(true);
		} catch (err){
			setAccessToken(null);
			setIsLoggedIn(false);
		}
	};
	const value = {
		isLoggedIn,
		setIsLoggedIn,
		accessToken,
		setAccessToken,
		role,
		setRole,
		refreshAccessToken
	};

	useEffect(() => {
		const callRefreshAccessToken = async () => {
			await refreshAccessToken();
		};
		callRefreshAccessToken();

	}, []);
	return <AuthContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>
};

export const useAuth = () => useContext(AuthContext);

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { searchExperiences } from '../api/aiApi';

export default function AiSearchTestPage() {
	const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
	const [results, setResults] = useState([]);
	const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
	const [error, setError] = useState('');

	const handleSearch = async (e) => {
		e.preventDefault();
		if (!query.trim()) return;

		setLoading(true);
		setError('');
		setResults([]);

		try {
			const res = await searchExperiences(query.trim(), 5);
			setResults(res.data.data);
		} catch {
			setError('Something went wrong while searching. Please try again.');
		} finally {
			setLoading(false);
		}
	};

	return (
		<div className="max-w-2xl mx-auto p-6">
			<h1 className="text-2xl font-semibold mb-4">AI Semantic Search (Test)</h1>

			<form onSubmit={handleSearch} className="flex gap-2 mb-6">
				<input
					type="text"
					value={query}
					onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
					placeholder="e.g. Redis and system design questions"
					className="flex-1 border rounded px-3 py-2"
				/>
				<button
					type="submit"
					disabled={loading}
					className="bg-black text-white px-4 py-2 rounded disabled:opacity-50"
				>
					{loading ? 'Searching...' : 'Search'}
				</button>
			</form>

			{error && <p className="text-red-600 mb-4">{error}</p>}

			<div className="space-y-4">
				{results.map((r) => (
					<div key={r.id} className="border rounded p-4">
						<div className="flex justify-between items-center mb-1">
							<span className="font-medium">{r.companyName} — {r.batch}</span>
							<span className="text-sm text-gray-500">score: {r.score.toFixed(3)}</span>
						</div>
						<p className="text-sm text-gray-700">{r.preview}</p>
					</div>
				))}
			</div>

			{!loading && results.length === 0 && !error && (
				<p className="text-gray-500">No results yet — try a search above.</p>
			)}
		</div>
	);
}

                    </svg>
                  </span>
                  {error}
                </div>
              )}

              {/* Submit */}
              <button className="cu-submit" type="submit" disabled={loading || !isValid}>

                  <><div className="cu-spinner" /> Sending…</>

import React, { useEffect, useState, useRef } from 'react';
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext';
import { useParams, useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';
import { onApprove, onReject } from '../api/experienceApi';
import api from '../api/axios';
import { createSocket } from "../socket";
import { formatDistanceToNow } from 'date-fns';

const rejectionReasons = ['SPA', 'DUPLICATE', 'INCOMPLETE DETAILS', 'OTHER'];

const statusConfig = {
  approved: { label: 'Approved', dot: '#1a7a4a', bg: 'rgba(26,122,74,0.10)', color: '#1a7a4a', border: 'rgba(26,122,74,0.2)' },
  pending:  { label: 'Pending',  dot: '#b45309', bg: 'rgba(247,201,72,0.15)', color: '#92660a', border: 'rgba(247,201,72,0.35)' },
  rejected: { label: 'Rejected', dot: '#c0392b', bg: 'rgba(192,57,43,0.09)', color: '#c0392b', border: 'rgba(192,57,43,0.2)' },
};

// ✅ FIX: Decodes HTML entities (e.g. &lt;p&gt; → <p>) before injecting as HTML
function decodeHTMLEntities(str) {
  if (!str) return '';
  const txt = document.createElement('textarea');
  txt.innerHTML = str;
  return txt.value;
}

export default function ExperienceDetailsPage() {
  const { id } = useParams();
  const { accessToken, role } = useAuth();
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const messagesEndRef = useRef(null);

  const [experience, setExperience] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState('');
  const [rejecting, setRejecting] = useState(false);
  const [reason, setReason] = useState('');
  const [remark, setRemark] = useState('');
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const [approving, setApproving] = useState(false);
  const [messages, setMessages] = useState([]);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');
  const [socket, setSocket] = useState(null);
  const [actionError, setActionError] = useState('');
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => { const t = setTimeout(() => setVisible(true), 80); return () => clearTimeout(t); }, []);

  // Fetch experience
  useEffect(() => {
    const getExperience = async () => {
      try {
        const headers = accessToken ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } : {};
        const res = await api.get(`/api/experiences/${id}`, { headers });
        setExperience(res.data.experience);
      } catch (err) {
        if (err.response?.status === 403) setError("You are not allowed to view this experience.");
        else if (err.response?.status === 404) setError("Experience not found.");
        else setError("Something went wrong!");
      } finally {
        setLoading(false);
      }
    };
    getExperience();
  }, [id, accessToken]);

  // Fetch messages
  useEffect(() => {
    const fetchMessages = async () => {
      try {
        const res = await api.get(`/api/messages/${id}`);
        setMessages(res.data.data);
      } catch {}
    };
    fetchMessages();
  }, [id]);

  // Socket setup
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!accessToken) return;
    const newSocket = createSocket(accessToken);
    setSocket(newSocket);
    return () => newSocket.disconnect();
  }, [accessToken]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!socket) return;
    socket.on('connect', () => socket.emit('joinRoom', id));
    socket.on('connect_error', () => {});
    return () => { socket.off('connect'); socket.off('connect_error'); };
  }, [id, socket]);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!socket) return;
    const handler = (data) => setMessages(prev => [data, ...prev]);
    socket.on('receiveMessage', handler);
    return () => socket.off('receiveMessage', handler);
  }, [socket]);

  const handleApprove = async () => {
    setApproving(true);
    setActionError('');
    try {
      await onApprove(id, accessToken);
      setExperience(prev => ({ ...prev, status: 'approved', remark: null, reason: null }));
      navigate('/admindashboard');
    } catch { setActionError('Failed to approve. Please try again.'); }
    finally { setApproving(false); }
  };

  const handleReject = async () => {
    if (!reason) { setActionError('Please select a rejection reason.'); return; }
    setSubmitting(true);
    setActionError('');
    try {
      await onReject(id, accessToken, reason, remark);
      setExperience(prev => ({ ...prev, status: 'rejected', reason, remark }));
      navigate('/admindashboard');
    } catch { setActionError('Failed to reject. Please try again.'); }
    finally { setSubmitting(false); }
  };

  const sendMessage = () => {
    if (!message.trim() || !socket) return;
    socket.emit('sendMessage', { experienceId: id, text: message });
    setMessage('');
  };

  const handleKeyDown = (e) => {

                  <path d="M21 15a2 2 0 01-2 2H7l-4 4V5a2 2 0 012-2h14a2 2 0 012 2z"/>
                </svg>
                Discussion
                <span className="edp-msg-count">{messages.length}</span>
              </span>
            </div>

            {messages.length === 0 ? (
              <div className="edp-empty-msgs">
                <div className="edp-empty-msgs-icon">💬</div>
                <p>No comments yet — be the first to ask!</p>
              </div>
            ) : (
              <div className="edp-messages">
                {[...messages].reverse().map((msg, i) => {
                  const name = msg.userId?.name || 'Anonymous';
                  const initial = name.charAt(0).toUpperCase();
                  return (
                    <div key={i} className="edp-msg">
                      <div className="edp-msg-avatar">{initial}</div>
                      <div className="edp-msg-bubble">
                        <div className="edp-msg-top">
                          <span className="edp-msg-name">{name}</span>
                          <span className="edp-msg-time">
                            {formatDistanceToNow(new Date(msg.createdAt), { addSuffix: true })}
                          </span>
                        </div>
                        <p className="edp-msg-text">{msg.text}</p>
                      </div>
                    </div>
                  );
                })}
                <div ref={messagesEndRef} />
              </div>
            )}

            <div className="edp-input-row">
              <textarea
                className="edp-chat-input"
                placeholder="Write a comment or ask a question…"
                value={message}
                onChange={(e) => setMessage(e.target.value)}
                onKeyDown={handleKeyDown}
                rows={1}
              />
              <button
                className="edp-send-btn"
                onClick={sendMessage}
                disabled={!message.trim() || !socket}
                title="Send (Enter)"
              >
                <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round">
                  <line x1="22" y1="2" x2="11" y2="13"/><polygon points="22 2 15 22 11 13 2 9 22 2"/>
                </svg>
              </button>
            </div>
          </div>

        </div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

import ExperienceCard from "../components/ExperienceCard";

// Animated counter hook
function useCountUp(target, duration = 1200) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!target) return;
    let start = 0;
    const step = target / (duration / 16);
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      start += step;
      if (start >= target) { setCount(target); clearInterval(timer); }
      else setCount(Math.floor(start));
    }, 16);
    return () => clearInterval(timer);
  }, [target, duration]);
  return count;
}

// Strip HTML tags for searching inside content
function stripHTML(str) {
  if (!str) return '';
  const div = document.createElement('div');
  div.innerHTML = str;
  return div.textContent || div.innerText || '';
}

// Skeleton card component
function SkeletonCard() {
  return (
    <div className="exp-skeleton">
      <div className="skel-img" />
      <div className="skel-body">
        <div className="skel-line w-60" />
        <div className="skel-line w-40" />
        <div className="skel-line w-full" />
        <div className="skel-line w-80" />
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

                      </svg>
                    ) : (
                      <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round">
                        <path d="M1 12s4-8 11-8 11 8 11 8-4 8-11 8-11-8-11-8z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/>
                      </svg>
                    )}
                  </button>
                </div>
              </div>

              {/* Error */}
              {error && (
                <div className="lp-error">
                  <svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round">

              )}

                </svg>
                Share New Experience
              </Link>
            </div>
          </div>

                  <div className="mep-stat-label">Approved</div>
                </div>
                <div className="mep-stat">
                  <div className="mep-stat-num" style={{ color: 'var(--accent)' }}>{pending}</div>
                  <div className="mep-stat-label">Pending</div>
                </div>
                <div className="mep-stat">
                  <div className="mep-stat-num" style={{ color: '#c0392b' }}>{rejected}</div>
                  <div className="mep-stat-label">Rejected</div>
                </div>
              </div>
            </div>
          )}

          {/* ── CONTENT ── */}
          <div className={`mep-body${visible ? ' visible' : ''}`}>
            {userExps.length === 0 ? (
              <div className="mep-empty">
                <div className="mep-empty-icon">📝</div>
                <h3>No experiences yet</h3>
                <p>You haven't shared any placement experiences. Be the first to help your juniors!</p>
                <Link to="/uploadpage" className="mep-empty-cta">
                  <svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round">
                    <line x1="22" y1="2" x2="11" y2="13"/><polygon points="22 2 15 22 11 13 2 9 22 2"/>
                  </svg>
                  Share Your First Experience
                </Link>
              </div>
            ) : (
              <>
                <div className="mep-section-header">
                  <h2 className="mep-section-title">Your Submissions</h2>
                  <span className="mep-count"><strong>{userExps.length}</strong> total · <strong style={{ color: 'var(--accent)' }}>{pending}</strong> pending review</span>
                </div>
                <div className="mep-grid">
                  {userExps.map((exp, i) => (
                    <div
                      key={exp._id || exp.id}
                      className="mep-card-wrap"
                      style={{ animationDelay: `${Math.min(i * 55, 380)}ms` }}
                    >
                      <ExperienceCard {...exp} showAdminActions={false} />
                    </div>
                  ))}
                </div>
              </>
            )}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

import React, { useEffect, useState } from 'react'
import { useNavigate, Link } from 'react-router-dom'
import api from '../api/axios';

const STEPS = { EMAIL: 0, OTP: 1, PASSWORD: 2 };

function StepIndicator({ current }) {
  const steps = ['Email', 'Verify', 'Password'];
  return (
    <div className="su-steps">
      {steps.map((label, i) => (
        <React.Fragment key={i}>
          <div className={`su-step${i < current ? ' done' : i === current ? ' active' : ''}`}>
            <div className="su-step-circle">
              {i < current ? (
                <svg width="12" height="12" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="3" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><polyline points="20 6 9 17 4 12"/></svg>
              ) : (
                <span>{i + 1}</span>
              )}
            </div>
            <span className="su-step-label">{label}</span>
          </div>
          {i < steps.length - 1 && <div className={`su-step-line${i < current ? ' done' : ''}`} />}
        </React.Fragment>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

export default function SignUpPage() {
  const [step, setStep] = useState(STEPS.EMAIL);
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
  const [otp, setOtp] = useState('');
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('');
  const [confirmPassword, setConfirmPassword] = useState('');
  const [showPassword, setShowPassword] = useState(false);
  const [showConfirm, setShowConfirm] = useState(false);
  const [passwordMatch, setPasswordMatch] = useState('');
  const [error, setError] = useState('');
  const [success, setSuccess] = useState(false);
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  const [sendingOtp, setSendingOtp] = useState(false);
  const [verifyingOtp, setVerifyingOtp] = useState(false);
  const [creatingAccount, setCreatingAccount] = useState(false);

  const navigate = useNavigate();

  useEffect(() => { const t = setTimeout(() => setVisible(true), 60); return () => clearTimeout(t); }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!confirmPassword || !password || password === confirmPassword) setPasswordMatch('');
    else setPasswordMatch('Passwords do not match.');
  }, [password, confirmPassword]);

  // Reset OTP step if email changes
  useEffect(() => {
    if (step > STEPS.EMAIL) { setStep(STEPS.EMAIL); setOtp(''); }
  }, [email]);

  const sendOtp = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    setError('');
    setSendingOtp(true);
    try {
      await api.post('/api/auth/send-otp', { email });
      setStep(STEPS.OTP);
    } catch {
      setError('Failed to send OTP. Please check your email and try again.');
    } finally {
      setSendingOtp(false);
    }
  };

  const verifyOtp = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    setError('');
    setVerifyingOtp(true);
    try {
      await api.post('/api/auth/verify-otp', { email, otp });
      setStep(STEPS.PASSWORD);
    } catch {
      setError('Invalid OTP. Please check and try again.');
    } finally {
      setVerifyingOtp(false);
    }
  };

  const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (passwordMatch) return;
    setError('');
    setCreatingAccount(true);
    try {
      await api.post('/api/auth/set-password', { email, password });
      setSuccess(true);
      setTimeout(() => navigate('/loginpage'), 1800);
    } catch {
      setError('Failed to create account. Please try again.');
    } finally {
      setCreatingAccount(false);
    }
  };

  const stepTitles = ['Create your account', 'Verify your email', 'Set your password'];
  const stepSubs = [
    'Enter your college email to get started.',
    `We sent a 6-digit code to ${email}`,
    'Choose a strong password to secure your account.',
  ];

        .su-left {

        <div className="su-left">
          <div className="su-left-bg" /><div className="su-left-noise" /><div className="su-orb" />
          <div className="su-left-top">
            <Link to="/" className="su-left-logo">
              <div className="su-logo-mark">IV</div>
              <span className="su-logo-text">Inter<span>VJTI</span></span>
            </Link>
          </div>
          <div className="su-left-bottom">
            <p className="su-left-quote">Join the<br /><em>community</em><br />of achievers.</p>
            <p className="su-left-sub">Share your placement journey and help future VJTIans navigate theirs.</p>
            <div className="su-perks">
              {['Access all student experiences', 'Share your own interview story', 'Ask questions in real-time discussion', 'Help your juniors succeed'].map(p => (
                <div key={p} className="su-perk">
                  <div className="su-perk-check">
                    <svg width="10" height="10" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="3" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><polyline points="20 6 9 17 4 12"/></svg>
                  </div>
                  {p}
                </div>
              ))}
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>

        {/* ── RIGHT PANEL ── */}
        <div className={`su-right${visible ? ' visible' : ''}`}>
          <div className="su-card">

            {/* Mobile logo */}
            <Link to="/" className="su-mobile-logo">
              <div className="su-mobile-logo-mark">IV</div>
              <span className="su-mobile-logo-text">Inter<span>VJTI</span></span>
            </Link>

            <StepIndicator current={step} />

            <div className="su-header">
              <div className="su-eyebrow"><span className="su-eyebrow-line" />Step {step + 1} of 3</div>
              <h1 className="su-title">{stepTitles[step]}</h1>
              <p className="su-subtitle">{step === 1 ? <><strong>{email}</strong> — check your inbox.</> : stepSubs[step]}</p>
            </div>

            <form className="su-form" onSubmit={(e) => e.preventDefault()}>

              {/* ── STEP 0: EMAIL ── */}
              {step === STEPS.EMAIL && (
                <>
                  <div className="su-field">
                    <label className="su-label">College Email</label>
                    <div className="su-input-wrap">
                      <span className="su-input-icon">
                        <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M4 4h16c1.1 0 2 .9 2 2v12c0 1.1-.9 2-2 2H4c-1.1 0-2-.9-2-2V6c0-1.1.9-2 2-2z"/><polyline points="22,6 12,13 2,6"/></svg>
                      </span>
                      <input className="su-input" type="email" placeholder="you@vjti.ac.in" value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} autoFocus required disabled={success} />
                    </div>
                  </div>
                  {error && <div className="su-feedback error"><span className="su-feedback-icon"><svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><line x1="12" y1="8" x2="12" y2="12"/><line x1="12" y1="16" x2="12.01" y2="16"/></svg></span>{error}</div>}
                  <button className="su-submit" onClick={sendOtp} disabled={sendingOtp || !email || success}>
                    {sendingOtp ? <><div className="su-spinner" />Sending OTP…</> : <>Send OTP <svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><line x1="22" y1="2" x2="11" y2="13"/><polygon points="22 2 15 22 11 13 2 9 22 2"/></svg></>}
                  </button>
                  <p className="su-footer-link">Already have an account? <Link to="/loginpage">Log in</Link></p>
                </>
              )}

              {/* ── STEP 1: OTP ── */}
              {step === STEPS.OTP && (
                <>
                  <div className="su-field">
                    <label className="su-label">6-Digit Code</label>
                    <input className="su-otp-input" type="text" inputMode="numeric" maxLength={6} placeholder="••••••" value={otp} onChange={(e) => setOtp(e.target.value.replace(/\D/g, ''))} autoFocus required disabled={success} />
                  </div>
                  {error && <div className="su-feedback error"><span className="su-feedback-icon"><svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><line x1="12" y1="8" x2="12" y2="12"/><line x1="12" y1="16" x2="12.01" y2="16"/></svg></span>{error}</div>}
                  <button className="su-submit" onClick={verifyOtp} disabled={!otp || otp.length < 6 || verifyingOtp || success}>
                    {verifyingOtp ? <><div className="su-spinner" />Verifying…</> : <>Verify Code <svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><polyline points="20 6 9 17 4 12"/></svg></>}
                  </button>
                  <p className="su-resend">Didn't get it? <button onClick={sendOtp} disabled={sendingOtp}>{sendingOtp ? 'Resending…' : 'Resend OTP'}</button></p>
                  <p className="su-footer-link"><button style={{ background:'none', border:'none', color:'var(--muted)', fontSize:12, cursor:'pointer', fontFamily:"var(--font-body)" }} onClick={() => { setStep(STEPS.EMAIL); setError(''); setOtp(''); }}>← Change email</button></p>
                </>
              )}

              {/* ── STEP 2: PASSWORD ── */}
              {step === STEPS.PASSWORD && (
                <>
                  <div className="su-field">
                    <label className="su-label">Password</label>
                    <div className="su-input-wrap">
                      <span className="su-input-icon"><svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><rect x="3" y="11" width="18" height="11" rx="2"/><path d="M7 11V7a5 5 0 0 1 10 0v4"/></svg></span>
                      <input className="su-input" type={showPassword ? 'text' : 'password'} placeholder="Min. 8 characters" value={password} onChange={(e) => setPassword(e.target.value)} autoFocus required disabled={success} style={{ paddingRight: 40 }} />
                      <button type="button" className="su-pw-toggle" onClick={() => setShowPassword(p => !p)} tabIndex={-1}>
                        {showPassword
                          ? <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M17.94 17.94A10.07 10.07 0 0 1 12 20c-7 0-11-8-11-8a18.45 18.45 0 0 1 5.06-5.94"/><path d="M9.9 4.24A9.12 9.12 0 0 1 12 4c7 0 11 8 11 8a18.5 18.5 0 0 1-2.16 3.19"/><line x1="1" y1="1" x2="23" y2="23"/></svg>
                          : <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M1 12s4-8 11-8 11 8 11 8-4 8-11 8-11-8-11-8z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/></svg>
                        }
                      </button>
                    </div>
                    {/* Strength bars */}
                    {password && (
                      <div className="su-pw-strength">
                        {[1,2,3,4].map(n => {
                          const str = Math.min(4, [/.{8,}/, /[A-Z]/, /[0-9]/, /[^A-Za-z0-9]/].filter(r => r.test(password)).length);
                          const colors = ['#c0392b','#e8521a','#f7c948','#1a7a4a'];
                          return <div key={n} className="su-pw-bar" style={{ background: n <= str ? colors[str-1] : undefined }} />;
                        })}
                      </div>
                    )}
                  </div>

                  <div className="su-field">
                    <label className="su-label">Confirm Password</label>
                    <div className="su-input-wrap">
                      <span className="su-input-icon"><svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><rect x="3" y="11" width="18" height="11" rx="2"/><path d="M7 11V7a5 5 0 0 1 10 0v4"/></svg></span>
                      <input className="su-input" type={showConfirm ? 'text' : 'password'} placeholder="Re-enter password" value={confirmPassword} onChange={(e) => setConfirmPassword(e.target.value)} required disabled={success} style={{ paddingRight: 40 }} />
                      <button type="button" className="su-pw-toggle" onClick={() => setShowConfirm(p => !p)} tabIndex={-1}>
                        {showConfirm
                          ? <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M17.94 17.94A10.07 10.07 0 0 1 12 20c-7 0-11-8-11-8a18.45 18.45 0 0 1 5.06-5.94"/><path d="M9.9 4.24A9.12 9.12 0 0 1 12 4c7 0 11 8 11 8a18.5 18.5 0 0 1-2.16 3.19"/><line x1="1" y1="1" x2="23" y2="23"/></svg>
                          : <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M1 12s4-8 11-8 11 8 11 8-4 8-11 8-11-8-11-8z"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="3"/></svg>
                        }
                      </button>
                    </div>
                    {passwordMatch && (
                      <p className="su-pw-err">
                        <svg width="12" height="12" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><line x1="12" y1="8" x2="12" y2="12"/><line x1="12" y1="16" x2="12.01" y2="16"/></svg>
                        {passwordMatch}
                      </p>
                    )}
                  </div>

                  {error && <div className="su-feedback error"><span className="su-feedback-icon"><svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="10"/><line x1="12" y1="8" x2="12" y2="12"/><line x1="12" y1="16" x2="12.01" y2="16"/></svg></span>{error}</div>}

                  {success && (
                    <div className="su-feedback success">
                      <span className="su-feedback-icon"><svg width="13" height="13" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><polyline points="20 6 9 17 4 12"/></svg></span>
                      Account created! Redirecting to login…
                    </div>
                  )}

                  <button className="su-submit" onClick={handleSubmit} disabled={creatingAccount || !!passwordMatch || !password || !confirmPassword || success}>
                    {creatingAccount ? <><div className="su-spinner" />Creating account…</> : <>Create Account <svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2.5" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><line x1="5" y1="12" x2="19" y2="12"/><polyline points="12 5 19 12 12 19"/></svg></>}
                  </button>
                  <p className="su-footer-link">Already have an account? <Link to="/loginpage">Log in</Link></p>
                </>
              )}

            </form>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

import { useState, useEffect } from "react"
import RichTextEditor from "../components/RichTextEditor";
import { useAuth } from '../context/AuthContext';
import api from "../api/axios";

const MIN_CHARS = 50;

export default function UploadPage() {
  const { accessToken } = useAuth();

  const [studentName, setStudentName] = useState('');
  const [companyName, setCompanyName] = useState('');
  const [batch, setBatch] = useState('');
  const [content, setContent] = useState('');
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
  const [message, setMessage] = useState('');
  const [error, setError] = useState('');
  const [visible, setVisible] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => { const t = setTimeout(() => setVisible(true), 60); return () => clearTimeout(t); }, []);

  const charCount = content.replace(/<[^>]*>/g, '').length;
  const progress = Math.min(100, Math.round((charCount / MIN_CHARS) * 100));
  const isContentValid = charCount >= MIN_CHARS;

  const handleSubmit = async (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    setMessage(''); setError('');
    if (!isContentValid) { setError(`Please write at least ${MIN_CHARS} characters in your experience.`); return; }
    setLoading(true);
    try {
      const headers = accessToken ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${accessToken}` } : {};
      await api.post('/api/experiences', { studentName, companyName, batch, content }, { headers });
      setMessage("Experience submitted for approval! We'll review it shortly.");
      setStudentName(''); setCompanyName(''); setBatch(''); setContent('');
    } catch {
      setError("Failed to upload your experience. Please try again.");
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }

    { label: 'Your Name', value: studentName, set: setStudentName, placeholder: 'e.g. Rahul Sharma', icon: <svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" strokeWidth="2" strokeLinecap="round" strokeLinejoin="round"><path d="M20 21v-2a4 4 0 00-4-4H8a4 4 0 00-4 4v2"/><circle cx="12" cy="7" r="4"/></svg> },

  ];

    <>
